title: soc: espressif: add LLVM and LLD build support
labels: area: Build System;area: Documentation;area: Toolchains;area: native port;platform: ESP32;area: Kconfig;area: LED;area: Linker Scripts;Stale;manifest;manifest-hal_espressif;DNM (manifest);area: Boards/SoCs;platform: Realtek
body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **BLOCKED BY**: This PR is blocked by the corresponding HAL support changes in the `hal_espressif` repository: [hal_espressif PR](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/hal_espressif/pull/567).
> The build requires those HAL changes to be merged or present in the module tree to compile successfully under LLVM/Clang.

### Description
This PR enables compiling and linking all Espressif SoC targets (`esp32`, `esp32c2`, `esp32c3`, `esp32c5`, `esp32c6`, `esp32h2`, `esp32s2`, `esp32s3`) out-of-the-box using the LLVM/Clang compiler and the LLD linker.

Each change addresses strict constraints enforced by the LLD linker or LLVM integrated assembler compared to the GNU toolchain:

1. **`_instruction_reserved_end` mapping**:
   - *Problem*: GNU-ld allows creating an empty dummy `.flash_rodata_dummy (NOLOAD)` section and advancing the Location Counter (`. += ALIGN(...)`) inside it to map the DROM correctly. LLD entirely discards empty `NOLOAD` sections, breaking the memory layout.
   - *Fix*: Removed `.flash_rodata_dummy` and instead directly mapped the start of the `.flash.rodata` section to `_instruction_reserved_end` (`.flash.rodata _instruction_reserved_end : ALIGN(0x10)`).

2. **`LONG(0)` extraction (`.flash.rodata_pad`)**:
   - *Problem*: GNU-ld handles `LONG(0)` alignment padding inside `NOLOAD` or `.dram0.dummy` sections without side effects. LLD strictly interprets `LONG()` directives as allocated data, erroneously creating a Write-Allocate (WA) segment. `esptool` chokes on WA segments during `.bin` image generation.
   - *Fix*: Extracted the `LONG(0)` padding into a new, dedicated `.flash.rodata_pad` section in all `default.ld`, `default_appcpu.ld`, and `mcuboot.ld` scripts.

3. **`SECTION_DATA_PROLOGUE` redefinition**:
   - *Problem*: Espressif linker scripts use the `ALIGN_WITH_INPUT` keyword for output section alignments. LLD does not support `ALIGN_WITH_INPUT`.
   - *Fix*: Redefined `SECTION_DATA_PROLOGUE` under `#ifdef __LLD_LINKER_CMD__` to simply enforce `align` instead of using the GNU-ld specific keyword.

4. **Exception Vector Absolute Offsets (`vectors.S` & linker scripts)**:
   - *Problem*: LLD processes section grouping and alignments differently, causing exception vector routines to misalign.
   - *Fix*: Added explicit absolute offsets (`. = _init_start + 0x180; KEEP(...)`) for all interrupt vectors (`WindowVectors`, `Level2InterruptVector`, etc.) inside the linker scripts when compiled with LLD. Also fixed assembler syntax in `vectors.S` to conform to Clang's stricter parser.

5. **`MAX(., ORIGIN + SIZEOF)` in `.dram0.dummy` & `.rtc.dummy`**:
   - *Problem*: GNU-ld allows advancing the Location Counter relative to its current position even in `NOLOAD` sections. LLD requires a stricter bounds definition for these placeholder regions.
   - *Fix*: Replaced `. = ORIGIN(...) + ...` with `MAX(., ORIGIN(...) + ...)` to prevent negative pointer evaluation under LLD's multi-pass evaluation.

6. **Compiler-RT Library Mapping**:
   - *Problem*: `libclang_rt.builtins.a`, `libatomic.a`, and `atomic_stubs` were not explicitly mapped.
   - *Fix*: Added these libraries to the `.literal` and `.text` rules to ensure LLVM compiler intrinsics are correctly mapped to IROM/DROM.

7. **`.dbg_thread_info` alignment**:
   - *Problem*: Debugging thread info sections were being placed without strict boundaries.
   - *Fix*: Moved `.dbg_thread_info` into its own `ALIGN(4)` group linked to `RAMABLE_REGION` to satisfy LLD's RAM alignment requirements.

8. **Orphan Sections Error**:
   - *Problem*: When `CONFIG_LINKER_ORPHAN_SECTION_ERROR=y` is active, LLD emits errors for unhandled symbol table sections.
   - *Fix*: Explicitly mapped `.symtab`, `.strtab`, and `.shstrtab` via `SECTION_PROLOGUE` if LLD is used.

### Test Matrix & Verification
- **Platforms tested**: All ESP32-* targets
- **Toolchains**:
  - Zephyr SDK Clang / LLD (`zephyr/llvm`)
  - Host Clang/LLD versions 19 through 22 (`host/llvm`)

body:
net: route: fix ethernet route packet ll addr mismatch

    Ethernet route packet from another iface cannot have
    original iface link layer address.
    Because it has different subnet.

 net: shell: add iptables shell cmd

    Add iptables shell cmd to add and del iptable rules.
    Iptable rules are used to allow specific packets to
    be forwarded through interfaces and subnets.

    Example usage:
    net iptable add -i 1 -o 2 -s 192.168.2.2 -S 255.255.255.0
    -d 192.168.1.1 -D 255.255.255.0 -p 1 -P 1 -t 60 -T 300
    net iptable del 0

 net: add NAT for ipv4 packets

    Add ipv4 NAT (Network Address Translation) to allow packets to
    hop between interfaces.
    Add iptable rules to filter packets that can be forwarded.

    There are mainly 3 parts. Iptable, connection track and NAT.
    1. Iptable rules can be added. And packets from original interface
       that match these rules, will generate a new connection track.
    2. The connection track will record the tuples of both directions.
       And it will age out after inactive for some time.
    3. When packet matches a connection track, NAT will update the packet
       header to let it route in the other interface.
       Will do SNAT (Src NAT) for packets from input interface and forward
       it to output interface.
       Will do DNAT (Dst NAT) for packets from output interface and forward
       it to input interface.

title: drivers: audio: add native_sim DMIC driver
labels: area: Devicetree;area: Tests;area: native port;area: Devicetree Binding;area: Audio;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
The native_sim DMIC driver in drivers/audio/dmic_native_sim.c is a host-file-backed implementation of the Zephyr DMIC API for the native simulator. Instead of sampling real hardware, it reads PCM data from a file, feeds it into fixed-size capture blocks, and exposes those blocks through the normal configure, trigger, and read callbacks. That makes it useful for testing DMIC clients on native_sim without needing a real microphone or board-specific audio input.

Its core design is straightforward. Configuration validates channel layout, sample width, slab/block sizing, and the input path. A worker thread performs paced reads so block delivery roughly follows the configured PCM rate rather than dumping the file as fast as possible. Captured blocks are queued in a message queue for the application to read, and session IDs are used to invalidate in-flight work when pause, stop, reset, or reconfigure happens.

A few behavioral details define how it feels to use:

- Missing input files are treated as silence rather than a hard configuration failure. The lower-level open helper in drivers/audio/dmic_native_sim_bottom.c still emits a warning, but the main driver then provides zero-filled blocks.
- The driver supports command-line override of the configured file path, so tests can swap sources without rebuilding.
- Pause and release operate at block granularity, which keeps the implementation simple and deterministic for tests.
- Reset closes the file, flushes queued blocks, clears stream state, and returns the driver to its initialized state.

The related Kconfig in drivers/audio/Kconfig.dmic_native_sim exposes the main knobs: default input file path, receive queue depth, and worker thread priority. In practice, the driver is best thought of as a simulation backend for audio test coverage rather than a fidelity-focused microphone model. It is intentionally simple, deterministic, and integrated into the normal DMIC control flow, which is exactly what native_sim usually needs.

title: drivers: i2s: add native_sim file backend
labels: area: Samples;area: Devicetree;area: Tests;area: native port;area: I2S;area: Devicetree Binding;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
Add a native_sim file-backed I2S controller for RX, TX, and loopback tests.

The native_sim I2S driver in i2s_native_sim.c is a file-backed I2S controller for the native simulator. It lets Zephyr exercise RX, TX, and bidirectional loopback flows without real I2S hardware by mapping streams onto host files: RX consumes PCM data from a host file, TX writes PCM data to a host file, and loopback can feed transmitted blocks back into the receive path. The driver exposes the standard Zephyr I2S API, including configure, read, write, and trigger handling, so it behaves like a normal I2S device from the application side.

Internally, it keeps separate RX and TX stream state, each with its own queue, active block tracking, error state, pacing deadline, and file descriptor. A worker thread drives the backend and uses configured sample rate and frame layout to pace traffic so native_sim delivery roughly matches the intended stream timing instead of running flat out. RX can fall back to zero-filled data when the configured host input file is missing, while TX writes queued blocks through host-libc file I/O. The driver also supports command-line overrides for RX and TX file paths, which makes it practical for tests and local experiments without rebuilding.

Configuration lives in Kconfig.native_sim. That Kconfig enables the backend, allows separate RX and TX support, and exposes the default host file paths, queue depth, and worker priority.

title: soc: rp2350: Support basic AMP with Snippets
labels: area: Build System;area: Samples;area: IPC;area: Devicetree;area: Tests;area: Clock Control;area: Devicetree Binding;area: PM CPU ops;platform: Raspberry Pi Pico;area: mbox;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
Continuation of #93379. Creating a new PR because cherry-picked commits needed to be squashed with some changes. Thanks to @dsseng for the support!

Add support to launch the 2nd core (CPU1) of the rp2350 from the main core (CPU0) for the Cortex-M33 CPUs using the new `rp2xxx-cpu1` and `rp2xxx-cpu1-xip` snippets (naming suggestions appreciated). The `rp2xxx-cpu1[-xip]` snippets are modeled after the [`nordic-flpr`](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/snippets/nordic/nordic-flpr/README.html#).

Add support to launch the 2nd core (CPU1) of the rp2350 from the main core (CPU0) for the Cortex-M33 CPUs.

Add the rpi_pico2/rp2350a/m33/cpu1 board target that is has 256kB SRAM, gpio controller, and uart1 by default. CPU0 is responsible for launching CPU1 in a soc late init hook. When CPU0's board dts has `&cpu1`'s node with an `enable-method = "raspberrypi,pico-pcbs";` and a `cpu_enable` node with a matching compatible.

The `raspberrypi,pico-pcbs` node provides `source-memory` and `execution-memory` properties to the CPU0 board target.  

If CPU0's board dts has both `source-memory` and `execution-memory` properties in `cpu1-launcher`, CPU0 will copy CPU1's image from `source-memory` into `execution-memory` and assumes that CPU1's CONFIG_XIP=n (the default). If only `execution-memory` is present, it is assumed that CPU1's CONFIG_XIP=y. This is modeled after a combination of the [Analog Devices max78002evkit](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/adi/max78002evkit/doc/index.html) and Nordic's [vpr launcher driver](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/drivers/misc/nordic_vpr_launcher/nordic_vpr_launcher.c).

**Note:** Running both CPU0 and CPU1 XIP is much slower than running CPU1 from SRAM because of XIP cache contention between the 2 cores. However, it may be necessary if CPU1's image does not fit in SRAM.

Although CPU1 is a board variant, this PR does not yet support using it as an independent target like the `cpuflpr`. This would require some custom sysbuild.cmake magic as seen [here](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/soc/nordic/sysbuild.cmake).

---

Open Questions:
- Is it ok to have a board variant that can't be built on its own yet and leave that to some future work?
- Right now, we would have to make a `rpi_pico2/rp2350a/m33/cpu1/mcuboot` target to support the mcuboot board target. This is the same for other boards that has a different flash size/partition layout. This looks like we will have to have a partitioning scheme similar to [how espressif does it](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/dts/vendor/espressif).  Is that required for this PR to be merged?
- The [board porting guide recommendations](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/hardware/porting/board_porting.html#general-recommendations) says that a board should have a `zephyr,console` chosen node. Is that still required for the CPU1 board target if it's always a secondary core? I enabled &uart1, but there was previous conversation that adding the `uart1_default` pinctrl to the common pinctrl file is not acceptable. (see https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/93379#discussion_r2286093435). Is it ok in the cpu1 common dtsi?

Future work: 
- Support hazard3 rp2350 core launch CPU1: need to use an architecture agnostic `WFE` and `SEV` in CPU1 launch sequence and to set CPU1's architecture to the Hazard3 core.
- Verify AMP on more rp2350-based boards
- Support RP2040
- Support using CPU1 as independent target like `cpuflpr` if there is desire for it.

---

Testing:

Build the icmsg sample with: 

```
west build -p always -b rpi_pico2/rp2350a/m33 --sysbuild -S rp2xxx-cpu1 samples/subsys/ipc/ipc_service/icmsg/
# or for CPU1 with XIP: 
west build -p always -b rpi_pico2/rp2350a/m33 --sysbuild -S rp2xxx-cpu1-xip samples/subsys/ipc/ipc_service/icmsg/
```

Flash with west using the RaspberryPi OpenOCD fork according to [Programming and Debugging](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/raspberrypi/rpi_pico/doc/index.html#programming-and-debugging) section of rpi_pico's board docs.

```
west flash --openocd /usr/local/bin/openocd
```

title: bluetooth: hci: NXP: drain TX FIFO before uart_configure() in fw_upload
body:
This PR fixes a regression issue n FW download code. Below is the details:

> **Root cause:** Commit `f56935c46fdf` (`serial: uart_mcux_lpuart: remove call of LPUART_Deinit()`) replaced `LPUART_Deinit()` in `mcux_lpuart_configure()` with a bare `CTRL &= ~(TE|RE)` register write. `LPUART_Deinit()` had internally polled the TC (Transmission Complete) hardware flag and waited for the TX FIFO **and** shift register to fully drain before disabling the peripheral — providing an implicit TX drain every time `uart_configure()` was called. After the commit, `uart_configure()` immediately clears the TE bit and reprograms the baud-rate dividers with no drain wait.
>
> This exposed a pre-existing timing hazard in `fw_upload_change_speed()`: CMD5 is written with `fw_upload_write_data()`, which only guarantees bytes are accepted into the TX FIFO — not that they have been clocked out on the wire. `fw_upload_uart_reconfig()` is called immediately after, which calls `uart_configure()` to switch to 3 Mbaud. Before `f56935c46fdf` the implicit `LPUART_Deinit()` drain inside `uart_configure()` masked this race; after the commit the tail bytes of CMD5 are clocked out at 3 Mbaud instead of 115200 baud, corrupting the handshake. The IW612 controller never receives a valid CMD5, never switches to 3 Mbaud, and the host times out waiting for HDR SIG.
>
> **Fix:** In `fw_upload_uart_reconfig()`, after disabling TX IRQs, poll `uart_irq_tx_complete()` (with `uart_irq_update()`) for up to 20 ms before calling `uart_configure()`. This explicitly waits for the hardware TC flag — restoring the drain guarantee that `LPUART_Deinit()` previously provided implicitly.

/* Driver for Nordic Global Software Watchdog Timer (GSWDT)
 *
 * The GSWDT is a software-based watchdog that can be used in conjunction with
 * the MBOX peripheral to provide a watchdog functionality. The driver sends
 * messages to the system controller through the MBOX interface to feed the
 * watchdog. Maximum timeout is determined by the system controller configuration
 * and is set to 6s. Minimum feed interval should be 5s to avoid watchdog
 * expiration. Too short feeding intervals may cause increased power consumption.
 *
 * During wdt_nrf_gswdt_setup the driver sends a message to the system controller to start
 * the watchdog.
 * After that, the driver expects periodic calls to wdt_nrf_gswdt_feed to keep the watchdog from
 * expiring. If the watchdog expires, the system controller will reset the SoC.
 * Disable functionality is not supported, as the GSWDT cannot be disabled once started.
 */

title: Bluetooth: Host: Fix use-after-free in bt_att_sent on disconnect
body:
## Summary

Fix a use-after-free of `chan->att` in `bt_att_sent()` that faults when an ATT
bearer disconnects mid-transfer.

## Problem

When the peer disconnects, the BT RX thread runs
`att_chan_detach()` → `att_reset()`, which clears `chan->att` and then frees the
`bt_att` context via `k_mem_slab_free()`.

For an unenhanced ATT bearer, `bt_att_sent()` is invoked from the ATT TX buffer
destroy work on the **system workqueue**, concurrently with that disconnect path
on the RX thread. It cached `chan->att` into a local, null-checked the *local*,
and then dereferenced `att->reqs` / `att->tx_queue`. That null check is a TOCTOU
race: the context can be freed between the check and the use, faulting in
`sys_slist_get(&att->reqs)`.

Observed on an nRF52840 peripheral as a bus fault on `sysworkq`:

```
<err> os: ***** BUS FAULT *****
<err> os:   Precise data bus error
... PC -> z_snode_next_peek (slist.h), inlined into sys_slist_get(&att->reqs)
... LR -> bt_att_sent (att.c)
Current thread: sysworkq
```

## Fix

Hold the scheduler lock across the queue processing in `bt_att_sent()` and
re-read `chan->att` under it. `att_chan_detach()` clears `chan->att` *before*
`att_reset()` frees it, and the free runs on a schedulable thread, so a non-NULL
read of `chan->att` under the scheduler lock guarantees the context stays valid
until `k_sched_unlock()`. This mirrors the existing locking around
`bt_att_chan_send()` in `bt_att_chan_req_send()`; no new primitives, and the
send calls in the region are already known not to block (same precedent).

## Testing

The fault is a cross-thread timing race and is not deterministically
reproducible in a host/`bsim` test (a disconnect-mid-TX test passes even with
the bug most of the time). Verified by reasoning about the ordering above and by
HIL on nRF52840: forcing a central disconnect mid file-transfer no longer
faults/resets. Happy to add a `bsim` test under `tests/bsim/bluetooth/host/` if
maintainers feel it can usefully force the interleaving.

## Notes

- AI-assisted; disclosed via the `Assisted-by:` trailer in the commit per the
  contribution guidelines. The human author reviewed the change and is
  accountable for it.

body:
This PR extends the mesh statistic module with timestamp-based measurement of LPN friendship timing parameters (ReceiveDelay and ReceiveWindow).

Timestamps are captured at protocol events during each poll cycle:

T1: Poll TX complete
T2: Scanner enabled (ReceiveDelay elapsed)
T3: Friend response received / ReceiveWindow expired
From these, the module computes actual on-air ReceiveDelay (T2 - T1) and ReceiveWindow (T3 - T2) in microseconds, along with min/max tracking and cycle counters.

Shell commands mesh stat lpn_get / mesh stat lpn_clear are added for runtime access. Existing frame statistic commands are renamed to mesh stat adv_get / mesh stat adv_clear.

Documentation is updated accordingly.

title: drivers: modem: tune CMUX defaults for Telit LE910C1TX and LEX10Q1
body:
Improve CMUX stability on Telit LE910C1TX and LEX10Q1 modems under bursty traffic load.

Both modems can experience DLCI receive buffer pressure during high-throughput operations (e.g. FTP transfers). This may lead
to unstable communication due to frequent flow control activity or insufficient buffering.

Adjust CMUX defaults as follows:
- Increase MODEM_CMUX_WORK_BUFFER_SIZE_EXTRA to 256 to provide additional buffer headroom
- Tune MODEM_CMUX_MSC_FC_THRESHOLD per modem:
  - improve handling of bursty traffic on LE910C1TX
  - use a conservative configuration on LEX10Q1, where virtual channel flow control is not supported according to the modem documentation

Defaults apply only when the modem is enabled via devicetree (DT_HAS_TELIT_LE910C1TX_ENABLED or DT_HAS_TELIT_LEX10Q1_ENABLED) and can be overridden by application configuration.

title: drivers: display: add charlieplex LED matrix driver
labels: area: Samples;area: Devicetree;area: Tests;area: Display;area: Devicetree Binding;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
Add a generic Zephyr display driver for monochrome and grayscale LED matrices driven by charlieplexed GPIOs, and enable the on-board matrix on the Arduino UNO Q.

Charlieplexing drives up to N*(N-1) LEDs from N GPIO lines: each LED sits between an ordered pair of lines and is lit by driving one line high and one low while every other line is held at high impedance. Only one LED is lit at a time, so a timer scans the pixels fast enough for persistence of vision. The Arduino UNO Q carries a 13x8 (104 LED) matrix of this kind wired to the STM32U585 across port F lines PF0..PF10, scanned by TIM17.

 Rather than add a board-specific driver, this reuses the existing display interface and keeps the driver hardware independent. It is built only on the generic GPIO and counter APIs: the inactive lines are configured as disconnected to obtain the required high impedance state instead of touching GPIO registers directly, and any timer exposed through the counter API can be used as the scan source. All of the panel specifics, the GPIO bank, the per-pixel high/low pin-pair map, the scan timer, refresh rate and grayscale depth, are described in devicetree through the new charlieplex-led-matrix binding, so the driver works unchanged on any SoC and any charlieplexed panel layout.

The driver keeps a per-pixel framebuffer and lights the next pixel on each counter top-value callback. Grayscale is produced by duty modulation over a configurable number of sub-frames. It implements the mandatory display write and get_capabilities operations plus blanking, get_framebuffer, set_brightness and pixel-format negotiation, and reports the MONO01 pixel format.

The series adds the binding and driver, enables the matrix in the arduino_uno_q devicetree as the chosen zephyr,display, and adds a ztest suite that runs on native_sim using the emulated GPIO controller and software counter so it needs no hardware.

Tested on an Arduino UNO Q (matrix lights and updates correctly) and with the ztest suite under twister on native_sim.

title: kernel: rework cpu_mask and support other schedulers
body:
Now SCHED_CPU_MASK is no longer restricted to SCHED_SIMPLE. Dropped
  dependency on SCHED_SIMPLE and made SCHED_CPU_MASK work on all scheduler
  types by implementing z_priq_rb_mask_best and z_priq_mq_mask_best for
  both scalable and multiq schedulers.

  Update the help text and remove the stale claim that the feature only
  works with the simple scheduler and document the mask-aware best-thread
  search algorithm and its performance characteristics for each of the
  three supported backends:

    SCHED_SIMPLE:   O(N) sorted-list scan; terminates at the first
                    priority-eligible thread, so cost is proportional to
                    the number of higher-priority threads pinned away from
                    the current CPU.

    SCHED_SCALABLE: O(N) in-order rbtree walk; benefits from priority
                    ordering so the walk usually terminates early.

    SCHED_MULTIQ:   O(P) bitmap iteration over non-empty priority levels
                    plus an inner O(N) per-level list scan; fast when
                    affinity-constrained threads are sparse, degrades when
                    many same-priority threads are pinned away.

title: scripts: west: runners: esp32: support watchdog-reset via --reset-type
body:
The esp32 runner always passes esptool `--after hard-reset`. On targets flashed over the chip's built-in USB Serial/JTAG peripheral (common on ESP32-S3, C3 and C6 boards with no external USB to UART bridge), `hard-reset` relies on an RTS line that does not exist, so esptool cannot perform a real system reset. After a successful flash the chip reboots back into download mode (`rst:0x15 (USB_UART_CHIP_RESET), boot:0x0 (DOWNLOAD)`) and never starts the application until a manual reset or power cycle. The runner exposed no way to choose a different post-flash reset method.

This advertises the generic `reset_types` runner capability so users can select the esptool `--after` method:

    west flash --reset-type watchdog-reset

which Espressif documents as the fix for USB Serial/JTAG targets that get stuck in download mode. Supported values are `hard-reset` (the default, behavior unchanged), `watchdog-reset`, `no-reset` and `no-reset-stub`. This mirrors how the `jlink` and `stm32cubeprogrammer` runners already use `reset_types`. When reset is disabled with `--no-reset`, a non-default reset type is ignored with a warning.

The default path is byte for byte identical to before. A runner test covers the default, the `watchdog-reset` and `no-reset` values, and the `--no-reset` interaction. A note is added to the Espressif programming and debugging documentation.

References:
- esptool advanced options (`--after watchdog-reset`): https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esptool/en/latest/esp32s3/esptool/advanced-options.html

title: soc: nxp: mcxe24x: fix watchdog reset loop when CONFIG_WATCHDOG=n
labels: platform: NXP;size: XS;platform: NXP MCU;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
The use of 'configdefault' for 'WDT_DISABLE_AT_BOOT' prevents the symbol from being defined when the watchdog driver is disabled.

On MCXE24x series SOCs, the NXP SDK startup code (SystemInit) uses this symbol (via the DISABLE_WDOG compiler definition) to decide whether to disable the hardware watchdog. If the symbol is missing from the Kconfig output, the build system defaults to leaving the watchdog enabled (DISABLE_WDOG=0).

Since the MCXE hardware watchdog is enabled by default after reset, this leads to an infinite reset loop approximately 1 second after boot for all applications that do not explicitly enable the watchdog driver.   Many of the samples do not run due to this.  

Reverting to 'config' ensures the symbol is always defined and the watchdog is correctly disabled at boot unless explicitly overridden.

Hardware verification on frdm_mcxe247 confirms the reset loop is resolved with this change. I have used the blinky and hello_world sample to verify. Alternatively this board.conf addition can be used as a work-around.   
CONFIG_WATCHDOG=y
CONFIG_WDT_DISABLE_AT_BOOT=y   

I also verified that in v4.4.0-rc3 this error does not occur.  

Fixes: 3a7500de7484 ("soc: nxp: mcxe24x: enable LPTMR as system timer")
Assisted-by: Gemini-CLI:0.44.1

title: drivers: pcie: Introducing CONFIG_PCIE_HOST
labels: area: Ethernet;area: CAN;area: PCI;area: Disk Access;Stale;area: ARM64;area: Virtualization;area: SMBus;area: VIRTIO;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
The file `drivers/pcie/host/pcie.c` is compiled if `CONFIG_PCIE`
is enabled, but it depends on the actual PCIe controller,
and a contradiction occurs when the sub-option `CONFIG_PCIE_CONTROLLER`
is set to `n`.

CONFIG_PCIE_HOST defaults to y when CONFIG_PCIE_CONTROLLER or X86 is

Endpoint-only configurations can enable CONFIG_PCIE without pulling in the
host support.

title: drivers: i3c: validate nested CCC buffers in do_ccc syscall handler
body:
The do_ccc syscall verifier checked the outer payload and the
ccc/targets arrays but operated on the caller's live structure and
did not validate the per-target data buffers, unlike the i3c_transfer
verifier which snapshots its message array before use.

Make the two paths consistent: introduce copy_ccc_and_do(), which
snapshots the payload, allocates a kernel-side copy of the target
array via k_usermode_alloc_from_copy(), and validates each data
buffer with K_SYSCALL_MEMORY() before calling the implementation.
num_targets is capped at 31 as a sanity bound. The driver-written
num_xfer and err fields are copied back to the caller after the
transfer so results still propagate; data buffers are unaffected
as their pointers still reference user memory.

Signed-off-by: Ryan McClelland <rymcclel@gmail.com>

title: drivers: wifi: brcmfmac: add BCM43xxx SDIO Wi-Fi driver
labels: In progress;area: Wi-Fi;area: Devicetree Binding;area: MAINTAINER File
body:
Add a native-L2 Zephyr Wi-Fi driver for SDIO-attached Broadcom/Cypress combo chips speaking the brcmfmac SDPCM + BCDC protocol. Validated on a Pi Zero 2 W (BCM43430A1 / CYW43439), but the protocol layer is chip-agnostic: chip identity is read at runtime from chipcommon[0] on the AXI/SB backplane, and per-chip firmware/NVRAM blobs come from the `hal_broadcom` module.

The driver is split into six translation units inside the one commit:

- `brcmfmac_core.c`: entry point + chip-init orchestration; wires `wifi_mgmt` + `iface_api` callbacks.
- `brcmfmac_chip.c`: EROM (DMP/PL-368) scan, AI core reset/enable helpers, CM3 set_passive / set_active state transitions.
- `brcmfmac_sdio.c`: F1 backplane window, ramrw, firmware + NVRAM upload + readback verify.
- `brcmfmac_bcdc.c`: BCDC framing over SDIO F2; dedicated RX thread drains F2 and dispatches by SDPCM channel; TX ring + per-frame flow-control gate.
- `brcmfmac_net.c`: `net_if` + `wifi_mgmt` glue: iface init/send, RX → `net_recv_data`, escan scan, WPA2-PSK connect/disconnect, event parsing.
- `brcmfmac_fw_blob.c`: thin wrapper that `#include`s the two `.inc` files CMake generates from `hal_broadcom`'s blobs (fetched via `west blobs fetch hal_broadcom`).

Firmware blob handling uses the standard `west blobs` flow: `hal_broadcom` is a new external Zephyr module hosting sha256-pinned URLs pointing at `rpi-distro/firmware-nonfree` (the canonical Cypress/Infineon distribution). The module itself is ~51 lines of `module.yml` + license file; no blob content stored.

Hardware-verified on Pi Zero 2 W: `wifi scan` returns visible networks, `wifi connect -s <SSID> -p <PSK> -k 1` associates, DHCP completes, `net dns` resolves.

Depends on #110199 (SDIO bus) and the `hal_broadcom` west.yml entry (separate PR to come).

title: boards: m5stack: add support for M5Stack StickS3
body:
## What

Add initial Zephyr support for the **M5Stack StickS3**, an
ESP32-S3-PICO-1-N8R8 board in a stick form factor.

This first board PR is intentionally minimal:

- boot and console over the native USB Serial/JTAG
- the two user buttons (G11/G12) via `gpio-keys`
- the on-board Bosch BMI270 IMU on I2C0

`procpu` and `appcpu` CPU clusters are provided. The board uses ESP simple boot
(no MCUboot), matching `m5stack_stamps3`.

The LCD (ST7789), ES8311 audio codec, infrared, the M5PM1 PMIC and PSRAM are
intentionally left out of this PR and planned as focused follow-ups.

## Why

There is no upstream support for the M5Stack StickS3 yet; the nearest M5Stack
ESP32-S3 boards (`m5stack_atoms3`, `m5stack_stamps3`) target different hardware
and SoC packages.

## What was tested

Builds (Zephyr 4.4):

- `west build -b m5stack_sticks3/esp32s3/procpu samples/hello_world`
- `west build -b m5stack_sticks3/esp32s3/procpu samples/basic/button`
- `west build -b m5stack_sticks3/esp32s3/appcpu samples/hello_world`
- `scripts/checkpatch.pl`: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

Hardware (physical M5Stack StickS3, flashed with `esptool --after
watchdog-reset`): boot/console confirmed.

```
*** Booting Zephyr OS build v4.4.0 ***
Hello World! m5stack_sticks3/esp32s3/procpu
```

The buttons (G11/G12, `gpio-keys` input events) and the BMI270 IMU were also
exercised on the same hardware during development.

## Known limitations / follow-ups

- LCD, ES8311 audio, IR and the M5PM1 PMIC (the latter with a
  `zephyr,fuel-gauge-composite` on the PMIC VBAT ADC) are not part of this PR
  and will be added separately.
- PSRAM is present on the module but not enabled in this initial port.
- This PR uses ESP simple boot to match `m5stack_stamps3`; MCUboot/sysbuild can
  be added later if preferred.

body:

title: xtensa: userspace: support generated privilege stack
body:
This adds support to have generated privilege stack. When CONFIG_GEN_PRIV_STACKS is enabled, the privilege stack is no longer places directly before the thread stack and is placed elsewhere according to linker script. This is useful for MPU as there are limited MPU slots in hardware. If there are multiple threads in a memory domain, even with stack array, there will be interleaved MPU entries covering all these stacks. If generated privlege stack is used instead, this stack array can be covered with two entries (start and end addresses), while the privilege stack will not be occupying additional entries due to them being covered by blanket kernel only R/W access through other entries. Downside of this is that thread stack no longer has stack overflow guard since now the privilege stack is elsewhere.

title: boards: infineon: pse84: --cmd-erase for OpenOCD
body:
Add a `--cmd-erase` runner argument to the kit_pse84_eval and kit_pse84_ai board.cmake files so that `west flash --erase` works on these boards. Without it the OpenOCD runner aborts with "--erase not supported for target without --cmd-erase".

`--cmd-erase` only wires up the command that `west flash --erase` invokes; a plain `west flash` still takes the normal load path and does not erase. When `--erase` is used it runs the vendor `erase_all` OpenOCD proc, which erases the on-die `cat1d.cm33.main_ns` RRAM bank where the application image lives, along with every external SMIF/QSPI bank attached to the device. `cat1d.cm33.main_s` is a virtual alias of the same physical memory, so a single sector erase covers both secure and non-secure views.

title: net: quic: Add DPLPMTUD probe tracking
body:
The Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (DPLPMTUD) is described in RFC 9000 section 14.3.

Keep the peer's max_udp_payload_size transport parameter separate from the currently validated send limit. Add endpoint and sent-packet state for DPLPMTUD so QUIC can track validated payload size, pending probes, and probe retries.

Teach the QUIC/TLS send path to build exact-size PING+PADDING probe datagrams, send them with don't-fragment enabled, and raise the active TX payload limit only after probe ACKs. Repeated probe loss now clamps the search range instead of folding the peer limit into the current send cap.

There are also fixes for protecting TX buffer used for constructing the sent message, and preserving and tracking out-of-order messages properly.

title: drivers: sensor: tmp112: add one-shot conversion mode
body:
The TMP112 can stay in shutdown (SD) mode and perform a single conversion on
demand through its one-shot (OS) bit. This is the lowest idle-current mode of
the device and is useful for battery-powered designs that sample temperature
infrequently.

This PR exposes that mode through the existing `conversion-rate` device-tree
property:

- Setting `conversion-rate = <0>` keeps the sensor in shutdown and triggers a
  one-shot conversion on every `sample_fetch` call. The driver blocks until the
  OS bit reads back as `1` (typically ~10 ms per datasheet §7.4.3) or a timeout
  elapses.
- The periodic conversion rates (0.25/1/4/8 Hz) keep their previous behaviour.
- The same mode can be selected at runtime by setting a 0 Hz sampling frequency
  via `sensor_attr_set(SENSOR_ATTR_SAMPLING_FREQUENCY)`.

Because a new value (`0`) is prepended to the `conversion-rate` enum, the
device-tree enum index no longer maps directly onto the CR register field, so
the init path subtracts one for the periodic rates. The binding and driver are
therefore changed together in a single commit to keep every revision
buildable/bisectable.

## Changes

- `drivers/sensor/ti/tmp112/tmp112.c` — one-shot convert helper, shutdown
  handling in init/attr_set, one-shot trigger in `sample_fetch`
- `drivers/sensor/ti/tmp112/tmp112.h` — `TMP112_CONFIG_SD` bit, one-shot timing
  constants, `one_shot` flag in `tmp112_data`
- `drivers/sensor/ti/tmp112/Kconfig` — document the shutdown/one-shot behaviour
- `dts/bindings/sensor/ti,tmp112.yaml` — allow `conversion-rate = 0`

## Testing

Tested on an **nRF54L15-DK** with a TMP112 connected over I2C:

- Periodic rates (0.25/1/4/8 Hz) behave as before.
- `conversion-rate = <0>` returns correct temperature readings on demand while
  the sensor is held in shutdown between fetches.
- Verified via the sensor shell.

No new build warnings; `twister`/CI clean expected.

title: Bluetooth: Host: Fix use-after-free in bt_att_sent on disconnect
body:
## Summary

Fix a use-after-free of the ATT context in the deferred "sent" callback path when an unenhanced ATT bearer disconnects mid-transfer.

> Supersedes #110070 (auto-closed for losing common history). An earlier revision of this PR wrapped `bt_att_sent()` in `k_sched_lock()`; as noted in review that is a no-op — Bluetooth forces a cooperative system workqueue, so the handler is already non-preemptible. This revision takes a different approach.

## Problem

When the peer disconnects, the teardown runs on the system workqueue: `att_chan_detach()` + `att_reset()` free the `bt_att`, then `bt_att_released()` frees the `bt_att_chan`. The channel TX drain queues the ATT TX buffer destroy work (`att_tx_destroy_work`) on the **same** system workqueue without awaiting it.

Later, `att_tx_destroy_work_handler()` calls `att_on_sent_cb()` → (for UATT) `bt_att_sent()`. By then the `bt_att`/`bt_att_chan` are freed. `att_on_sent_cb()` does guard against a detached bearer, but it does so by dereferencing `meta->att_chan`, which is now a dangling pointer — it faults once the channel slab slot has been reused (the real-world trigger: disconnect, then reconnect). Observed as a bus fault on `sysworkq` in `sys_slist_get(&att->reqs)`.

## Fix

Null any pending ATT TX metadata that still references the channel in `bt_att_released()`, immediately before the channel is freed. The existing `att_on_sent_cb()` guard (its `!meta->att_chan` check) then drops the deferred callback instead of dereferencing freed memory. Teardown and the destroy work both run on the cooperative system workqueue, so this is serialized with the handler and needs no lock; aligned pointer writes are atomic.

## Testing

This is a cross-thread timing race: it is not deterministically reproducible in a host/`bsim` test, and on hardware it only fires intermittently (the deferred sent-work has to land in the window after the channel is freed/reused). I therefore can't offer a clean automated before/after, and want to be upfront that the low hit-rate is also why the earlier (no-op) `k_sched_lock` revision *appeared* to help. The fix is justified primarily by the lifetime/ordering reasoning above and in the commit message; it is being exercised on nRF52840 HIL with disconnect and disconnect-then-reconnect mid file-transfer, and I'll follow up here with results. Suggestions for a reliable repro (or a `bsim` angle that can force the interleaving) are welcome.

## Notes

- Targets the UATT deferred path (the reported fault). For EATT, `bt_att_sent` is L2CAP's direct `.sent` callback rather than the `meta`-based path; whether it needs separate handling is a question for maintainers.
- AI-assisted; disclosed via the `Assisted-by:` trailer in the commit per the contribution guidelines. The human author reviewed the change and is accountable for it.

Fixes: #112430

<summary>(shell script used for the biggest commit, click to expand)</summary>

The below script greps (using awk) DTS files for `pinctrl-0 = <&i2c_scl_pWX &i2c_sda_pYZ>;` (or swapped phandles) and adds `scl-gpios = <&gpioW X ...>`/`sda-gpios = <&gpioY Z ...>` in the node (possibly replacing existing occurrence in the node). It leverages STM32 SoC based DTS files use these pinctrl labels and all uses this single line format for I2C nodes defining their pinctrl default state (as shown running output from shell command `grep -rs _scl_p boards/ samples/ tests/ | grep -v _sda_p`).

The properties are printed after `pinctrl-names = ...`, to make the DTS files more readable.


```shell
#!/bin/bash
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright The Zephyr Project Contributors
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

set -o nounset
set -o errexit

tempfile=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tempfile"' EXIT

awk_cmd() {
  awk '
{
  # in case pinctrl-names is placed before pinctrl-0 in the node
  if ($0 ~ /^([[:space:]]*)pinctrl-names =/) {
    name_found = 1
  }

  if ($0 ~ /^([[:space:]]*)(scl|sda)-gpios =/) {
      props_present = 1
      # skip the line, it will be printed later
      if (props_added == 1) { next }
  }

  # Closing node: wipe our state
  if ($0 ~ /^([[:space:]]*)}/) {
    props_present = 0
    props_added = 0
    name_found = 0
  }

  # Matching pinctrl-0 = <&i2c1_scl_pXX &i2c1_sda_pXX>;
  if (match($0, /^([[:space:]]*)pinctrl-0[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*<&i2c([[:digit:]]+)_scl_p([[:alpha:]])([[:digit:]]+)[[:space:]]+&i2c([[:digit:]]+)_sda_p([[:alpha:]])([[:digit:]]+)>;/, m)) {
    desc_indent = m[1]
    P1 = m[3]
    B1 = m[4]
    P2 = m[6]
    B2 = m[7]
    pinctrl_found = 1
  }

  # Matching pinctrl-0 = <&i2c1_sda_pXX &i2c1_scl_pXX>;
  if (match($0, /^([[:space:]]*)pinctrl-0[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*<&i2c([[:digit:]]+)_sda_p([[:alpha:]])([[:digit:]]+)[[:space:]]+&i2c([[:digit:]]+)_scl_p([[:alpha:]])([[:digit:]]+)>;/, m)) {
    desc_indent = m[1]
    P2 = m[3]
    B2 = m[4]
    P1 = m[6]
    B1 = m[7]
    pinctrl_found = 1
  }

  print

  if (pinctrl_found == 1 && name_found == 1) {
    if (props_present != 1) {
      print desc_indent "scl-gpios = <&gpio" P1 " " B1 " GPIO_ACTIVE_HIGH>;"
      print desc_indent "sda-gpios = <&gpio" P2 " " B2 " GPIO_ACTIVE_HIGH>;"
      props_added = 1
    }
    pinctrl_found = 0
    name_found = 0
  }
}
' "$1" > "$2"
}

cnt=0
# Consider .dts, .dtsi and .overlay files that have a "_scl_p" occurrence
echo "Find matching files..."
files=`find boards/ samples/ tests/ \( -name "*.dts*" -o -name "*.overlay" \) -exec grep -l _scl_p {} \;`
echo "Process " `echo $files | wc -w` "matching files"

for f in $files; do
  awk_cmd "$f" "$tempfile"
  cmp -s "$f" "$tempfile" && continue
  echo $f
  cnt=$(($cnt+1))
  cat "$tempfile" > "$f"
done

echo "Done, $cnt files modified"
```
</details>

title: drivers: pulse_io: add vendor-neutral timed-edge IO subsystem
labels: area: Samples;area: Xtensa;area: RISCV;area: Devicetree;area: Tests;area: native port;platform: ESP32;area: LED;area: Devicetree Binding;area: Pinctrl;area: MAINTAINER File;area: Boards/SoCs;Release;platforms: RISCV
body:
## Pulse IO subsystem

This series introduces **pulse_io**, a vendor-neutral subsystem for
hardware that generates and captures timed digital edges on a single
GPIO line. Several MCU families ship a dedicated peripheral for this
under different names (Espressif RMT, RP2040 PIO, NXP FlexIO, STM32
timers with DMA, Nordic PWM with PPI and GPIOTE); pulse_io abstracts
that hardware class so client drivers - addressable LED strips, IR
transmit/receive, stepper pulse generation, frequency/duty measurement,
one-wire style protocols - can bind once and run on any SoC that
provides a backend.

Implements the RFC in #109586.
Fixes https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/72546

### What this adds

- A vendor-neutral API (`include/zephyr/drivers/pulse_io.h`): driver
  vtable, capability descriptor, two submission modes (SYMBOL for
  arbitrary `{level, duration}` pairs, CELL for fixed-period cells),
  sync and async transmit/receive, and a byte/symbol encoder + decoder.
- Userspace support: the channel lifecycle and transfer calls are
  exposed as syscalls with verification handlers.
- Optional RTIO integration: backends may expose an iodev submit path
  plus encoder/decoder vtables, mirroring the sensor subsystem.
- A functional `native_sim` backend that loops transmitted symbols back
  on receive, so the subsystem is exercised in CI without hardware.
- ztest suites covering capabilities, the channel lifecycle,
  configuration, codec encode/decode, sync/async transfer, streaming
  receive, the userspace syscall path, and the RTIO loopback (including
  chained transactions).
- Subsystem documentation, a release note, and a MAINTAINERS entry.

### Scope

This is the API plus a software reference backend only. Real hardware
backends follow a separate PRs once the API is settled.

### Testing

`west twister -p native_sim -p qemu_x86 -T tests/drivers/pulse_io`

Reading the TCP/UDP port fields via e.g `UNALIGNED_GET(&tcphdr->src_port)` takes the address of a packed struct member, which trips Clang's `-Waddress-of-packed-member` warning.

Since `net_tcp_hdr` and `net_udp_hdr` are already `__packed` structs, the compiler emits correct unaligned accesses for direct member reads, so read the port fields directly instead. This is consistent with how the rest of the file already accesses these members.

title: bluetooth: hci: ipc: Add config for closing HCI while keeping IPC alive
body:
As it currently stands, if you close an HCI connection e.g. `bt_disable()`, then `bt_hci_close()` will cause the IPC driver to deregister the IPC endpoint and close the connection. Generally, this means that we can no longer enable Bluetooth again on IPC-driven setups easily (on the nRF5340, it seems that the [net core would have to be restarted separately to re-bind](https://devzone.nordicsemi.com/f/nordic-q-a/114847/bt_enable-failed-after-bt_disable-in-nrf5340), for example).

This change poses a simpler alternative which adds a config option to allow `bt_hci_close()` to mask the IPC traffic, rather than actually closing the IPC session. The traffic can be later re-subscribed by defining a new receive callback with `bt_hci_open()`.

In my specific application, I have the use case: I switch between two uses of the HCI IPC. One is a USB HCI raw connection, where the app core just passes HCI messages through to the net core directly. Another is an SMP use, where the app core has the Bluetooth host stack to serve as a peripheral advertising SMP. These don't exist concurrently, but switch over who owns the receive callback as the current HCI authority (SMP or passthrough). Without this change, switching over the callback would inherently teardown the IPC connection and require the net core to be reset to sync the two cores again.

title: Infineon/wdt cat1d pse84 fixes
labels: area: UART;area: Samples;area: Watchdog;area: Devicetree Binding;area: Task Watchdog;platform: Infineon;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
## Summary

Three independent bugs in the Infineon WDT driver / PSE84 SoC made the WDT unusable on CAT1D / PSE84 and broke `samples/subsys/task_wdt` (the CI test for WDT reset / recovery on `kit_pse84_eval`). This PR fixes the SoC, driver, and the sample's UART-drain behavior so the test can run end-to-end.

## Root cause

1. **Boot loop on every cold boot.** On CAT1D / PSE84 the ROM hands control to the application with the WDT armed and a small match value. The window is short enough that the chip resets before *any* POST_KERNEL driver init can run, so the WDT driver itself cannot rescue this. The fix disables the WDT in `soc_early_init_hook()` on the secure M33 (the boot core in any PSE84 sysbuild configuration), well before any driver runs. A later `wdt_setup()` from the application re-enables it cleanly. Failure was deterministic; every cold boot of a stock build reproduced it.

2. **Counter not reset before `Cy_WDT_Enable()` on CAT1D.** `ifx_cat1_wdt_setup()` only called `Cy_WDT_ResetCounter()` when `COMPONENT_CAT1` was defined. On MXS40SSRSS / MXS22SRSS the reset was skipped, so the match landed close to the (potentially large) current counter and the chip reset almost immediately after enable. Extended the existing double-`Cy_WDT_ResetCounter()` workaround to cover those IPs.

3. **Wrong macro in `IFX_DETERMINE_MATCH_BITS` on 22-bit IP.** `IFX_DETERMINE_MATCH_BITS` used `IFX_WDT_MAX_IGNORE_BITS` instead of `IFX_WDT_MATCH_BITS`, producing `(MAX_IGNORE_BITS - ignore_bits)` instead of the documented `(MATCH_BITS - ignore_bits)`. A 1000 ms request (ignore_bits = 8) configured ~62.5 ms instead of ~1000 ms on MXS40SSRSS / MXS22SRSS. Gated on `SRSS_NUM_WDT_A_BITS == 22` so non-22-bit IPs are unaffected.

4. **UART TX truncation on `sys_reboot()`.** With the driver / SoC fixes the `task_wdt` sample reaches `sys_reboot()`, but the CI regex was still missing the second `Resetting device...` line because both PSE84 reset paths (`Cy_SysPm_TriggerSoftReset()` and `NVIC_SystemReset()`) tear down the SCB clock before the UART FIFO drains. Added an optional drain on PSE84 + enabled it in the sample's M55 board overlay.

## Changes (4 commits)

1. **`drivers: watchdog: wdt_infineon: fix CAT1D match-bits and reset-counter handling`** — `drivers/watchdog/wdt_infineon.c`. Fixes #2 and #3 above.
2. **`soc: infineon: pse84: disable WDT in early SoC init`** — `soc/infineon/edge/pse84/soc_pse84_m33_s.c`. Fixes #1; runs in `soc_early_init_hook()` so it preempts any POST_KERNEL driver.
3. **`soc: infineon: pse84: optional UART TX drain before soft reset`** — new `SOC_PSE84_REBOOT_UART_DRAIN` Kconfig (default n) + drain in `sys_arch_reboot()`. Default drain is 20000 us (covers a 16-byte SCB FIFO at 9600 baud: `16 * 10 / 9600 = 16.67 ms` + ~20 % margin).
4. **`samples: subsys: task_wdt: enable UART TX drain on kit_pse84_eval M55`** — sample board overlay opt-in.

## Validation

Verified locally on `kit_pse84_eval_pse846gps2dbzc4a` (M55):

- Without this PR: cold boot loops forever, no banner.
- With this PR: `samples/subsys/task_wdt` runs through its full lifecycle — banner, task-watchdog callback, `Resetting device...`, second banner after WDT reset. Matches the multi-line regex the CI test expects.

SonarCloud quality gate: passed. Compliance checks: green.

## Notes for reviewers

- The early WDT disable in `soc_early_init_hook()` is unconditional on PSE84 because the ROM-armed WDT will brick boot otherwise; there is no Kconfig knob to turn it off (such a knob would only let users brick their board). Applications that want WDT coverage from boot should call `wdt_install_timeout()` + `wdt_setup()` themselves.
- The 22-bit `IFX_DETERMINE_MATCH_BITS` branch is gated on `SRSS_NUM_WDT_A_BITS == 22` (a PDL-provided macro), so non-22-bit Infineon WDTs keep their existing behavior.
- Updated per @parthitce's review feedback: disable moved out of the driver into `soc_early_init_hook()`; UART drain default bumped to 20 ms; drain comment updated to cover both reset paths; `select HAS_WDT_DISABLE_AT_BOOT` + the `default y if SOC_SERIES_PSE84` block dropped (no longer relevant).

title: bluetooth: audio: vocs_client: dynamically discover CCC handle
body:
Currently, the VOCS client subscribes to characteristics by hardcoding the CCC handle offset to `attr->handle + 2.` While common, this layout is not strictly guaranteed by the Bluetooth specification and can fail if a server structures its GATT table differently. This commit updates the characteristic discovery callback to use the `CONFIG_BT_GATT_AUTO_DISCOVER_CCC` feature to dynamically locate the CCC. To support concurrent CCC discoveries safely, dedicated discovery parameter structures are added to the VOCS client instance. This prevents in-flight characteristic discoveries from clobbering each other's memory state. Additionally, the auto-discovery boundary is corrected to use the end of the service, rather than prematurely shrinking to the characteristic value handle. The hardcoded fallback and conditional compilation directives have been removed, as VOCS inherently relies on CCC auto-discovery being enabled via Kconfig.

title: Bluetooth: Add bt_conn_take() and bt_conn_drop() APIs and adopt treewide
body:
This PR introduces two new bt_conn reference-management APIs — bt_conn_take() and bt_conn_drop() — and sweeps the tree to adopt them, analogous to the recent work on introducing `net_buf_take()` and `net_buf_drop()`. It also fixes two latent use-after-unref bugs uncovered while doing the cleanup.

### New APIs

 - `bt_conn_take(struct bt_conn **conn)` — atomically transfers ownership of a connection reference from a pointer variable, leaving the source pointer NULL. The reference count is unchanged; the caller takes over ownership. Mirrors the existing net_buf_take().
 - `bt_conn_drop(struct bt_conn **conn)` — atomically drops a connection reference and clears the source pointer, replacing the common two-line pattern:
```
 bt_conn_unref(conn);
 conn = NULL;
```
`NULL` is handled internally, so external guards become unnecessary.

### Treewide adoption

`bt_conn_drop()` (and `bt_conn_take()` where applicable) is applied across:

 - Bluetooth Host, Classic, Audio, Mesh, ISO
 - OpenThread BLE platform glue
 - Bluetooth samples and the BBC micro:bit pong sample
 - Bluetooth tests (unit + bsim)

These changes are purely refactoring — no behavioral change intended — but they remove a recurring boilerplate footgun and tighten ownership semantics.

### Bug fixes

While auditing call sites, two genuine use-after-unref issues were found and fixed:

 - Bluetooth: Host — `bt_hci_le_enh_conn_complete()` dropped its local reference before dereferencing conn->role in the central-role scanner restart path. The bt_conn_unref() is moved to the end of the function.
 - Bluetooth: AVRCP — `bt_avrcp_cover_art_ct_l2cap_connect()` dropped its ACL reference before using the pointer for bt_conn_index() and bt_bip_l2cap_connect(). The unref is moved past the last use on each return path.

In both cases the object happened to survive in practice thanks to other references, but the code was incorrect per the reference-counting contract.

title: drivers: spi: nrfx_spim: chunk transfers exceeding EasyDMA MAXCNT
body:
The reworked SPIM driver passes the whole continuous chunk returned by spi_context_max_continuous_chunk() straight to the common transfer layer, which rejects anything larger than the controller MAXCNT with -EINVAL. On SoCs with a small EasyDMA MAXCNT (e.g. nRF91 SPIM with 13 bits, max 8191 bytes) a transfer of 8192 bytes or more fails outright.

The old monolithic driver used to cap the chunk to the MAXCNT limit and let the event handler walk the rest of the buffer. That behaviour was lost in the rework, so any caller pushing a buffer larger than MAXCNT now breaks. One example is the nRF70 firmware patch download, which copies the patch in 8192 byte chunks and ends up corrupting RPU memory, leading to a boot signature mismatch.

Restore the cap in transfer_start() so an oversized chunk is split across multiple EasyDMA transfers, with the remainder handled by the next call from the event handler once the current chunk completes.

title: drivers: gpio: infineon: implement pin_get_config callback
body:
The Infineon CAT1 and Cypress PSoC 6 GPIO drivers do not implement the
optional pin_get_config callback. With `CONFIG_USERSPACE=y` and
`CONFIG_GPIO_GET_CONFIG=y`, the syscall verifier invokes
`K_SYSCALL_DRIVER_GPIO(port, pin_get_config)`, which `K_OOPS`es the
kernel when the callback is `NULL` instead of letting
`z_impl_gpio_pin_get_config()` return `-ENOSYS`.

This PR implements the callback for both drivers, reverse-mapping the
PDL drive mode (`Cy_GPIO_GetDrivemode`) and HSIOM state back to
`gpio_flags_t`.

### Verification

Built and ran `tests/drivers/gpio/gpio_basic_api` on
`kit_pse84_eval/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m33` with
`CONFIG_USERSPACE=y` and `CONFIG_GPIO_GET_CONFIG=y` and a
P15.2 <-> P15.3 loopback. All four test suites pass, including the
`gpio_port` suite which calls `gpio_pin_get_config()` from a user
thread:

`
SUITE PASS - 100.00% [after_flash_gpio_config_trigger]: pass = 2, fail = 0, ...
SUITE PASS - 100.00% [gpio_port]: pass = 1, fail = 0, ...
SUITE PASS - 100.00% [gpio_port_cb_mgmt]: pass = 3, fail = 0, ...
SUITE PASS - 100.00% [gpio_port_cb_vari]: pass = 1, fail = 0, ...
PROJECT EXECUTION SUCCESSFUL
`

Without this change, the same test K_OOPSes in
`z_vrfy_gpio_pin_get_config()` as soon as the user thread reaches

title: drivers: wifi: native_sim: Add Wi-Fi driver using host nl80211
labels: area: Networking;area: Samples;area: Devicetree;area: Tests;area: native port;area: Wi-Fi;area: Devicetree Binding;manifest;manifest-net-tools;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
Add a Wi-Fi driver for the native_sim board so the Zephyr Wi-Fi stack (network manager / wpa_supplicant, net_mgmt, the wifi shell) can be exercised on the host against the Linux mac80211_hwsim simulated radio. It is meant for development and verification of the Wi-Fi APIs, not as a driver for any real hardware.

The Zephyr wpa_supplicant is the sole SME. The driver's host side brings up only the Linux nl80211 driver (compiled for the native_simulator runner) and runs its event loop in a thread; it does not run a second, host-side supplicant. It provides its own wpa_supplicant_event() that forwards nl80211 driver events (scan results, auth, assoc, deauth, disassoc, mgmt rx) to the Zephyr supplicant over an in-process socketpair, read by the interface RX thread and dispatched to the supplicant callbacks. The supplicant driver ops (scan, authenticate, associate, set_key, get_capa, ...) call the nl80211 ops table directly. Data frames, including the EAPOL 4-way handshake, flow over an AF_PACKET socket bound to the host interface and the Zephyr networking stack.
    
Notes on the host integration:

* The Zephyr interface adopts the host radio MAC address, so frames addressed to the associated STA are accepted by the Ethernet L2 and the frames it transmits are not rejected by the AP.
* control-port-over-nl80211 is disabled in the driver capabilities so the kernel delivers EAPOL as data frames to the supplicant's l2_packet.
* The interface uses carrier-up plus dormant, leaving dormant on association so the handshake can use the data path, and re-entering it on disconnect.
* A small supp_api hook lets the supplicant connect path notify this proxy driver; the connection itself is driven by the Zephyr SME.

Tested on native_sim with mac80211_hwsim: scan, connect (open and WPA2-PSK), status, disconnect and data transfer all work.

Currently the testing needs to be done manually, similarly as LWM2M interop tests. User can either setup the host manually using net-tools scripts, or run the provided Docker script that does all automatically.

Bluetooth: Switch bt_addr_le_t string format to a prefix-based encoding
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Networking;area: Samples;area: Tests;area: Wi-Fi;area: Bluetooth Controller;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth Audio;area: Bluetooth ISO;area: Bluetooth Classic;area: Boards/SoCs;Release
body:
### Summary

Switches the `bt_addr_le_t` string encoding from the space-separated `"11:22:33:44:55:66 (random)"` form to a compact prefix-based form, `"R:11:22:33:44:55:66"` / `"P:..."`. The motivation is to make shell input parsing trivial (a single token carries both the address and its type) and to remove the embedded whitespace from log lines.

The wire-level meaning of `bt_addr_le_t::type` is unchanged. Only the human-readable representation moves.

As agreed in the Bluetooth WG meeting on Aug 13, no compatibility with the old format is retained, neither for output nor for input. The deprecated Kconfig, the two-token input fallback and the shell helper from the earlier revisions are gone.

### What changed

- `bt_addr_le_to_str()` emits the `P:`/`R:` form. Address type values carrying HCI-level extension bits (the Controller-resolved identity types) are formatted by their base type; the Host log sites that handle raw HCI event addresses print a separate `(resolved)` annotation so the information is not lost. `BT_ADDR_LE_STR_LEN` shrinks from 30 to 20.
- `bt_addr_le_from_str()` loses its `type` argument and parses only the prefixed form. The prefix is case-insensitive, like the hex digits already were.
- All shell commands taking an LE address now take it as a single argument. Argument counts, positional indices, help strings and the shell documentation are updated. `bap_scan_delegator add_src` also gets its argv indices fixed (the error messages and the metadata parsing referred to the wrong slots), and `bt id-create` no longer proceeds after failing to parse its address.
- `bt id-create` and `bt id-reset` document their optional address as a static random address, which is all `bt_id_create()`/`bt_id_reset()` accept.
- Sample READMEs and the stm32wb5mmg board page show the new output format.
- ZTEST coverage for both conversion functions under `tests/bluetooth/addr/`.
- Migration guide entry.

### Verification

- `tests/bluetooth/addr` on native_sim: 51/51 test cases pass.
- All 75 `tests/bluetooth/shell` scenarios build on native_sim (full sweep on v3; default scenario rebuilt on every push since).
- Compliance checks clean (ClangFormat advisory warnings only).

title: release: list_backports: add --check mode for PR issue enforcement
body: Add a --check flag intended for use in the GitHub Actions workflow. When --check is passed with a single -p PR number, the script verifies that the PR body contains a 'Fixes #N' (or equivalent URL) reference. If no issue is found, a comment is posted on the PR asking the contributor to add one, and the script exits with a non-zero status, failing the CI check.

title: net_buf: Use net_buf_drop() to replace unref + NULL pattern
labels: area: Networking;area: USB;platform: Microchip SAM;area: Ethernet;area: CAN;area: mcumgr;area: ec_host_cmd;platform: Infineon
body:
Replace the recurring two-line pattern:
```
     net_buf_unref(buf);
     buf = NULL;
``` 
with `net_buf_drop(&buf)`, which performs both operations atomically in a single step. This is a pure refactor with no functional change, just fewer lines and less room for the pointer-zeroing step to be forgotten.
 
 Affected areas:
 - `drivers/ethernet` (eth_sam_gmac, eth_xmc4xxx)
 - `subsys/mgmt/mcumgr/transport` (smp_shell)
 - `subsys/net/ip/tcp`
 - `subsys/usb/device_next` (bt_hci, usbd_device)
 - `subsys/usb/device/class/bluetooth` (legacy USB)
 - `subsys/canbus/isotp`
 - `subsys/mgmt/ec_host_cmd` USB backend — here `net_buf_drop()` also fixes a dangling pointer on the persistent `ctx->usb_rx_buf` field on error paths.

title: drivers: bluetooth: hci: Fix send() buffer ownership contract
body:
The `bt_hci_driver_api` `send()` contract requires that the buffer reference is only consumed (unref'd) on success. On error, the caller retains ownership and is responsible for unref'ing the buffer.
 
Two HCI drivers were violating this contract by unconditionally calling `net_buf_unref()` at a `goto done` label, consuming the buffer on every error path:
 
 - `hci_bflb` — buffer incorrectly consumed on every error path.
 - `hci_bee` — same issue, plus a use-after-free where `buf->len` was
   accessed after the unref.
 
Both are fixed by returning early on each error path (without unref'ing) and only unref'ing on the success path.

Fixes: #112555

title: cmake: sca: fix Unix Makefiles generator byproduct dependency
body:
With the Unix Makefiles generator, BYPRODUCTS declared in
add_custom_command(TARGET ... POST_BUILD ...) are not registered as
Make rules. The clang and codechecker SCA targets depended on sentinel
files (clang-sca.ready, codechecker.ready) that were byproducts of the
zephyr ELF POST_BUILD step, causing:

  No rule to make target 'sca/clang/clang-sca.ready'

Replace the sentinel file mechanism with cmake_language(DEFER CALL ...)
to add a direct add_dependencies() on logical_target_for_zephyr_elf
after it is defined. This works correctly with both the Ninja and Unix
Makefiles generators and preserves the same ordering guarantee: SCA
analysis runs only after the full ELF build completes.

Fixes #104755

title: cmake: clang: fix MVE FP disabled on Cortex-M55 with -mfpu=fpv5-sp-d16
body:
Two related problems caused clang/LLVM to disable MVE floating-point
(-mve.fp) when targeting Cortex-M55:

1. cmake/gcc-m-fpu.cmake set FPU_FOR_cortex-m55 to fpv5-sp-d16 (commit
   6612580d9e4) to allow precision selection via PRECISION_TOKEN. For
   GCC this is harmless because GCC derives MVE capability from -march.
   For clang, -mfpu=fpv5-sp-d16 explicitly overrides the CPU's default
   FPU capabilities, which disables mve.fp:

     clang -mcpu=cortex-m55 -mfpu=fpv5-sp-d16 -> +nomve.fp  (wrong)
     clang -mcpu=cortex-m55                    -> +mve.fp    (correct)

   restore FPU_FOR_cortex-m55 to "auto". The +nomve.fp, +nomve and
   +nodsp variants keep fpv5-sp-d16 because they explicitly restrict FPU
   capabilities.

2. cmake/compiler/clang/target_arm.cmake unconditionally passed
   -mfpu=${GCC_M_FPU} when CONFIG_FPU is set, with no guard for "auto".
   The equivalent armclang fix was applied in commit f30235f56aa but was
   never ported to the standalone clang toolchain path.

   add the same NOT "auto" guard as armclang/target.cmake.

Fixes #109009

title: drivers: i2s: add I2S shell
body:
## Summary

Add a generic `i2s` shell for testing and validating I2S controllers from the Zephyr shell.

The new shell provides commands to generate and stream a test sine tone over any I2S device using the generic `i2s.h` API. It is transport-only and can be used together with the existing codec shell to route audio through a codec.

### New Commands

* `i2s tone <device> [frequency_hz] [sample_rate] [bits]`

  * Start streaming a generated sine tone.
  * Defaults: 440 Hz, 48000 Hz, 16-bit.
  * Supports 16, 24, and 32-bit audio formats.

* `i2s stop`

  * Stop the active tone stream.

* `i2s info`

  * Display current stream configuration and status.

### Testing

Verified by streaming tones on I2S hardware with multiple sample rates and word sizes (16/24/32-bit).

Companion to the `codec` shell `configure` work in #110693.

Example, routing through a codec with the `codec` shell:

```shell
i2s tone i2s@28000 440 48000 16
codec configure tas2563@4c 48000 16 2 playback
codec start tas2563@4c
codec set_prop tas2563@4c volume all -6
codec stop tas2563@4c
```

title: gpio: RFC: Add Fast GPIO API Extension (closes #106831)
labels: area: GPIO;area: Devicetree;platform: STM32;platform: nRF;platform: NXP;area: Tests;platform: Microchip SAM;platform: ESP32;area: Devicetree Binding;platform: Raspberry Pi Pico;area: MAINTAINER File;Release
body: This commit creates the Fast GPIO API via RFC #106831. It adds low-latency set, clear, toggle, get, etc. functions and helpers for implementing fast bit-bang drivers. Closes #11917, closes #106831. **UPDATE:** This has been refactored to use DT instead of overrides; see more recent commits. ~~**NOTE:** This is starting as a draft. I want to get some feedback from @nandojve before opening to other reviewers. Before marking as ready I will separate the WS2812 driver parts into a new PR. It is combined here at first for ease of testing/hardware verification.~~ This is now complete: #111218. OK, this was a tough one! Here are some notes compared to the original RFC: 1. I was unable to implement `gpio_fast_send_stream()`. The timing requirements for a driver like WS2812 are too tight to abstract the data out into a struct and for loops. I was only able to make it work by creating a specific 2-operations-per-bit set/clear mode, which defeats the point of the abstraction. It is likely possible, but will take a lot more work and I think should go in a followup PR. 2. The only way I could make the timings reliable across all platforms was to use `nop`. 3. I could not use `LISTIFY()` because it created a mess of Kconfig math. We can now automatically calculate timing offsets via the number of CPU cycles required for set and clear in the header/source, so the WS2812 driver no longer requires per-board timing config in Kconfig/DTS. 4. When implementing future vendor Fast GPIO drivers, it is really a **requirement** that it is tested on real hardware. There are so many edge cases where you may need `__ramfunc` or calculating the cycle offsets are weird. The good thing is, **none of these edge cases are visible from the user-facing API.** 5. The number of cycles to do operations varies per platform, but **the driver can fully realize if timings can be met at compile time.** The part I am really proud of: I have verified this works on **6 different platforms!** - Adafruit Circuit Playground Express: `sam0` - Adafruit Feather ESP32: `esp32` - Adafruit KB2040: `rpi_pico` - Teensy 4.0: `mcux` - STM32 Nucleo-F401RE: `stm32` - nRF52840 Dongle : `nrf52840` All of these work without custom timing in DTS. @nandojve I added your copyright to some files since you did a lot of work in the RFC. Please let me know if you would prefer me to remove them. I used the help of Claude Opus 4.7 on this PR, and it mostly helped me with vendor-specifics for each platform that I am less familiar with. I have physically tested the set/clear functions on each platform. I do not use this tool for issue/PR comments and take full responsibility for this code. Assisted-by: Claude:claude-opus-4.7

title: drivers: counter: infineon_tcpwm: fix set_top_value HW counter reset
body:
## Summary

Fix `ifx_tcpwm_counter_set_top_value()` so that it actually resets the
TCPWM hardware counter when a new top value is configured, and add the
test overlays needed to exercise this on Infineon TCPWM boards.

## Driver fix

Previously the function only updated the software cache
(`data->value`) and the TCPWM `PERIOD` register; the hardware `CNT`
register was never written. When the new top value was smaller than
the current counter value, the counter had to roll over the full
16-bit / 32-bit range before terminal count, instead of the new
period. On a 16-bit counter clocked at 10 kHz this took about 6 s,
which broke `test_set_top_value_with_alarm` in
`tests/drivers/counter/counter_basic_api`.

The patch:

- writes `0` to the HW counter via `Cy_TCPWM_Counter_SetCounter()`
  when `COUNTER_TOP_CFG_DONT_RESET` is **not** set,
- returns `-ETIME` when `DONT_RESET` is set but the current counter
  value is already past the new top (matching the counter API
  contract), and additionally resets the counter to `0` in that case
  when `COUNTER_TOP_CFG_RESET_WHEN_LATE` is set,
- reorders the write so the new period is programmed before the
  reset-vs-late comparison.

## Test overlays

`counter_basic_api` previously had no overlay for the PSE84 or
CYW20829 boards, so it never ran on the affected hardware. New
overlays are added for:

- `cyw920829m2evk_02` (b0lkml, b1010, b1340)
- `kit_pse84_ai/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m33` and `/m55`
- `kit_pse84_eval/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m33` and `/m55`

The existing `kit_psc3m5_evk` overlay is updated to use the unified
`clock-div` property and drop legacy properties
(`divider-type`/`divider-sel`/`divider-val`/`clock-frequency`/
`scb-block`/`div-value`) that are not declared by the current
`infineon,tcpwm` / `infineon,peri-div` bindings.

## Verification

`tests/drivers/counter/counter_basic_api` was run on real hardware
with the driver fix applied. All subtests pass on:

| Board | Result |
|-------|--------|
| `kit_pse84_eval/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m33` | 8 PASS, 2 SKIP |
| `kit_pse84_eval/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m55` | 8 PASS, 2 SKIP |
| `kit_pse84_ai/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m33`   | 8 PASS, 2 SKIP |
| `kit_pse84_ai/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m55`   | 8 PASS, 2 SKIP |
| `cyw920829m2evk_02/cyw20829b0lkml`    | 8 PASS, 2 SKIP |

(The two skips are the existing `test_multiple_alarms` /
`test_cancelled_alarm_does_not_expire` cases that are already gated
on driver capabilities not provided by `infineon,tcpwm-counter`.)

title: net: shell: quiet ping with statistics
body:
**Issue**
When the underlying UART is shared with the logging subsystem, extensive logging can prevent `net ping` from printing its response for over 100 ms. The network stack then appears unresponsive to subsequent pings, which looks like a network stack bug but is not — logging is contending with `shell_print()`.

**Solution**
The Linux ping command supports a quiet mode and end-of-session statistics.
- Add `-q` flag to suppress per-reply output
- Add end-of-session statistics printed on termination
```
--- ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss
rtt min/avg/max = 87/91/93 ms
```

**Pre-work for the above**
The shell print functions for IPv4 and IPv6 are unified to reduce code duplication, which is required to implement the statistics without repeating logic.

**Spotted bug while fixing the initial issue**
Fixed incorrect RSSI reporting on multi-interface devices: when CONFIG_IEEE802154 is enabled, RSSI was previously read regardless of interface type. It is now only read for IEEE 802.15.4 links, checked at runtime.

title: Add support RFC 8899 generic DPLPMTUD
body:
The #110315 added DPLPMTUD support to QUIC but that PR did not implement the DPLPMTUD in generic way so that other transports could use it. This PR adds generic APIs for DPLPMTUD and converts QUIC to use them.

Summary:

RFC 8899 describes Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (DPLPMTUD), a method for discovering the maximum packet size a path supports without relying on ICMP. Here are the transports that benefit:

* SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) (currently not relevant for Zephyr): SCTP uses datagram-style packetization and previously lacked a robust PMTUD mechanism. DPLPMTUD gives it a reliable, ICMP-independent way to probe path MTU.
* QUIC: runs over UDP and needs to know the path MTU to size its packets correctly. Since QUIC implements its own reliability and congestion control, it naturally fits the PL (Packetization Layer) model DPLPMTUD targets.
* UDP Applications (generic): Any application sending UDP datagrams directly (DNS over UDP, game protocols, media streaming, tunneling protocols) can implement DPLPMTUD at the application or middleware layer to avoid fragmentation.

Transports That Fit the Model:

* DTLS (Datagram TLS): Runs over UDP and has a record-size limit tied to MTU. DPLPMTUD helps DTLS-based apps (e.g., WebRTC data channels, VPNs) avoid fragmentation or silent packet loss.
* IPsec / ESP in tunnel mode (currently not relevant for Zephyr): Encapsulation adds overhead that reduces effective MTU. DPLPMTUD helps tunnel endpoints discover the usable MTU after encapsulation overhead is accounted for.
* WireGuard / VPN protocols: Similar to IPsec, encapsulation overhead makes accurate MTU discovery important for throughput and avoiding fragmentation.
* RTP/RTCP (real-time media): Used in VoIP and video conferencing. DPLPMTUD helps size RTP packets to avoid mid-path fragmentation, which is especially harmful for latency-sensitive media.

Details:

* This PR will add a generic Datagram Packetization Layer PMTU Discovery core in `subsys/net/ip/dplpmtud.[ch]`. The new code keeps per-path DPLPMTUD state such as the validated PLPMTU, probe size, retry counters, and search bounds required by RFC 8899.

* It also adds a transport-facing API for the generic DPLPMTUD subsystem. Transports can now create a path handle, query the current validated PLPMTU, request probe sizes, and report probe sent, probe acked, and probe lost events back to the core.

* Extend the existing no-fragment socket and packet handling so UDP transports can request no-fragment behavior on a per-datagram basis. This avoids transport code having to toggle socket state around probe sends and provides a cleaner foundation for generic DPLPMTUD probes.

* Refactor QUIC to use the generic DPLPMTUD subsystem for path MTU search state, probe bookkeeping, and validated payload size management. QUIC keeps transport-specific responsibilities such as building PING+PADDING probes and confirming them through ACK and loss processing.

* Add generic DPLPMTUD tests, and convert QUIC tests when needed

title: net: quic: Re-advertise flow control limits on loss
body:
MAX_DATA and MAX_STREAM_DATA carry the most recent flow-control limit, but unlike STREAM frames they were not retransmitted when lost. If such an update was lost while a peer was flow-control blocked, the peer had already sent STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED for the stale limit (and does not repeat it), so the window was never reopened and the connection deadlocked. This was seen under packet loss in the net.quic retransmission test, which hung indefinitely.

Make quic_detect_lost_packets_locked() report whether any in-flight packet was declared lost, and when so re-advertise the current connection MAX_DATA and per-stream MAX_STREAM_DATA after the ACK is processed (RFC 9000 Section 13.3). Streams are snapshotted under contexts_lock and the updates are sent with the lock released, matching handle_stream_data_blocked_frame().

Tested with tests/net/lib/quic (net.quic) under 10% packet drop on native_sim and qemu_x86; the retransmission test now completes.

title: ci: compliance: add support for loading linters from directory
body:
The compliance_check.py is becoming increasingly complex as more linters are
added, and the number of shared utilities and globals grows.

Auto-load all compliance linter modules from the compliance/ sub-directory.
Each module is expected to define one or more ComplianceTest subclasses,
which are auto-discovered by the inheritors() walk used by the runner.

Introduce scripts/ci/compliance/_context.py as a shared namespace for
runtime globals (GIT_TOP, COMMIT_RANGE) that linter modules in the
compliance/ directory need but which are only available after _main()
runs.

The loader in check_compliance.py now loads _context.py first (before
any linter module) and registers it in sys.modules as
'_compliance_context'.  _main() populates the context immediately after
setting its own globals.

_context.py now exposes all symbols that linter modules need,
split into two categories:

  Static symbols — populated by the loader before any linter module
  is imported (ComplianceTest, EndTest, get_files, get_shas, git,
  get_set_from_file, zephyr_doc_detail_builder, ZEPHYR_BASE, magic).
  Safe to use at class-definition time.

  Dynamic symbols — populated by _main() after argument parsing
  (GIT_TOP, COMMIT_RANGE). Must only be accessed inside method bodies.

The loader (_load_compliance_linters) now populates all static symbols
into _ctx immediately after registering _context.py in sys.modules,
before any linter module is imported.

The canonical pattern for a new linter module is now:

  import _compliance_context as _ctx

  class MyChecker(_ctx.ComplianceTest):
      doc = _ctx.zephyr_doc_detail_builder("...")

      def run(self):
          for f in _ctx.get_files():
              ...

This PR moves a few of the linters with the goal of moving everything out in the next step.

This PR includes two improvements to the VOCS (Volume Offset Control Service) client:

1. **CCC Auto Discover**: Replace the hardcoded CCC handle assumption (`attr->handle + 2`) with `BT_GATT_AUTO_DISCOVER_CCC_HANDLE` to properly discover the CCC descriptor.
