title: Coredump smp thread support
body:
Enable MEMORY_DUMP_THREADS coredump mode on SMP platforms and add ARM64 (Cortex-A) support for thread stack capture. The
  coredump_threads test is updated for SMP stability and verified on versalnet_apu/amd_versalnet_apu/smp hardware.

  Motivation

  DEBUG_COREDUMP_MEMORY_DUMP_THREADS was previously restricted to uniprocessor builds (depends on !SMP), so SMP systems
  could not dump all thread stacks and metadata after a fatal error. ARM64 also lacked the arch hooks needed for THREADS
  mode (ARCH_SUPPORTS_COREDUMP_THREADS, arch_coredump_stack_ptr_get()).

  Changes

  arch: arm64 — THREADS mode support

  * Select ARCH_SUPPORTS_COREDUMP_THREADS and ARCH_SUPPORTS_COREDUMP_STACK_PTR for CPU_CORTEX_A.
  * Implement arch_coredump_stack_ptr_get() using thread->callee_saved.sp_elx (saved EL1 SP from context switch). For the
  faulting thread, callee_saved is stale, so the full stack allocation is dumped (conservative and correct).

  subsys: debug — SMP support for MEMORY_DUMP_THREADS

  * Remove !SMP dependency from DEBUG_COREDUMP_MEMORY_DUMP_THREADS and DEBUG_COREDUMP_THREADS_METADATA.
  * On SMP, walk _kernel.threads under z_thread_monitor_lock taken via k_spin_trylock(): this stabilizes the list against
  concurrent thread create/exit on other CPUs while avoiding a self-deadlock if the crashing CPU already holds the lock.
  If the lock is contended or held, fall back to a bounded lock-free walk (racy read of one entry beats losing the whole
  dump). The walk is capped at a fixed sanity bound as insurance against a corrupted/cyclic list.
  * Dump ISR stacks for all CPUs (CONFIG_MP_MAX_NUM_CPUS), not only cpus[0].
  * On SMP, select THREAD_MONITOR instead of DEBUG_THREAD_INFO (not SMP-safe: K_CURR_THREAD reflects only 
  cpus[0].current). Document this in Kconfig help.

  tests: coredump_threads — SMP enablement and stability

  * Keep the existing CONFIG_DEBUG_COREDUMP_MEMORY_DUMP_THREADS filter (runs broadly, skips cleanly on unsupported 
  platforms) and add versalnet_apu/amd_versalnet_apu/smp to integration_platforms so the new SMP path is exercised in CI 
  without narrowing overall platform coverage.
  * Fix SMP test stability:
    * Replace busy-loop k_sem_take(K_NO_WAIT) + k_sleep(0) with blocking k_sem_take(K_MSEC(...)) to avoid IPI storms 
  during coredump.
    * Use atomic_cas so only one thread calls k_panic().
    * Override k_sys_fatal_error_handler() to return only for K_ERR_KERNEL_PANIC (allows k_thread_join() to complete);
  halt on other fault types.
    * Increase STACK_SIZE from 1024 to 2048 (SMP blocking path needs more stack).

  Testing

  Ran tests/subsys/debug/coredump_threads on real versalnet_apu/amd_versalnet_apu/smp hardware (4-core Cortex-A78):

  * Confirmed all 4 cores boot up (primary + 3 secondaries) before the test triggers the crash.
  * Fault triggered a Kernel panic on CPU 2 (a secondary core), exercising the SMP-crash coredump path this series adds — 
  including the k_spin_trylock()/bounded-walk thread list capture and the per-CPU ISR stack dump.
  * Exactly one ZEPHYR FATAL ERROR occurred, with no cascading panics and no z_arm64_mm_init/MMU re-entry (the IPI-storm

title: net: lib: coap: client: Do not hold lock in callback
body:
An application may hold its own lock while calling `coap_client_req()` (which takes the client lock), and the response callback may in turn take that same lock. Holding the client lock across the callback is then an AB-BA deadlock.

Invoke the callback with the lock released. The `in_callback` atomic already guards the slot, so additionally skip in-callback slots in `get_free_request()` and defer their release on cancel, preventing reuse or reset under a running callback.

title: stm32h7: fix invalid smps-direct + VOS0 combination (Vcore overvoltage)
body:
## Summary

On STM32H74x/H75x boards configured for `power-supply = "smps-direct"`, the
clock-control driver selects voltage scale VOS0 (`ODEN=1`). VOS0 is only valid
when Vcore is supplied through the LDO (DS12919 Table 23; `stm32h7xx_hal_pwr.h`
comment). In smps-direct mode the LDO is bypassed (`LDOEN=0`), so setting
`ODEN=1` drives the SMPS output out of spec — **~1.5 V Vcore measured on an
STM32H755**, above the 1.40 V absolute maximum, risking permanent damage.

This was latent until commit `66fb4e16a0a` correctly started honoring `ODEN`
when requesting VOS0 on H74x/H75x. Before that the ODEN write was silently
dropped and the part stayed at VOS1, so the incompatible board configuration
went unnoticed.

`nucleo_h755zi_q` and `nucleo_h745zi_q` both select `smps-direct` in their
`.dtsi` (factory-default supply config per UM2408 Table 10) while requesting
480 MHz on the M7 — a combination that is simply invalid: smps-direct tops out
at VOS1 / 400 MHz.

## Changes

1. **`drivers: clock_control: stm32h7`** — cap the voltage scale at VOS1 when
   the `pwr` node selects `smps-direct`, instead of unconditionally selecting
   VOS0. The LDO-supplied VOS0 path is unchanged.
2. **`boards: st: nucleo_h745zi_q` / `nucleo_h755zi_q`** — set the *default* M7
   PLL to 400 MHz (`mul-n` 120 → 100, VCO 800 MHz, /P = 400 MHz) so SYSCLK
   matches the voltage scale that the factory-default smps-direct supply
   supports. The H755 `pll2` (FDCAN source) is unchanged.

   This is intentionally the default-hardware value. A board reworked for an
   LDO-supplied Vcore (`power-supply = "ldo"`/`"smps-ldo"`/`"smps-ext-ldo"`)
   can run the M7 at 480 MHz again by restoring `mul-n = <120>` /
   `clock-frequency = <DT_FREQ_M(480)>` in an overlay — the driver change in
   (1) then selects VOS0 automatically for those supplies. A DTS comment in
   each board documents this.

## Test / measurement

Measured on a Nucleo-H755ZI-Q in factory-default smps-direct config (VCAP pin):

| Build | VCAP |
| --- | --- |
| Mass-erased, no firmware | 1.215 V |
| Affected build (VOS0 written in smps-direct) | **1.509 V** (out of spec) |
| With this fix (VOS1 / 400 MHz) | ~1.22 V |

## References

- DS12919 Rev 2 (STM32H755 datasheet) Table 23 — SMPS section has no VOS0 row; VOS1 max = 400 MHz
- `stm32h7xx_hal_pwr.h`: "configuring Voltage Scale 0 is only possible when Vcore is supplied from LDO"
- PR #104749 / commit `66fb4e16a0a` — the fix that exposed this
- ST community confirmation: Nucleo-H7x5ZI-Q factory default is 400 MHz + SMPS-direct; 480 MHz needs an LDO hardware mod

Fixes #108941

title: Introduce mux control API for hardware signal multiplexer
labels: area: PWM;area: Sensors;area: Samples;area: Devicetree;platform: NXP;area: Tests;area: Clock Control;area: Devicetree Binding;platform: ADI;platform: NXP MCU
body:
Introduce a way to control muxes based on DT description through a generic API. 
The DT description is based on Linux: https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/devicetree/bindings/mux/mux-controller.txt 
The API refer to Linux: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/include/linux/mux/consumer.h

### Overview

This PR introduces a generic MUX (multiplexer) device model for Zephyr and adds
initial controller drivers, devicetree bindings, driver integrations, documentation

It includes:

- generic devicetree bindings for MUX controllers and consumers
- a common MUX driver API
- SoC-specific (NXP) and generic (GPIO) MUX controller drivers, plus an external
  analog-switch backend (ADI ADGM3121)
- integration of existing drivers with the MUX device model

Conceptual diagram:
```
   inputs                   mux controller
   in0 ──┐              ┌─────────────────────┐
   in1 ──┤              │   mux_control_set    │
   in2 ──┼──────────────│   / mux_state_apply  │────────▶ output line (outN)
   ...   │              │                     │
   inK ──┘              └─────────────────────┘

```

### Motivation

Signal routing and multiplexer configuration are commonly needed for both SoC
internal routing blocks and external multiplexers. Before this PR/change, support
for this kind of hardware was controller-specific and not expressed through a
common device model;

This PR/change addresses the following problems:

- no common API for configuring and querying MUX controllers
- no generic devicetree model for MUX consumers
- On different chips, the MUX devices used can vary. For IPs that require MUX configuration, since there's no MUX driver model available, users must distinguish between them based on the chip model

This PR introduces a reusable MUX device model so drivers can describe routing in
devicetree and configure it through a common interface.

### Design Details

This PR adds the following building blocks.

#### 1. Devicetree bindings

Add generic MUX bindings:

- `mux-controller.yaml`
- `mux-consumer.yaml`

Add controller-specific bindings:

- `nxp,inputmux.yaml`
- `nxp,trgmux.yaml`
- `nxp,mcux-xbar.yaml`
- `gpio-mux.yaml`
- `adi,adgm3121.yaml`
- `adi,adgm3121-gpio.yaml`

A consumer node references a mux controller via one of two phandle-array properties:

- mux-controls = <&ctrl addressing-cells>
  Consumer holds a reference to a control line and supplies the state value at runtime. Use when the route changes during operation (e.g. ADC source selection).
- mux-states = <&ctrl addressing-cells state-value>
  The desired state is baked into devicetree. The consumer applies it once at init and never touches it again. Use when integration-time wiring is fixed (e.g. routing a QDEC's phase-A to a specific external pin)

Each controller declares #mux-control-cells / #mux-state-cells so the addressing layout matches the underlying hardware.

For example:
```
trgmux: trgmux@... {
        compatible = "nxp,trgmux";
        #mux-control-cells = <2>;
        #mux-state-cells = <3>;
};

adc-trigger {
        /* device=5, input-slot=1, source=7, fixed in DT */
        mux-states = <&trgmux 5 1 7>;
};

```

#### 2. Generic MUX driver API

Add a common MUX API in `include/zephyr/drivers/mux.h`

The API includes:

Function | Purpose
-- | --
mux_control_set(dev, ctrl, state) | Drive ctrl on dev to the given state. Used by mux-controls consumers.
mux_state_apply(dev, mstate) | Convenience for mux-states consumers — applies the DT-defined state in one call.
mux_state_get(dev, ctrl, *state) | Read back the current state. Optional.
mux_control_disconnect(dev, ctrl) | Physically open/disconnect the addressed control line. Orthogonal to routing — it does not select a route, it opens the line. Optional.

**Disconnect axis.** `mux_control_disconnect()` is orthogonal to routing: instead of
selecting a route, it drives the addressed control line into its open/off state; a
later `mux_control_set()` reconnects it. How the open state is reached is
backend-specific — a dedicated enable gate (e.g. the `gpio-mux` optional
`enable-gpios`, or an external switch's enable pin) or the all-open state of a
switch array. Backends that cannot reach an open state (e.g. a plain GPIO select
bus with no enable line) leave the op unimplemented and it returns `-ENOSYS`.

#### 3. Controller drivers

Add the following MUX controller drivers:

- NXP `INPUTMUX`
- NXP `XBAR`
- NXP `TRGMUX`
- Generic `gpio-mux` — a select bus driven by GPIOs (state encoded as a binary
  pattern across the lines), with an optional `enable-gpios` property that adds
  `mux_control_disconnect()` support
- ADI `ADGM3121` — external DPDT MEMS analog switch exposed as a MUX controller,
  supporting both SPI (`adi,adgm3121`) and parallel-GPIO (`adi,adgm3121-gpio`)
  control modes; `mux_control_disconnect()` opens all switches

These cover SoC routing peripherals, generic GPIO-driven muxes, and external
analog switches.

#### 4. Driver integration

Convert existing drivers to use the MUX device model instead of controller-specific
handling:

- `qdec_mcux`
- `qdc_mcux`
- `eqdc_mcux`
- `pwm_mcux_ctimer`
- `pwm_mcux_sctimer`

This allows these drivers to consume MUX routing information from devicetree
through the generic MUX API.

title: kernel: guard primitives with CHECKIF instead of __ASSERT
body:
## Summary
Standardise the kernel's caller-error and illegal-context checks on the `CHECKIF()` macro, replacing the mix of `__ASSERT()` and open-coded checks.
Behaviour is governed by the existing "Error checking behavior for CHECK macro" choice.

## Motivation

Misuse such as calling a blocking primitive from an ISR was guarded by `__ASSERT()`, which is compiled out in common builds. The checks never fired and real bugs shipped.
`CHECKIF()` lets the same condition:
- assert under `CONFIG_ASSERT_ON_ERRORS`,
- k_panic() / return an error under the default `CONFIG_RUNTIME_ERROR_CHECKS`,
- compile out under `CONFIG_NO_RUNTIME_CHECKS`.

Under the shipped default (`RUNTIME_ERROR_CHECKS`) these checks are now active, catching the misuse at the call site with no debug build required.
Production builds should set `CONFIG_NO_RUNTIME_CHECKS=y` to regain the size and performance of the kernel.

## What's included
- Illegal context (panic): every pend-capable primitive panics when called from an ISR with `timeout != K_NO_WAIT`, unconditionally ISR-forbidden blocking APIs panic on any ISR use.
- Illegal argument checks now return error instead of `__ASSERT()`.
- Each check runs before the primitive's spinlock is taken.

Behaviour changes
- `k_poll()` and `k_thread_join()` now permit ISR callers when `timeout == K_NO_WAIT` matching the other pending primitives.
- Default (`RUNTIME_ERROR_CHECKS`) builds gain a small text increase from the panic/return branches. `CONFIG_NO_RUNTIME_CHECKS` removes them entirely.

title: tracing: Configurable init level
body:
The tracing backend initialized at a fixed `APPLICATION` level. Make the `SYS_INIT` level (`TRACING_INIT_LEVEL`) and priority (`TRACING_INIT_PRIORITY`) configurable so tracing can come up earlier and capture more of the boot sequence.

The earliest level is `PRE_KERNEL_2` (sync tracing only — async needs the kernel for its drainer thread), and it requires a priority above the system timer (`SYSTEM_CLOCK_INIT_PRIORITY`) so the cycle counter is live and event timestamps are valid. The defaults (`APPLICATION`, priority 0) preserve the previous behavior.

The kernel already calls `sys_trace_sys_init_enter/exit` around every `SYS_INIT` and device init, but the CTF backend stubbed them out. Implement them so per-init timing is captured.

Record the device name when the entry is a device, so the event is self-describing in any CTF reader. Bare `SYS_INIT` entries have no runtime name, so the `init_fn` pointer is recorded instead for offline resolution. The init level and result are included as well.

title: drivers: timer: add NXP RTC (rtc_jdp) system timer
labels: area: Kernel;area: Counter;area: Timer;platform: NXP;area: Tests;platform: NXP MCU;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
## Summary

Add a Zephyr system timer driver for the NXP RTC (`rtc_jdp`) IP on the MCXE31x family, letting the RTC serve as the kernel tick source. Because the RTC keeps counting across all low-power states, it works as a low-power system timer with no companion timer. The RTC counter driver already exists; this PR adds the system-timer role on the same IP plus the arbitration so the two roles coexist.

## Design

It is a chosen-selected singleton (enabled via `zephyr,system-timer` -> an `nxp,rtc-jdp` node, like `mcux_lptmr_timer.c`), tickless against the RTC's single absolute compare register (RTCVAL), with the free-running 32-bit counter as the cycle counter. A RTCVAL write synchronizes into the slow RTC clock domain and sets `INV_RTC` while in progress (further writes are ignored), so the driver waits for `INV_RTC` to clear before each write per the reference manual. The scheduling horizon is capped at half the counter range so an absolute compare can never wrap past the counter and look like the past (mirroring `mcux_os_timer.c`/`mcux_gpt_timer.c`). The MCXE31x defconfig disables SysTick and derives the clock rate from the chosen node when this timer is selected (prescaler = 1 -> 32 kHz, 1000 ticks/s). The counter driver yields the RTC instance when it is the chosen system timer so both drivers never bind the same hardware. The role is opt-in; the board default (SysTick + RTC-counter calendar) is unchanged.

## Testing

Validated on `frdm_mcxe31b`: `tests/kernel/timer/timer_api` passes 15/15, and `tests/kernel/timer/timer_behavior` passes with zero drift and zero jitter over 10,000 samples (mean exactly 32 cycles/tick, `late_callbacks = 0`). Default-build regressions confirm SysTick stays the default and the RTC counter still instantiates when the RTC is not the system timer.

title: tracing: ctf: keep 64-bit timestamps monotonic on 32-bit counters
body:
The CTF timestamp helper computed the interval from a fixed bigbang of
0, so timing_cycles_get() returned the raw timing counter value. On
boards whose timing counter is narrower than 64 bits (e.g. a 32-bit
hardware cycle counter) that value wraps back to near zero every time
the counter rolls over, which made the 64-bit nanosecond timestamp jump
backwards. Non-monotonic timestamps crash CTF readers such as
babeltrace2 with "timestamp is less than muxer's last returned
timestamp".

Accumulate the per-call cycle delta into a persistent 64-bit total
before converting to nanoseconds. timing_cycles_get() resolves a single
counter rollover between two readings, so the running total stays
monotonic across wraps as long as no more than one rollover happens
between consecutive traced events. A spinlock protects the shared
accumulator, since the CTF_EVENT macro only took irq_lock, which is not
SMP safe.

Fixes #111651

title: ci: set_assignees: diff manifest/maintainers against PR fork point
body:
The assigner compared the PR's west.yml and MAINTAINERS.yml against the
checked-out base-branch tip. For pull_request_target the working tree is
the base branch HEAD, while pr_west.yml/pr_MAINTAINERS.yml come from the
asynchronously-recomputed pull/<N>/merge ref, whose base can lag well
behind that tip. The diff therefore reported not only the projects/areas
the PR actually changed but also everything that advanced on the base
branch after the PR was created, and added all of those maintainers and
collaborators as reviewers.

Compare instead against the merge ref's first parent (FETCH_HEAD^1), the
base the merge was computed from, so the diff isolates exactly the PR's
own changes regardless of how stale the merge ref is. The workflow now
writes base_west.yml and base_MAINTAINERS.yml from FETCH_HEAD^1 and
passes them via the new --base-manifest and --base-maintainer-file
options. Both options default to the checked-out files when omitted, so
local and manual invocations keep working.

Fixes #110422

title: scripts: checkpatch: recognize __aligned() in declarations
body:
checkpatch reported a false-positive LINE_SPACING "Missing a blank line
after declarations" for local variables declared with __aligned(), e.g.:

	uint32_t eicr, embr, eicr_val;
	uint32_t __aligned(4) data32 = 0;

The LINE_SPACING heuristic decides whether a line is a declaration with
a regex that lets the type absorb trailing modifiers/attributes. But
__aligned was missing from the $Attribute list, so the type matched only
"uint32_t", $Ident then matched "__aligned", and the following "(" did
not match the expected [=,;:[] terminator. The line was therefore not
seen as a declaration and a blank line was demanded after the preceding
one.

Add __aligned to $Attribute, consuming its parenthesized argument
(including one level of nesting such as __aligned(sizeof(x))). This is
the root cause: __aligned(N) is now understood as a type attribute
everywhere, not only in the LINE_SPACING check.

Fixes #110417

title: net: lib: coap: client: Wake poll() when a request is scheduled
body:
`coap_client_schedule_poll()` only gives the `recv` semaphore, which wakes the `recv` thread when it is idle but does not interrupt a `poll()` that is already blocked. A request submitted mid-poll - in particular one whose socket changed after a reconnect - is then not watched until the current `poll()` returns, up to `COAP_PERIODIC_TIMEOUT` later, so its response is invisible for that window.

Write the recv-thread wakeup `eventfd` from `schedule_poll()` so a blocked `poll()` returns at once and the `recv` loop rebuilds `fds[]` with the current socket set. The `eventfd` is the same channel cancellation already uses; the resulting ack-sem pulse is harmless since the cancel path resets it under the cancel mutex before waiting. Update the eventfd documentation to cover the dual use.

title: kernel: obj_core: register object types from a single init point
body:
Each kernel object type that participates in the object core framework
previously supplied its own SYS_INIT routine to initialize its
k_obj_type and to walk its static-object linker section, linking each
object core. These routines were near-identical across 11 object types
and differed only in the type id, the object struct and the obj_core
offset.

Replace that per-type boilerplate with a declarative K_OBJ_TYPE_DEFINE()
macro that emits a const descriptor into a new iterable ROM section, and
walk those descriptors once from a single SYS_INIT in obj_core.c. The
descriptor captures the type storage, type id, obj_core offset, the
static object section bounds and the object stride, which is all the
shared loop needs to initialize and link every statically defined
object.

stack and timer. The non-uniform initializers (thread, mem_slab and the
internal cpu/kernel objects) are left unchanged and will be dealt with

* tests: bluetooth: classic: sim: add L2CAP channel test

Add Bluetooth Classic L2CAP (Logical Link Control and Adaptation Protocol) channel test for the simulation testing infrastructure.

The test validates L2CAP client-server functionality across multiple link modes including basic mode, retransmission mode, flow control mode, enhanced retransmission mode (ERTM), and streaming mode. It uses two simulated Bumble controllers connected via TCP to test client and server roles performing device discovery, connection establishment, SDP service discovery to obtain L2CAP PSM, L2CAP channel connection, data transmission, and disconnection.

* tests: bluetooth: classic: sim: add L2CAP echo test

Add Bluetooth Classic L2CAP echo request/response test for the simulation testing infrastructure.

The test validates L2CAP echo functionality by testing the echo request and echo response commands defined in the L2CAP specification. It uses two simulated Bumble controllers connected via TCP to test bidirectional echo operations between devices.

The test also validates error handling for invalid echo response operations, including checks for invalid identifiers and buffer states. Both devices perform device discovery, connection establishment, echo command exchanges, and graceful disconnection.

* tests: bluetooth: classic: sim: add L2CAP connectionless test

Add Bluetooth Classic L2CAP connectionless channel test for the simulation testing infrastructure.

The test validates L2CAP connectionless data transmission functionality by testing the connectionless channel operations defined in the L2CAP specification. It uses two simulated Bumble controllers connected via TCP to test bidirectional connectionless data exchange between devices.

The test suite includes three scenarios:

1. Basic send/receive: Validates single-PSM connectionless data transmission where Device 1 sends to Device 2, and Device 2 replies. Tests BR/EDR inquiry, ACL connection establishment, and PSM verification.

2. Multiple PSM: Tests simultaneous registration of multiple PSMs (`0x1001` and `0x1003`) plus a wildcard callback (PSM 0). Validates correct delivery to PSM-specific callbacks and verifies wildcard callback receives frames for any PSM.

3. Register/unregister errors: Validates error handling including double-registration (`-EEXIST`), unregistering already-unregistered callbacks (`-ENOENT`), and NULL callback handling (`-EINVAL`).

Both devices perform device discovery, connection establishment, connectionless data transmission using `bt_l2cap_br_connless_send()`, and graceful disconnection. The test uses proper buffer management with `BT_L2CAP_CONNLESS_RESERVE` for headroom allocation.

title: bluetooth: classic: l2cap: refactor SDU length tracking
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth Classic
body:
Refactor SDU (Service Data Unit) length tracking in Bluetooth Classic L2CAP to use closure-based storage instead of channel state variables.

The change introduces a new l2cap_br_closure structure that extends the base closure with an sdu_len field, allowing SDU length to be stored per-buffer rather than in the channel structure. This eliminates the need for _sdu_total_len tracking in both bt_l2cap_br_chan and bt_l2cap_br_window structures.

title: bluetooth: classic: l2cap: optimize dynamic CID allocation
body:
Optimize the L2CAP BR/EDR dynamic CID allocation by using a static counter to track the last allocated CID instead of always starting from the beginning of the range.

The change introduces a br_cid_next array that maintains the position of the next CID to allocate for each connection. The allocation now searches from the last allocated position through the range, wrapping around if needed. This reduces the search time for available CIDs in scenarios with multiple active channels by avoiding repeated scans of already-allocated CIDs at the start of the range.

Additionally, this modification has the advantage of preventing a recently disconnected CID from being assigned to a new channel. This avoids data from the channel disconnection process being sent to this newly assigned channel.

The allocation still validates that CIDs are not in use by checking against bt_l2cap_br_lookup_rx_cid() before assignment, maintaining the same correctness guarantees as the previous implementation.

title: bluetooth: classic: l2cap: add state validation in receive path
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth Classic;backport v3.7-branch;backport v4.3-branch;backport v4.4-branch
body:
* bluetooth: classic: l2cap: add state transition for fixed channel

Add proper state management to Bluetooth Classic L2CAP fixed channel connection by setting the channel state to `CONNECTED` before invoking the connected callback.

The change ensures that fixed channels follow the same state transition pattern as other L2CAP channel types. When a fixed channel is connected, the state is now explicitly set to `BT_L2CAP_CONNECTED` before calling the channel's connected callback.

The changes ensure the channel state accurately reflects its lifecycle status.

* bluetooth: classic: l2cap: use chan state to manage fixed channel

Refactor the fixed channel accept functions to use channel state for direct check if the channel is available instead of checking `conn` field of channel. And also refactor the fixed channel accept functions to use connection index for direct lookup instead of iterating through the pool arrays.

The changes affect the L2CAP BR signaling channel, connectionless channel, and SMP BR channel accept functions.

The functions now check if the channel is in the `DISCONNECTED` state before accepting a new connection, returning `-EBUSY` if the channel is not idle. This ensures proper channel state validation and prevents reuse of channels that are still in use.

Additionally, instead of searching through the entire pool to find an available channel context, the code now uses `bt_conn_index()` to directly access the corresponding entry in the pool array.

The L2CAP BR fixed channel connection now also sets the channel state to CONNECTING, ensuring proper state transitions.

* bluetooth: classic: l2cap: add state validation in receive path

Add state validation check in the L2CAP BR/EDR receive path to ensure channels are in a valid connected state before processing incoming data.

The change adds a check after the fixed channel validation to verify that the channel state is at least BT_L2CAP_CONNECTED before proceeding with data reception. If the channel is in an earlier state (CONNECTING or DISCONNECTED), an error is logged and the packet is dropped.

This prevents potential issues from processing data on channels that are not yet fully established or are in the process of being torn down, improving the robustness of the L2CAP receive path.

Fixes: #113698

title: samples: bluetooth: l2cap_coc: Fix missing advertising, scan filters, and bugs
body:
This commit fixes several severe structural bugs in the l2cap_coc samples:

 **Acceptor Fixes:**
 - Adds connectable advertising (`BT_LE_ADV_CONN_FAST_1`) so the device is actually visible to the Initiator over the air.
 - Auto-restarts advertising on disconnect using a `k_work` item to prevent `-ENOMEM` collisions.
 - Fixes a severe memory corruption hard-fault by allocating the `l2cap_chans` array as `bt_l2cap_le_chan` instead of the base `bt_l2cap_chan`.
 - Configures `CONFIG_BT_DEVICE_NAME` in `prj.conf` and uses it in the advertising array instead of hardcoding magic strings.
 
 **Initiator Fixes:**
- Adds `bt_data_parse` scan filters to prevent the Initiator from blindly connecting to random unrelated LE devices (e.g., phones, TVs).
- Replaces magic numbers for device name array sizes with the `MAX_NAME_LEN` macro.
- Fixes a buffer overflow bug where the `NET_BUF_POOL_FIXED_DEFINE` pool lacked space for L2CAP headers by using the `BT_L2CAP_SDU_BUF_SIZE()` helper macro.
- Fixes an `-EINVAL` reference leak by correctly clearing the `default_conn` pointer on disconnect.
- Fixes an L2CAP packet corruption race condition by statically spawning the `send_task` thread in `main()` instead of dynamically re-spawning it on every reconnect.

title: kernel: dynamic: combine thread state checks in stack free
body:
z_impl_k_thread_stack_free() tested _THREAD_DUMMY and _THREAD_DEAD
with two separate z_is_thread_state_set() calls combined with a
logical OR. z_is_thread_state_set() returns (thread_state & state)

bits ORed into the mask. Collapse them into one call; this is

title: kernel: thread: factor out thread name initialization
body:
The strncpy + NUL-termination + arch_thread_name_set() hook sequence
behind CONFIG_THREAD_NAME was duplicated in z_impl_k_thread_name_set()
and z_setup_new_thread(). Extract it into a single set_thread_name()
helper and call it from both places, removing the duplicated logic and
the risk of the two copies drifting apart.

The helper treats a NULL name as "clear the name" (writes an empty
string), matching the previous z_setup_new_thread() behavior; the
k_thread_name_set() path always passed a non-NULL string, so its
behavior is unchanged.

title: kernel: timeslicing: avoid recomputing the slice size on rearm
body:
z_time_slice() computed z_time_slice_size(curr) to decide whether the
slice had expired, and then z_time_slice_reset() computed it a second
time to rearm the slice timeout. Cache the value instead: split the
rearm body into a slice_reset(slice_size) helper (z_time_slice_reset()
becomes a thin wrapper that still computes the size for its other
callers) and pass the already-known size from z_time_slice().

The size is still only computed when the slice has actually expired, so
the per-tick fast path is unchanged. In the CONFIG_TIMESLICE_PER_THREAD
case the expiry handler runs with the scheduler lock dropped and may
change the thread's slice configuration, so the cached value is
recomputed after the handler returns; behavior is therefore unchanged.

title: tests: kernel: sys_sem: skip basic_sem_test without userspace
body:
## Summary

`test_basic_sem_test` checks the argument validation performed by the
userspace `sys_sem_init()` (it returns `-EINVAL` for invalid parameters).
The supervisor-mode `sys_sem_init()` is a thin `k_sem` wrapper that performs
no such validation, so the test was guarded with `#ifdef CONFIG_USERSPACE`
and compiled out on non-userspace builds.

Because the case is compiled out, the test image of a non-userspace build
never reports it, while twister still expects it from its source scan of the
test file. The result is a spurious
`WARNING - A None status detected ... sys_sem.basic_sem_test` for that case
on platforms built without userspace.

## Change

Keep the test always compiled and `ztest_test_skip()` at runtime when
`CONFIG_USERSPACE` is not enabled. The case is now reported as *skipped* on
non-userspace builds and runs normally with userspace, so no false None
status remains. This matches the documented intent of `CONFIG_TEST_USERSPACE`
that such tests "should still run on those platforms, just with all threads
in supervisor mode".

## Testing

Run on hardware (`kit_pse84_eval/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m33`):

- Non-userspace scenario `kernel.memory_protection.sys_sem.nouser`:
  14/14 test cases, `basic_sem_test` reported as **skipped**, no
  None-status warning.
- Userspace scenario `kernel.memory_protection.sys_sem`: 14/14 test cases,
  `basic_sem_test` **passed** (behavior unchanged).

title: modem: cellular: add operational statistics
body:
Adds an optional operational-statistics API to the cellular driver, implemented
in `modem_cellular`, for link-health telemetry on fielded devices.

`cellular_get_stats()` returns a typed `struct cellular_stats` of cumulative
counters (`outage_ms`, `registration_losses`, `link_drops`, `command_failures`,

title: bluetooth: l2cap: optimize LE dynamic CID allocation
body:
Optimize the L2CAP LE dynamic CID allocation by using a per-connection counter to track the next CID to allocate instead of always starting from the beginning of the range.

The change introduces a `le_cid_index_next` array that maintains the position of the next CID index to allocate for each connection. The allocation now searches from the last allocated position through the range, wrapping around if needed. This reduces the search time for available CIDs in scenarios with multiple active channels by avoiding repeated scans of already-allocated CIDs at the start of the range.

Additionally, this modification has the advantage of delaying the reassignment of a recently disconnected CID to a new channel. This makes it less likely that data from the channel disconnection process is sent to the newly assigned channel. Note that it is not a guarantee: if the cursor happens to point at the index of a CID whose channel has just been freed, the next allocation still returns that CID immediately.

The allocation still validates that CIDs are not in use by checking against `l2cap_le_lookup_rx_cid()` before assignment, maintaining the same correctness guarantees as the previous implementation.

Also add checks to following three functions, including `l2cap_accept()`, `bt_l2cap_ecred_chan_connect()`, and
`bt_l2cap_chan_connect()`.

title: boards: shields: nrf7002eb2: drop spurious nRF54LM20 pin workarounds
body:
The nRF54LM20 SoC overlay for the `nrf7002eb2` shield redirected the
application console from UART20 to UART30 and deleted `button_3`/`sw3`.
Both were copied from the nRF54L15 overlay, where they resolve **real**
conflicts:

- **nRF54L15 DK**: UART20 uses P1.4–P1.7 and `led1` sits on P1.10, all of
  which are routed to the nRF7002 EB II expansion header (the shield
  SPI-CS lands on P1.10). The redirect/delete is justified.

None of these conflicts exist on the **nRF54LM20 DK**:

| Signal | Pin | On the EB II expansion header? |
|---|---|---|
| UART20 TX/RX/RTS/CTS | P1.16 / P1.17 / P1.18 / P1.19 | No |
| Shield SPI-CS (spi22) | P3.2 | — |
| `button_3` / `sw3` | P0.5 | No |

The conflict only ever existed on the downstream pre-production kit, not
on the production DK.

## Change

- Remove the workaround from `boards/shields/nrf7002eb2/nrf54lm20.overlay`
  so UART20 (VCOM1) stays the default console — matching standard
  nRF54LM20 DK behaviour — and all buttons remain usable. SPI and GPIOs
  continue to come from the root overlay.
- Scope the shield doc's "Console and UART impact" section to the
  nRF54L15 DK and note that the nRF54LM20 DK is unaffected.
- The workaround shipped in v4.4.0, so add a 4.5 migration note telling
  existing nRF54LM20 DK shield users to move their serial terminal from
  VCOM0 back to VCOM1.

The nRF54L15 overlay is intentionally left unchanged; its conflict is real.

title: drivers: hdlc_rcp_if: spi: add CONFIG_HDLC_RCP_IF_SPI_DEFERRED_INIT
body:
Some RCP modules (e.g. IW61X) require an asynchronous firmware load
sequence before the 15.4 SPI interface becomes operational.
The firmware is uploaded via a separate transport (e.g. BT UART H4),

Without this option, Zephyr's net_if_post_init() automatically brings up
the OpenThread interface at boot, before the RCP is ready, causing Spinel
command failures and NULL dereferences.

Add CONFIG_HDLC_RCP_IF_SPI_DEFERRED_INIT (default n, preserves existing
behavior) which:
- hdlc_iface_init(): skip ieee802154_init(), set NET_IF_NO_AUTO_START
  to block net_if_post_init() from starting the interface
  before the RCP is ready.
- hdlc_rcp_if_spi_init(): skip SPI IRQ arming and RCP reset,
- hdlc_deferred_init(): arms the SPI IRQ and clears NET_IF_NO_AUTO_START.

title: net: ipv6: send unsolicited Neighbor Advertisements
body:
Add `CONFIG_NET_IPV6_UNSOLICITED_NA`. When enabled, the node multicasts an
unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement (RFC 4861 chapter 7.2.6) to the
all-nodes address, with the Override flag set and the target set to the
address, when one of its unicast addresses is added or passes Duplicate
Address Detection. This is the IPv6 counterpart of gratuitous ARP: it lets
neighbors that still hold an entry correct a stale link-layer address
without waiting for Neighbor Unreachability Detection. A neighbor that has
already dropped its entry ignores it (RFC 4861 chapter 7.2.5).

title: net: sockets: Fix incorrect connection drop in zsock_accept()
body:
zsock_accept() included some obsolete code related to the old TCP stack
behavior, which caused that incoming TCP connections that were already
closed generated an error instead of having FD assigned. This made the
server side unreliable, as it prevented the server from reading out data
received on such connections in case of late accept().

Also the accepted/closed net context flags are not set/checked anywhere
else in the network stack, so there's no need to use them at the socket
layer anymore.

Fixes #112419

title: net: mdns: Rejoin multicast groups when interface comes back up
body:
When a network interface is brought fully down (for example by the connection manager after an Ethernet cable is removed) the network stack leaves the mDNS multicast groups. When the interface comes back up the stack only rejoins groups that are still marked in use, so the mDNS groups are not restored automatically.

The NET_EVENT_IF_UP handler only rejoined the IPv4 IGMP group, and did so using a fragile net_if_get_by_iface() - 1 index into the per-family context array. The IPv6 MLD group (ff02::fb) was never rejoined, so after a link down/up cycle the responder stopped receiving queries and the incoming packets were dropped at the IPv6 input as being destined to an unjoined multicast address.

Rejoin both the IPv4 and IPv6 mDNS groups on NET_EVENT_IF_UP. The well-known group addresses are constant, so construct them directly with create_ipv4_addr()/create_ipv6_addr() instead of indexing the context array.

Add a regression test that probes the responder, cycles the interface down and up, and verifies the responder still answers afterwards. The test fails without this fix and passes with it.

The PR has fixes for mDNS resolver and responder, also LLMNR responder is fixed. LLMNR resolver does not join a multicast group.

Fixes #112266

title: net: dns: Deprecate LLMNR support
body:
Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR, RFC 4795) is being phased out. Microsoft is retiring the protocol and it is disabled by default on modern Windows for security reasons. mDNS is the modern replacement and Zephyr already provides both an mDNS resolver and responder.

Deprecate the LLMNR resolver and responder Kconfig options by selecting DEPRECATED and marking the prompts with [DEPRECATED]. Enabling either option now emits a deprecation warning when the Kconfig tree is parsed. The feature still works during the deprecation period; per the API lifecycle policy it can be removed after two full releases (5.0 at the earliest).

Document the deprecation in the 4.5 release notes and migration guide, pointing users to mDNS (CONFIG_MDNS_RESOLVER / CONFIG_MDNS_RESPONDER).

title: fs: virtiofs: validate READ response length before returning
body:
virtiofs_read() validated only error/used_len but passed expected_len=-1
to virtiofs_validate_response(), skipping the length check. The host-
supplied out_header.len was then used to compute the return value; a
value smaller than sizeof(out_header) underflowed, and a value larger
than the read buffer would misrepresent the bytes read.

Guard against both cases before returning.

title: net: ipv6: add neighbor cache clear helper
body:
Add `net_ipv6_nbr_clear_cache`, which removes all non-static IPv6 neighbor
cache entries of an interface. It is meant to be called when the interface
link goes down so that the entries are re-resolved on link-up;
the re-resolution Neighbor Solicitation carries the Source Link-Layer
Address option (RFC 4861 chapter 7.2.2), letting a peer that dropped
its entry for this node relearn it. This is the IPv6 counterpart of
clearing the ARP cache on link down.

Call `net_ipv6_nbr_clear_cache`() from the interface-down path so that stale
IPv6 neighbor entries are dropped when the link goes down and re-resolved
once it is back.

title: tracing: Add existed object check in SYS_TRACK_LIST_PREPEND
body:
The SYS_TRACK_LIST_PREPEND unconditionally prepends an object in the list without checking if the object is already in the list.

This is problematic and will corrupt the list if an object is initiallized multiple times.

For example if you define an event with the macro: K_EVENT_DEFINE(my_event)

and then you also initialize the object in code:
k_event_init(&my_event)

This will corrupt the list. Even though you don't need to run the k_event_init after you statically define the event it is not explicitely forbitten either so it should not corrupt anything.

To fix that I updated the SYS_TRACK_LIST_PREPEND to check if an object is already in the list and only prepend it if it does not exist.


If you want to test this I also created a minimal sample that I run with native_sim 64 that show cases the problem.
If you run this sample without my PR the list will get corrupted immediately after the first call to the k_event_init.
[obj_tracking_event_poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29597418/obj_tracking_event_poc.zip)

title: tests: drivers: uart: async_api: give kit_pse84_eval DUT own clock divider
body:
The `uart_async_api` test overlay for `kit_pse84_eval` assigned the DUT
(`&scb5`) the peripheral clock divider `peri0_group1_16bit_1`, which is
also the divider used by the board console (`&scb2`). The `read_abort`
subtest is the only one that reconfigures the DUT baud rate (to 9600), so
`ifx_cat1_uart_set_baud()` reprograms that shared divider. That
simultaneously dropped the console from 115200 to 9600, corrupting all
subsequent console output and making the device appear to hang partway
through the suite.

Point the DUT at a dedicated, otherwise-unused 16-bit divider
(`peri0_group1_16bit_2`) so baud-rate changes on the DUT no longer disturb
the console. The same fix is applied to the m33 and m55 overlays.

### Testing

Ran `drivers.uart.async_api` on `kit_pse84_eval/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m33` with
twister `--device-testing`:

- Before: the suite locked up during `uart_async_read_abort` — the console
  output was truncated and the harness lost the device.
- After: the console stays alive through `read_abort`; the whole suite runs
  to completion and reports results normally.

body:
Add a clock_monitor back-end for the NXP BASIC Frequency Measurement
(FREQME / fmeas) peripheral on RT5xx / RT6xx / RW6xx SoCs, wrapping
the MCUX SDK fsl_fmeas HAL.

The hardware has no interrupt line, so only MEASURE (one-shot) mode is
supported; completion is polled from a workqueue. The reference window
is HW-fixed at 2^20 reference cycles (window_ns is ignored). Reference
and target clocks are routed through INPUTMUX via the mux subsystem;
the reference rate is queried from clock_control to convert the raw
counter to Hz.

had no help text. Without it, a developer browsing the config has no

title: Bluetooth: Controller: Align PAST sync_offset_us calc with CIS_IND
body:
The `ull_sync_setup_from_sync_transfer()` function computed the adjustment to `sync_offset_us` from the `Connection Event Counter` carried by LL_PERIODIC_SYNC_IND using a signed difference (`conn_event_count - conn_evt_current`) narrowed to `int16_t`. The narrowing conversion of an unsigned subtraction result is implementation-defined, and the resulting arithmetic mixed signed and unsigned types.

Refactor the computation to mirror the CIS_IND LLCP procedure handling of `instant_latency` in `rp_cc_check_instant_by_counter()` and `lp_cc_check_instant()`: compute the difference as an unsigned wrap-safe value `(conn_evt_current - conn_event_count) & 0xFFFF` and dispatch on the `<= 0x7FFF` range test.

Also explicitly handle both directions:
- Reference connection event in the past (peripheral processes the LL_PERIODIC_SYNC_IND at a connection event later than the one indicated by the PDU): deduct the elapsed time from `sync_offset_us`; when the resulting anchor would fall into the past, advance the periodic advertising event counter by the required whole number of periodic advertising intervals.
- Reference connection event in the future: add the remaining time to `sync_offset_us`.

The behavior for a valid signed offset in the range supported by the previous implementation is preserved, while the arithmetic is now portable and matches the CIS_IND pattern.

title: RFC: Add DMX subsystem
body:
This is a proposal to add support for the DMX512 (ESTA E1.11) in Zephyr. If you have been to a theater, concert, or architectural lighting installation anytime in the past 30-ish years, then you have likely been in the presence of one, dozens, or hundreds of DMX devices. DMX receiver devices can be lighting dimmers, LED lights, moving lights, atmospheric effects, and more. Controllers can be lighting consoles, architectural controllers, splitters, network gateways, and etc.

E1.11 is an ANSI standard. It can be downloaded for free here: https://tsp.esta.org/tsp/documents/published_docs.php

I decided to start with just the receiver, as it is more difficult than the transmitter.

### Protocol

The DMX protocol uses a half-duplex RS-485 bus. A bus consists of one controller and many receivers. The most frequent and common packet (the NULL start code packet) contains 512 bytes of data and is sent at a maximum of 44 Hz. Packets begin with a break signal, the mark-after-break (MAB), and then the packet start code (SC). A valid, active DMX signal consists of a non-stop stream of packets.

  ```
     ┌─BREAK─┐ MAB ┌──SC──┐┌─Slot 1─┐┌─Slot 2─┐     ┌─Slot N─┐ MBB ┌─BREAK─┐
     │ ≥88µs │     │ 8N2  ││  8N2   ││  8N2   │ ... │  8N2   │     │ ≥88µs │
 ───┘       └─────┘      ┘└────────┘└────────┘     └────────┘─────┘       └───
    LOW      HIGH  ← 250 kbaud, 1 start + 8 data + 2 stop bits →   LOW
```

### Receiver Data flow
1. The DMX transmitter writes continuously.
2. The backend waits for a framing error or break detection interrupt and reads the first byte (start code).
3. If the break-to-break timings are valid, the subsystem allocates the maximum possible data size for the start code on the `spsc_pbuf`.
4. The backend writes in the bytes with `dmx_rx_byte()`.
5. The slot in `spsc_pbuf` is finalized to the actual final size and the application is notified.
6. The application reads the packet with `dmx_rx_claim()` and then releases it with `dmx_rx_free()`.

Because the packets are quite large (512 bytes), I implemented this with a zero-copy ring buffer (`spsc_pbuf`). Bytes are read straight into the buffer, processed (without moving/copying), and then a pointer is sent to the API consumer.

A DMX receiver device typically needs either a) all of the DMX data slots (512 bytes) or b) only a small subset (~50ish channels for current generation moving lights). On more constrained hardware you might only store the slots that you need, and this was the way to do it for a long time. However, on the modern MCUs supported by Zephyr (typically with 16 kB+ of RAM), it is much simpler to always store the whole packet. This also makes chunked backend implementations (i.e. DMA, PIO, etc.) much easier to implement. Once the actual packet size is known, we reduce the allocation size in the `spsc_pbuf`.

I could not use a single packet struct with a union because `data[]` must be variable size in some packets. So, the consumer gets a header struct with the type (from `dmx_rx_claim()`) and then uses that type to cast the rest of the packet.

This PR implements DMX receiver support using UART ISR. The files and API are structured to allow for a future Async UART backend (which I am working on now) and peripheral-specific backends (i.e. PIO). There are API methods to allow for chunked input (instead of byte-by-byte).

```
  UART HW ──► ISR ──► dmx_rx_byte() ──► spsc_pbuf ──► dmx_rx_claim()
                │         │                  │              │
                │     writes directly        │          returns pointer
                │     into spsc_pbuf    k_sem_give()    to packet in
                │     allocation             │          the buffer
                │                            │              │
           framing error               ┌────────────┐   dmx_rx_free()
           = break detect              │ app thread │   releases slot
                                       └────────────┘
```

### UART ISR Receiver Backend
The UART ISR backend handles the breaks/framing errors differently depending on where it thinks it is in the packet. This validates the DMX timing constraints. Per specification, the first packet sent on the line (or after the last packet times out) is discarded.

Not all UART peripherals detect breaks specifically, so we also detect framing errors as the start of a packet. If a second break/framing error occurs before the minimum timings are met (for the following packet), then it is treated as an error.

There are a few different common schemes that UART peripherals use to handle bytes received after breaks/framing errors. This makes receiving DMX tricky, as we need to save the first byte that is sent after the break. PR #111721 adds a notation to UART peripherals so that this subsystem can understand how to handle the upstream peripheral. Normally, writing a cross-platform DMX receiver would be quite difficult, but Zephyr really makes this attainable.

The UART ISR method validates that the packet rate is valid, which is what is needed for probably 98% of receivers. However, it does not validate the actual break time duration. In practice, this is not necessary unless you are trying to analyze the DMX signal. There are lots of other ways to read a DMX signal (UART + second pin with hardware timer, FPGA, etc.), but this way is definitely the most cross-platform (and only uses 1 pin!).

The NULL start packet (and other packets) can technically be less than 512 slots (although very uncommon now). Since there is no length field, we commit the packets smaller than 512 slots when the next packet starts (this is the standard method of doing this). The SIP packet (will fully implement in a future PR) theoretically solves this, but in practice nobody uses the SIP packet.

```
                 ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
                 │           signal lost            │
                 │          (1.25s timer)           │
                 ▼                                  │
            ┌────────┐   break   ┌────────┐   break (valid timing)
  enable ─► │  IDLE  │ ────────► │  SYNC  │ ──────────────────────┐
            └────────┘           └────────┘                       │
                 ▲                    │                           │
                 │               break (bad timing)               │
                 └────────────────────┘                           │
                 ▲                                                ▼
                 │                                           ┌─────────┐
                 │            break (bad timing)             │  BREAK  │
                 ├───────────────────────────────────────────│(wait SC)│
                 │                                           └─────────┘
                 │                                                 │
                 │                                          clean byte
                 │                                          (start code)
                 │                                                 │
                 │    break (bad timing)   ┌────────┐              ▼
                 └─────────────────────────│  DATA  │◄─────────────┘
                                           │(slots) │
                                           └────────┘
                                             │    │
                          early-commit ──────┘    └────── break (valid timing)
                          (all slots rx'd)                = break-commit
                                │                              │
                                ▼                              ▼
                           ┌────────┐                     ┌─────────┐
                           │  SYNC  │                     │  BREAK  │
                           └────────┘                     └─────────┘
```

### Application API
Applications use these methods to set up the receiver, receive packets, and read the receiver state:
- **`dmx_set_mode(dev, DMX_MODE_INPUT)`:** Set DMX port to input/output (this is intentionally configurable at runtime)
- **`dmx_set_filter(dev, &filter)`:** Configure which start codes to accept
- **`dmx_enable(dev)`**: Start receiving
- **`dmx_disable(dev)`**: Stop receiving
- **`dmx_rx_claim(dev, &hdr, timeout)`**: Wait for a packet to be received and then return a pointer into the ring buffer. Application then looks at `hdr->start_code` and chooses a struct to cast the data to:
  - **`DMX_SC_NULL` (`0x00`):** `struct dmx_null_packet`
  - **`DMX_SC_TEST` (`0x55`):** `struct dmx_test_packet`
  - **`DMX_SC_TEXT` (`0x17`):** `struct dmx_text_packet`
  - **`DMX_SC_UTF8` (`0x90`):** `struct dmx_utf8_packet`
  - **`DMX_SC_MFR` (`0x91`):** `struct dmx_manufacturer_packet`
  - **`DMX_SC_SIP` (`0xCF`):** `struct dmx_sip_packet`
  - **All others:** `struct dmx_raw_packet`
- **`dmx_rx_free(dev, hdr)`**: Release the packet in the ring buffer
- **`dmx_rx_is_receiving(dev)`**: Returns true if packets are being continuously received within timing constraints (this is useful for status LEDs and messages)
- **`dmx_rx_stats_get(dev, &stats)`**: Get packet drop/error counts
- **`dmx_rx_stats_reset(dev)`**: Reset packet drop/error counts

Packet Header (common to all types):
```c
struct dmx_rx_header {
	/** Uptime in milliseconds when the BREAK was detected. */
	uint32_t timestamp;
	/**
	 * 16-bit ones complement additive checksum of all received bytes (start code + slot data)
	 * per ANSI E1.11 Annex D5.5. Usually computed incrementally during reception.
	 */
	uint16_t checksum;
	/** DMX start code of the frame. */
	uint8_t start_code;
};
```

NULL Packet (start code `0x00`):
```c
struct dmx_null_packet {
	/** Common packet header. */
	struct dmx_rx_header hdr;
	/** Number of data slots received (1-512). */
	uint16_t slot_count;
	/** Slot data (slot_count bytes, data[0] = DMX slot 1). */
	uint8_t data[];
};
```

### Backend API
Backends implement these methods in `struct dmx_driver_api`:
- **`set_mode(dev, mode)`**: Configure input/output modes
- **`enable(dev)`**: Configure peripherals, interrupts, and etc. Start receiving.
- **`disable(dev)`**: Stop receiving
- **`is_receiving(dev)`**: Return true if signal present

Backends call these methods to the subsystem:
- **`dmx_rx_begin_frame()`**: Allocate initial `spsc_pbuf` slot
- **`dmx_rx_byte()`**: Receive one byte (and sets up data after start code received)
- **`dmx_rx_bytes()`**: Receive a chunk of bytes (useful for DMA-based backends)
- **`dmx_rx_end_frame()`**: Finalize and commit a frame

### Hardware Testing

I have validated this with physical hardware using an Enttec DMX USB Pro on:
- PL011 (RP2040)
- nRF UARTE (nRF52840)
- STM32 USART (STM32L4)
- NXP LPUART (i.MX RT1060)
- Atmel SAM0 SERCOM (SAMD21)
- Espressif UART (ESP32-S3)

### Future Work

Followup PRs will implement:
- Async UART (DMA) receiver backend
- DMX SIP packet validation (although rarely used, this will make the receiver fully compliant)
- DMX transmitter
- Tests
- RDM responder
- RDM controller
- E1.31 Streaming ACN (sACN): DMX over network

### Associated PRs

This PR requires the following:
- #111721

This PR led to the following bugfixes for serial peripherals:
- #111222
- #111726
- #112717
- #114810
- #114911

---

This has been an exciting project to work on! I'm not aware of any other fully cross-platform DMX peripheral frameworks. Once I get the Async UART backend to work, there will truly be a performant option for every MCU that Zephyr supports.

Disclaimer: While I am a member of the ESTA Control Protocols Working Group (CPWG), this work was produced independently from ESTA.

title: fixes to failing tests with llvm/riscv
labels: area: Kernel;area: RISCV;area: Tests;area: Architectures;Hotfix;area: Userspace
body:
Fix two miscompilation issues exposed by building RISC-V with the LLVM toolchain, both causing kernel.threads.apis to hang forever on qemu_riscv32e (expected-fault tests looped in the fatal error handler).

- z_riscv_fatal_error() may legitimately return when a fatal error is handled (e.g. ztest expected faults), and isr.S already handles that return path. The CODE_UNREACHABLE hint made LLVM emit a trapping unimp instruction on the return path, causing an endless illegal-instruction fatal error loop. GCC builds only worked by chance.

- clang silently miscompiles any global variable named tp while the register ... __asm__("tp") declaration from syscall.h is in scope (loses static linkage, section attribute, and initializer). This broke ZTEST_DMEM placement in the userspace partition, causing PMP faults. Use __builtin_thread_pointer() instead, which gcc and clang both lower to a plain register read.

title: drivers: virtio: allow enumerating an unused zero-size virtqueue

The virtio device enumeration asserts that every advertised queue size is

## Subsystem: Drivers / PCIe Host

### Problem Statement & Architectural Context
The current PCIe host shell module implementation (`drivers/pcie/host/shell.c`) is entirely passive. While it permits early boot device discovery, configuration dump reading, and capability tree parsing via `pcie ls`, it lacks an interactive mechanism to perform real-time, runtime configuration updates or write instrumentations from the command canvas.

This presents a development bottleneck during pre-silicon platform validation (e.g., when debugging complex ARM-FPGA SoC interconnects such as Intel/Altera or AMD/Xilinx AXI-to-PCIe bridges) where engineers need to rapidly toggle interface control registers, force-enable bus-master states, or dynamically alter memory maps without modifying code and repeatedly recompiling the firmware image target.

### Proposed Feature Enhancements
This patch introduces a runtime interactive sub-command wrapper: 
`pcie write <bus:device.function> <register_word_offset> <32bit_hex_data>`

**Underlying Execution Steps:**
1. Intercepts terminal panel strings, isolating target registers and data components.
2. Checks configuration space link responsiveness to prevent system lockups.
3. Invokes the underlying hardware abstraction layer function `pcie_conf_write()` natively over the specified index.
4. Executes an immediate configuration read-back loop pass to verify bit-latch and alignment stability.

### Verification Matrix
- **Compilation Toolsuite:** Zephyr SDK 1.0.1 (`aarch64-zephyr-elf-gcc`)
- **Validation Architecture:** Out-of-tree workspace layout running on top of a 64-bit multi-core simulator (`qemu_cortex_a53`).
- **Code Standards Compliance:** Evaluated cleanly via `checkpatch.pl` linting scripts, logging `0 errors, 0 warnings, 446 lines checked`.
- **Live Functional Logs:** Successfully toggled the Bus Master Enable (BME) and Memory Space Enable (MSE) bits inside the Command/Status register from `0x00000000` to `0x00000006` dynamically with real-time verification feedback.

title: drivers: pcie: controller: ecam: validate bus range bounds
body:
## Subsystem: Drivers / PCIe Controller

The generic Enhanced Configuration Access Mechanism (ECAM) host bridge controller driver (`drivers/pcie/controller/pcie_ecam.c`) accepts raw 32-bit `pcie_bdf_t` coordinate inputs natively within its read and write routines with zero validation parameters. 

On hardware configurations or virtual motherboard platforms mapping multi-bus topologies, passing an out-of-bounds bus index variable can cause a critical bit-field overflow. Because of automatic truncation masking in downstream macro layouts, raw boundary spillage shifts overflow bits into upper address coordinates. The driver then executes memory transactions over unallocated regions inside the ECAM window, causing the hardware to return unhandled dummy data blocks (`0xFFFFFFFF`) or leak address spaces silently, completely masking critical software configuration or hardware mapping flaws instead of trapping the failure.

### Proposed Architecture Fix
This patch introduces strict `__ASSERT` parameter validation gates directly at the thresholds of both primary configuration read and write device instance handlers:
- `__ASSERT((bdf & 0xFF000000U) == 0, "%s: Corrupted BDF token bounds detected", __func__);`

By checking the raw bits before any bitwise shifts or extraction macros are applied, this patch successfully halts out-of-bounds parameter execution at the lowest hardware choke point without interfering with multi-bus hierarchies conforming to the PCI Express Base Specification.

### Verification Matrix & Test Strategy
- **Compiler Variant:** Zephyr SDK 1.0.1 (`aarch64-zephyr-elf-gcc`)
- **Coding Standards:** Validated using `checkpatch.pl`, returning `0 errors, 0 warnings`.
- **Fault-Injection Reproduction:** Tested using an out-of-tree testing sandbox on `qemu_cortex_a53`. Standard bus sweeps execute natively with zero regression slips. Injecting a corrupted test coordinate token (`Bus 260`) successfully fires the raw assertion gate, logs the correct function name via `__func__`, and triggers an immediate, controlled kernel panic to preserve system memory boundaries when `CONFIG_ASSERT=y` is compiled.

title: drivers: timer: cortex_m_systick: fix 32-bit overflow in LPM tick accounting
body:
When the SysTick LPM counter-companion (CONFIG_SYSTEM_TIMER_LPM_COMPANION_COUNTER) is used to keep time across a low-power state, sys_clock_idle_exit() reconstructs the elapsed time and announces it to the kernel. Two intermediate values were computed in 32 bits, which overflows once a single low-power sleep exceeds 2^32 core cycles (~134 s at 32 MHz):

- dcycles (the unannounced cycle delta) was uint32_t. Truncation makes the announced tick count far too small, so k_sleep() never completes and the MCU appears to never wake from STOP.

- announced_cycles += dticks * CYC_PER_TICK evaluated the product in 32 bits before adding to the 64-bit accumulator. Truncation under-counts announced_cycles by a multiple of 2^32, so each subsequent sleep's dcycles is too large and kernel time runs progressively fast.

Widen dcycles to 64 bits and cast the multiply to cycle_t so both operations are performed in 64 bits. Only affects builds with a 64-bit cycle counter (CONFIG_CORTEX_M_SYSTICK_64BIT_CYCLE_COUNTER) using the counter companion; verified on STM32L151 (32 MHz core, LSE RTC companion) with 5- and 9-minute STOP intervals.

title: net: quic: Add 0-RTT support
body:
**What it is**: 0-RTT (Zero Round Trip Time) is a feature of the QUIC transport protocol that allows a client to send application data to a server immediately, in the very first packet of a connection, before completing the standard handshake.

**How it works normally**: Establishing a secure connection typically requires at least one full round trip (client → server → client) to negotiate encryption keys before any real data can be sent. 0-RTT eliminates this wait for returning clients by reusing cryptographic parameters from a previous session.

The mechanism:

* On a first connection, the server issues the client a session ticket containing cached parameters (keys, negotiated settings).
* On a subsequent connection, the client presents that ticket and immediately encrypts and sends application data alongside its handshake initiation—no waiting required. The server validates the ticket and can decrypt that data right away.

**Key benefit**: Reduced latency. For repeat visitors, this can effectively make a secure connection feel instantaneous, which matters a lot for mobile networks, page-load speed, and API calls with many small requests.

**Key trade-off - replay risk**: Because 0-RTT data isn't protected by a fresh handshake, it's vulnerable to replay attacks: an attacker could capture that first packet and resend it, potentially causing the server to process the same request twice. This is why 0-RTT is generally only considered safe for idempotent operations (e.g., a GET request), not for state-changing actions (e.g., a financial transaction) unless the application layer adds its own replay protection.

**Practical implications:**

* Servers often implement anti-replay defenses (e.g., single-use tickets, deduplication caches).
* Applications must explicitly decide which requests are safe to send via 0-RTT.
* It's a "best-effort" speed optimization, if 0-RTT fails or isn't supported, QUIC gracefully falls back to a standard 1-RTT handshake.

**Where it's used**: 0-RTT is part of QUIC (the transport underlying HTTP/3) and is closely related to TLS 1.3's 0-RTT resumption feature, which QUIC builds on for its cryptographic handshake.

title: bluetooth: mesh: dfu distributor self-update
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Tests;area: Bluetooth Mesh;platform: nRF BSIM
body:
## Summary

Fixes correctness and resumability issues in Bluetooth Mesh DFU when the
Distributor is also an Update Target (self-update) with no CDP change
— i.e. the Distributor stays provisioned after the update.

## Root causes

1. **Spec mismatch on Apply terminal state.** The DFU Client treated
   `Firmware Update Status { SUCCESS, APPLYING }` as in-progress and kept
   polling. Per MshDFUv1.0 §7.1.2.6 / §7.1.2.8, this response is the
   terminal *keep* condition for the Apply Firmware On Target Nodes
   procedure — Idle verification is handled by Refresh.
2. **Distributor state not persistent.** DFD Server and DFU Client state
   lived only in RAM, so a reboot mid-distribution — unavoidable during
   self-update — left the procedure unrecoverable.
3. **Self-target Apply raced with distribution completion,** losing
   track of remaining targets across the reboot.

## Changes

| # | Commit | What it does |
|---|--------|--------------|
| 1 | `tests: bsim: tune SAR config for DFU and BLOB tests` | Enables retries and tightens ACK timing so segmented unicast survives contention |
| 2 | `dfu_cli, dfu_srv: accept SUCCESS + APPLYING as terminal` | Aligns Apply completion with MshDFUv1.0 §7.1.2.6 |
| 3 | `persist dfd srv state for self-update resume` | Adds settings-backed persistence for DFD Server |
| 4 | `restore dfu client state for self-update resume` | Restores DFU Client procedure state on boot |
| 5 | `decouple dfu srv persisted state from runtime struct` | Splits stored state from live state |
| 6 | `fix dfu srv state persistence on failure paths` | Prevents stale persisted state after errors |
| 7 | `defer self-target apply until distribution completes` | Applies self-image only after all remaining targets are done |
| 8 | `resume self-update confirm step after reboot` | Continues the Apply/Refresh follow-up after Distributor reboots |
| 9 | `tests: cover DFD self-update post-reboot resume` | bsim coverage for the resume path |

## Notes

- No API changes.
- New persisted state uses a new settings subtree; old stored state is
  ignored on first boot (equivalent to no in-progress distribution).
- SAR retuning is scoped to the bsim test config only — no impact on
  production defaults.

title: tests: kernel: condvar: fix coherence fault on intel_adsp
body:
test_condvar_wait_timeout_relocks_mutex declared its k_condvar and
k_mutex as stack locals. On CONFIG_KERNEL_COHERENCE platforms (Xtensa
SMP DSP targets such as intel_adsp/ace20_lnl and ace30/ptl) thread
stacks live in cached, non-coherent memory, while a wait_q a thread
pends on must be memory-coherent -- it can be manipulated from another
CPU under _sched_spinlock.

When k_condvar_wait() timed out and pended the current thread on the
stack-resident condvar wait_q, the assert in pend_locked()

  __ASSERT_NO_MSG(wait_q == NULL || sys_cache_is_mem_coherent(wait_q));

fired, producing an EXCCAUSE 63 fatal exception and CPU panic. This was
the only test in the suite using stack-local kernel objects; every other
object here is file-scope and therefore already coherent.

Make the two objects static so they land in coherent .bss. The test is
single-shot and single-threaded, so static is safe.

Fixes #112846

title: kernel: kheap: keep static heap init as a PRE_KERNEL_1 SYS_INIT

Static heap init was converted from SYS_INIT(PRE_KERNEL_1, OBJECTS) to a

heap init. With the hook, sys_heap_init() ran first, heap->kasan_ba
stayed NULL and tracking was silently disabled. On the system heap this
let the tests/lib/heap_kasan overflow cases corrupt real chunk metadata
and panic with "heap corruption (free chunk linkage)".

init as SYS_INIT(PRE_KERNEL_1, CONFIG_KERNEL_INIT_PRIORITY_OBJECTS),
restoring the ordering the KASAN shadow registration depends on. The
mem_slab and mailbox conversions in the same series are unaffected and
stay on K_KERNEL_INIT_PRE. A comment records why kheap must remain a
SYS_INIT so it is not reconverted.

title: cmake: gcc: fix GCC emitting double-precision FP instructions on single-precision Cortex-M55
body:
## Problem

  The Realtek RTL87x2G (Cortex-M55) is an unusual configuration:
  it has **full MVE** (both integer MVE and MVE with float, i.e.
  `ARMV8_1_M_MVEI` + `ARMV8_1_M_MVEF`) and **DSP**, but only a
  **single-precision FPU** — double-precision instructions are not
  implemented in hardware.

  Because both MVE variants are present, `gcc-m-cpu.cmake` resolves
  `GCC_M_CPU` to the bare `cortex-m55` (the first branch, no `+nomve.*`
  suffix).  This means `gcc-m-fpu.cmake` looks up `FPU_FOR_cortex-m55`,
  and whatever value that holds is what GCC receives for `-mfpu=`.

  ### Timeline of regressions

  1. **Before commit 6612580** — `FPU_FOR_cortex-m55` was `auto`.
     GCC inferred double-precision from `-mcpu=cortex-m55`, so
     double-precision FP instructions could be emitted on a chip that
     does not support them.

  2. **commit 6612580** (`cmake: gcc-m-fpu: Support Cortex-M55 with
     single-precision FPU`) — changed `FPU_FOR_cortex-m55` to
     `fpv5-${PRECISION_TOKEN}d16`.  With `CPU_HAS_FPU_DOUBLE_PRECISION`
     unset, `PRECISION_TOKEN = "sp-"`, so GCC received `-mfpu=fpv5-sp-d16`.
     **This correctly prevented double-precision codegen on RTL87x2G.**

  3. **commit 570ef09** (`cmake: clang: fix MVE FP disabled on Cortex-M55
     with -mfpu=fpv5-sp-d16`) — reverted `FPU_FOR_cortex-m55` back to
     `auto` in the shared `gcc-m-fpu.cmake` to fix a clang regression
     (clang treats `-mfpu=` as an explicit capability override, so
     `-mfpu=fpv5-sp-d16` silently disables `mve.fp`).  The clang fix was
     correct, but editing the shared file also reverted the GCC behaviour.
     **Double-precision instructions can be emitted on RTL87x2G again.**

  ## Fix

  GCC and clang have different semantics for `-mfpu=`:

  - **GCC**: MVE capability comes from `-mcpu`/`-march` only; `-mfpu=`
    controls scalar FP precision and does not affect MVE.  Passing
    `-mfpu=fpv5-sp-d16` is safe and correct.
  - **clang**: `-mfpu=` is a full capability override; any feature not
    listed is disabled, so `fpv5-sp-d16` removes `mve.fp`.

  The right fix is therefore toolchain-specific.  This PR adds a guard
  in the **GCC-only** `cmake/compiler/gcc/target_arm.cmake`: when
  `GCC_M_FPU` is `"auto"` and `CPU_HAS_FPU_DOUBLE_PRECISION` is not set,
  explicitly pass `-mfpu=fpv5-sp-d16` to prevent GCC from assuming
  double-precision.

  The clang and armclang paths already skip `-mfpu=` entirely for `"auto"`
  (via guards added in commits 570ef09 and f30235f respectively) and are
  not changed.

  ## Impact

  No behaviour change for:
  - Any platform where `CPU_HAS_FPU_DOUBLE_PRECISION` is set
  - Any platform where `GCC_M_FPU != "auto"` (e.g. `cortex-m55+nomve.fp`)
  - clang or armclang builds

  Fixes double-precision FP codegen for any GCC build targeting a
  Cortex-M55 (or similarly resolved `auto` CPU) with a single-precision
  FPU only.

Assisted By Claude

title: Feature/pcie dynamic masking
body:
## Subsystem: Drivers / PCIe Controller & Host Core

### Technical Problem Statement & Structural Risk
During pre-silicon hardware-software co-design, platform bring-up, or out-of-tree custom driver development, triaging unstable, malfunctioning, or unsecure PCIe endpoints presents a severe development bottleneck. Currently, Zephyr's internal bus scanning infrastructure (`pcie_scan()`) recursively enumerates every available BDF coordinate blindly. 

If a faulty or unmapped hardware endpoint is probed during early boot sweeps, it can trigger asynchronous data aborts, memory pool leaks, or catastrophic kernel panic freezes. Bypassing or disabling these hardware slots traditionally requires hardcoding structural alterations directly within the architecture-specific DeviceTree files, forcing slow, repetitive compilation cycles.

### Proposed Architecture Fix
This patch introduces a dynamic software-based masking tracking layer to the common host subsystem processing layers to allow selective device isolation at runtime.
- Declares a global function pointer hook (`pcie_scan_override_hook`) inside the core `drivers/pcie/host/pcie.c` processing fabric.
- Implements a localized tracking matrix array (`masked_bdfs[]`) and evaluation callback handlers directly inside `drivers/pcie/host/shell.c`.
- Updates the central `scan_dev` device bus enumerator to query the hook before issuing configuration transactions. If a target coordinate is registered within the software mask, the loop intercepts execution and skips the slot natively.

This enables developers to interactively blacklist BDF slots on the fly from the live terminal canvas without forcing firmware re-builds or hardware descriptions resets.

## Subsystem: Drivers / PCIe Controller & Host Core

### Technical Problem Statement
Real-world physical edge devices running Zephyr frequently require low-power mode transitions or dynamic performance scaling. Currently, the native shell utilities provide zero options to interactively alter or retrain physical link parameters at runtime. This forces engineers to alter hardware initializers or recompile the system image simply to triage bus power profiles during platform bring-up.

### Proposed Architecture Fix
This patch extends the PCIe command tree by introducing a standalone link-management sub-tree:

- Dynamically updates the Target Link Speed bitfield inside the Link Control 2 register.

title: drivers: pcie: host: add interactive interrupt line diagnostic utility
body:
## Subsystem: Drivers / PCIe Controller & Host Core

Triage of asynchronous hardware interrupt line assignment anomalies, incorrect vector mappings, or silent interrupt masking states within embedded real-time systems (RTOS) is historically difficult. Currently, Zephyr's shell diagnostics emit passive, un-decoded register metrics. 

When a developer needs to verify whether a peripheral is successfully operating in legacy `INTx` mode or has correctly migrated to a Message Signaled Interrupt configuration, they must manually read raw hex configuration offsets and cross-reference device specs. This fragmentation severely dampens velocity during pre-silicon platform bring-up and device validation phases.

###  Proposed Architecture Fix
This patch introduces a robust, interactive multi-layer interrupt verification tree directly into the core PCIe host shell layer:
 `pcie irq status <bus:device.function>`

The execution infrastructure operates cleanly across three targeted triage tiers:
1. **Legacy INTx Parsing**: Decodes the standard `PCIE_CONF_INTR` boundaries, extracting explicit physical pin routing mappings (`INTA` through `INTD`) and hardware IRQ lines.
2. **Standard MSI Capability Block (Cap ID `0x05`)**: Automates traversal of the device capability pointer chains. It decodes the Message Control register, identifies whether MSI is active, tracks vector allocation counts, and prints the 32/64-bit Target Message Addresses and Message Data words.
3. **Extended MSI (MSI-X) Capability Block (Cap ID `0x11`)**: Traces extended multi-vector structures, monitoring global masking, complete vector table sizing boundaries, and outputs the exact Base Address Register (BAR) offset locating the active vector assignment table.

### Verification Matrix & Test Telemetry
