title: drivers: display: ssd16xx: add support for SSD1683
body:
The Solomon Systech **SSD1683** is a Gen2 SSD16xx EPD controller (functionally
equivalent to the SSD1619A, **400 sources × 300 gates**). It uses the same
command set as the already-supported SSD1680/SSD1681 and loads its refresh
waveforms from OTP, so support is just a new devicetree binding plus a
`ssd16xx_quirks` entry with the correct maximum resolution — no custom LUT.

Used by e.g. the **WeAct Studio 4.2" 400×300** module and the GoodDisplay
**GDEY042T81** 4.2" 400×300 mono panel.

Per the driver's own convention (`struct ssd16xx_quirks`: `max_width` = gate
lines, `max_height` = source outputs; cross-checked against SSD1680 =
176 sources × 296 gates → `max_width=296, max_height=176`), SSD1683
(300 gates, 400 sources) → `max_width=300, max_height=400`.

## Changes
- `drivers/display/ssd16xx.c`: add `quirks_solomon_ssd1683` + registration.
- `dts/bindings/display/solomon,ssd1683.yaml`: new binding (includes
  `solomon,ssd16xx-common.yaml`, mirrors the existing `solomon,ssd1680.yaml`).

## Test overlay used
```dts
&spi0 {
    status = "okay";
    cs-gpios = <&gpio0 0 GPIO_ACTIVE_LOW>;

    epd: ssd1683@0 {
        compatible = "solomon,ssd1683";
        reg = <0>;
        mipi-max-frequency = <4000000>;
        width  = <296>;   /* gates; see note below on the /8 constraint */
        height = <400>;   /* sources, multiple of 8 */
        busy-gpios = <&gpio0 1 GPIO_ACTIVE_HIGH>;
        full { };         /* empty -> OTP waveform */
    };
};
```

## Tested on hardware
Verified on a **Nordic nRF52840 (pro micro dev board)** driving a **WeAct Studio 4.2" 400×300**
e-paper module (SSD1683 controller) over SPI, via LVGL. Both **full and partial
refresh** render correctly in both orientations:
- **Landscape** — native geometry (the byte-packed axis is the 400-source side,
  which is a multiple of 8).
- **Portrait** — with `width = 296` (a /8-safe value ≤ 300 gates), matching the
  workaround for the LVGL-glue limitation described below.

## Known limitation
A GDEY042T81 has 300 gates, and 300 is **not a multiple of 8**. Zephyr's LVGL
mono glue (`modules/lvgl/lvgl_display_mono.c`) mis-strides 1-bit buffers whose
width is not a multiple of 8. That is an **LVGL-glue issue, not an ssd16xx
issue**, so this PR is deliberately limited to enabling the controller. Use
`width = 296` (a /8 value ≤ 300 gates) or landscape orientation (the 400-source
axis is /8). A proper stride fix belongs in a separate LVGL-glue PR.

## Checks run locally
- `checkpatch.pl`: 0 errors, 0 warnings
- `yamllint` (Zephyr config): clean
- devicetree binding schema (edtlib): parses, compatible matches filename,
  include resolves (46 inherited props), no underscore/`required:false` issues
- `gitlint` (Zephyr config): clean
- DCO: author == Signed-off-by (`Marcus Voß <meav33@gmail.com>`)

Signed-off-by: Marcus Voß <meav33@gmail.com>

title: modem: cellular: skip power-on pulse when modem already on
labels: area: Devicetree;area: Devicetree Binding;area: Modem Drivers
body:
The bring-up path pulses the power key unconditionally. On modems that toggle power with the key, that turns off a modem still running after an MCU-only reset, and the driver then times out against a dead bus until the modem completes a full power cycle.

Add an optional `mdm-status-gpios` input reporting modem power state. When it is present and asserted at start-up, skip the power-on pulse and bring up the bus directly. The init script confirms the modem responds, and if it does not, the driver powers the modem on.

Boards without the GPIO behave as before.

title: net: dns: datagrams queued on a DNS dispatcher socket are never drained by the socket service — global RX net_pkt slab exhausted, permanent RX blackout on all interfaces
body:
## Summary

On a dual-interface device (Ethernet + PPP-over-cellular warm standby), an Ethernet link
flap triggers DNS queries to a carrier DNS server reachable only over a 9600-baud PPP
link. The responses arrive after the 5 s query timeout has cancelled the queries, and
instead of being consumed and dropped, the datagrams remain **unread in the DNS
dispatcher's UDP socket receive queue** while the `net_socket_service` thread sits inside
`zsock_poll()` and never receives POLLIN for that socket. Each queued datagram pins one
`net_pkt` from the single global RX slab (`CONFIG_NET_PKT_RX_COUNT`), so the slab is
exhausted within seconds and **packet reception dies on every interface in the system**
(Ethernet included: `eth_stm32_hal: Failed to obtain RX buffer` for every frame; PPP:
`modem_ppp: Dropped frame, no net_pkt available`).

The condition is **persistent**: it was observed standing for 23+ minutes with no
recovery; only a reboot restored service. (An earlier apparent self-recovery during our
debugging was traced to a watchdog reset caused by a debugger halt, not to the stack
recovering.)

A 9600-baud side channel permanently starving a 100 Mb/s Ethernet interface is a severe
availability issue for any product combining the DNS resolver with a slow secondary link
— a very common cellular-failover topology.

Reproduced 4/4 on v4.3.1. The relevant code paths are unchanged in **v4.4.1** and current
**main** (f4509a09915) — see "Version check".

## Environment

- Zephyr v4.3.1, STM32F407 (custom board)
- Ethernet: `eth_stm32_hal` (HAL v2)
- Cellular: SIM800L via `modem_cmux`/`modem_ppp`/PPP L2 at 9600 baud, PPP interface up
  in warm standby (not default route; `CONFIG_NET_DEFAULT_IF_ETHERNET=y`)
- DNS: `CONFIG_DNS_RESOLVER=y`, `CONFIG_DNS_RESOLVER_MAX_SERVERS=2` — slot from DHCP
  (Ethernet) + slot from PPP IPCP (`CONFIG_NET_L2_PPP_OPTION_DNS_USE=y`, carrier DNS);
  MDNS/LLMNR responders and resolver disabled, so `DNS_RESOLVER_MAX_POLL` = 2
- `CONFIG_ZVFS_POLL_MAX=3` (socket service polls eventfd + 2 DNS sockets = exactly 3)
- `CONFIG_NET_SOCKETS_DNS_TIMEOUT=5000`
- `CONFIG_NET_PKT_RX_COUNT=4` (also reproduced with 8 — the retention consumes whatever
  is available; data-buf pools stay mostly free)
- 3 TLS/TCP clients (2× MQTT, 1 custom) re-resolving a hostname on reconnect

## Steps to reproduce

1. Both interfaces up; PPP negotiated (IPCP adds the carrier DNS server); TCP/TLS clients
   connected via Ethernet using a hostname only the LAN-side DNS can resolve.
2. Pull the Ethernet cable ~60 s. Client reconnect loops resolve via both servers; only
   the carrier server (over PPP) is reachable. It answers NXDOMAIN — at 9600 baud each
   answer lands after the 5 s query timeout has already cancelled the query.
3. Replug the cable. RX starvation begins within seconds and does not recover.

## Observed

```
<err> eth_stm32_hal: Failed to obtain RX buffer            (every incoming frame)
<wrn> modem_ppp: Dropped frame, no net_pkt available
```

`net mem` during the outage — RX pkt slab exhausted, data bufs mostly free:

```
Address        Total    Avail    MaxUsed    Name
0x200017b0    8    0    -    RX
0x200017e8    4    4    -    TX
0x20001b40    20    12    10    RX DATA (rx_bufs)
0x20001b78    30    30    21    TX DATA (tx_bufs)
```

`net allocs` (`CONFIG_NET_DEBUG_NET_PKT_ALLOC`): all pinned pkts allocated by the PPP RX
reassembler, i.e. complete frames handed to the stack:

```
0x2001cf98/1  used  RX  modem_ppp_process_received_byte():234
... (8 identical entries — 100% of the RX slab)
```

`net pkt 0x2001cf98` decodes a held pkt: complete, valid UDP datagram — DNS NXDOMAIN
response from the carrier server, destination = the resolver's live UDP socket
(port matches `net conn`):

```
IPv4 213.131.32.34:53 -> 172.27.231.240:53252, UDP len 101
DNS response, RCODE=3 (NXDOMAIN)
```

`net conn`: no TCP connections; the DNS socket context alive and bound (one additional
UDP context shows `AF_UNSPEC` / iface `-1` during the window).

Thread forensics via debugger while wedged (`k_thread.base.pended_on` resolved against
symbols; stack walked from `callee_saved.psp`):

- `net_socket_service` thread: parked **inside `zsock_poll()`**
  (`z_impl_k_poll` ← `zvfs_poll_internal`, wait object = zvfs poll event) — its normal
  wait state — while 8 datagrams sit queued on a DNS socket it should be watching.
- DNS resolver `ctx->lock`: **free** (`owner = 0x0`, `lock_count = 0`) — no lock convoy.
- RX traffic-class thread `rx_q[0]`: idle, pending on its own empty FIFO — the pinned
  packets are not in the RX queue; they were delivered to the socket's `recv_q`.
- No thread in the system is deadlocked; the MQTT client threads are in their normal
  poll/backoff states.

So: a level-triggered `zsock_poll()` never reports a socket whose `recv_q` holds 8
datagrams, for tens of minutes. This points at the socket's fd not being represented
(or not readable-flagged) in the socket service's active poll array — e.g. lost/raced
poll-set rebuild — rather than at packet processing.

## Analysis notes

The datagrams reached the socket receive queue (packets held, allocated by the L2
driver, addressed to the bound port), so the failure is between "datagram queued on
socket" and "socket service drains it". Relevant mechanics in v4.3.1
(`subsys/net/lib/sockets/sockets_service.c`):

- The service thread polls a private copy `ctx.events[]` that is rebuilt from
  `svc->pev[]` only on an eventfd-signalled `restart:`; `net_socket_service_register()`
  (called from `dns_resolve_reconfigure()` paths — which fire in bursts on link
  flaps when `NET_L2_PPP_OPTION_DNS_USE` is enabled) rewrites `svc->pev[]` and signals
  the eventfd.
- `call_work()` temporarily masks an fd (`pev->fd = -1`) in the active array around
  each callback and restores it afterwards.
- In this configuration the poll array is at exact capacity
  (`CONFIG_ZVFS_POLL_MAX=3` = eventfd + 2 DNS sockets).

Additionally, `recv_data()` (`subsys/net/lib/dns/dispatcher.c:155`) allocates from
`dns_msg_pool` *before* reading the socket and returns without `recvfrom()` on
allocation failure — so under pool pressure a queued datagram is neither consumed nor
dropped. That did not appear to be the blocking site in our captures (the service thread
was in `zsock_poll`, not in an alloc wait), but it makes the retention worse once the
system is degraded.

Independent of the exact race, two structural issues turn this into a system-wide,
unrecoverable outage:

1. **Unbounded per-socket RX retention from the shared slab:** one unserviced UDP socket
   may pin the entire `NET_PKT_RX_COUNT` slab and take down RX for every interface and
   protocol, with no aging/purge of queued-but-never-read datagrams.
2. **No forward-progress guarantee in the drain path** (alloc-before-read in
   `recv_data()`).

We can re-run the reproduction and capture the live poll array vs. the registered
dispatcher fds if that would help pinpoint the race — the setup is available.

## Version check

- v4.3.1 → v4.4.1: no functional change in `dispatcher.c` / `sockets_service.c`
  (rename-only commits aadb23a1889, d45cd6716bb); `resolve.c` changes are feature work.
- main (f4509a09915): 8e8dd62cf3f initializes the dispatcher mutex (assert fix — not
  this), 620480f6176 ("avoid timeout-bound alloc in cancel helper") is adjacent but does
  not change the drain path; da0a4290857 (query multiple servers) would *increase* the
  number of doomed queries in this topology.

## Workarounds used

- Per-link DNS policy at the application layer (never query the cellular-side server for
  LAN-only names) — removes the late-response flood.
- Keeping the PPP link down until Ethernet actually fails (cold standby) — avoids the
  dual-server topology during flaps.

Both only remove our trigger; the underlying "one slow socket pins the global RX slab
permanently" hazard remains reachable by any delayed UDP responses.

title: drivers: mspi: stm32: add STM32Cube2 (HAL2) XSPI driver variant
body:
## What this PR does

Makes the existing XSPI MSPI driver (`mspi_stm32_xspi.c`) build and work with both STM32Cube HAL generations: the legacy one and STM32Cube2 ("HAL2", `CONFIG_STM32_HAL2`), which is the only HAL shipped for newer series such as STM32C5. The two HALs use different names for the XSPI types, structure fields and enum constants, and a few functions changed their call shape, so the legacy-only driver could not compile there.

This is the rework requested in the earlier review round: no second driver file and no renaming of HAL primitives. The HAL-dependent code lives in one `#if defined(CONFIG_STM32_HAL2) / #else / #endif` section of HAL adapter functions at the top of the file, with one implementation per HAL generation. Everything below that section is compiled unchanged for both generations and never references a HAL name that differs between them. The key piece is a small driver-local command description (opcode, operation type, address and length, dummy cycles, data length) that the shared logic fills in and a single adapter, `mspi_stm32_xspi_send_cmd()`, translates into the HAL command structure - so the command-building logic exists only once.

No new files, no new Kconfig options and no device tree changes; this also keeps the door open for the factorization of the xspi/ospi/qspi driver variants that ST is considering, since the shared logic is already HAL-agnostic.

The controller lock lifecycle bug found during the first review round was split off as requested and is already merged (#113624), so this PR is now driver-rework only.

## What is HAL-specific and what is shared

HAL adapter functions (one implementation per HAL generation):

| Adapter | Difference between the HALs |
|---|---|
| `prepare_cmd()`, `send_cmd()` | command type, field and constant names (`XSPI_RegularCmdTypeDef`/`.Instruction` vs `hal_xspi_regular_cmd_t`/`.instruction`, ...) |
| `is_memorymap()` | reads `CR.FMODE` vs `HAL_XSPI_GetState()` |
| `memmap_off()` | `HAL_XSPI_Abort()` vs `HAL_XSPI_StopMemoryMappedMode()` |
| `memmap_start()` | memory-mapped config structure and start call |
| `autopoll_start()` | auto-polling config structure and start call |
| `abort()` | HAL2 `HAL_XSPI_Abort()` takes a timeout argument |
| `is_busy()` | `HAL_XSPI_GET_FLAG()` vs `HAL_XSPI_IsActiveFlag()` |
| `mspi_hal_init()` | handle `Init` fields vs `HAL_XSPI_Init(instance)` + `HAL_XSPI_SetConfig()` + `HAL_XSPI_SetFifoThreshold()` |
| `mspi_configure_delay_block()` | `DLYB_GetClockPeriod()`/`PhaseSel / 4` vs `DLYB_CalculateMaxClockPhase()`/`SetConfigDelay(max / 4)` |
| `dma_init()` | `hdma->Init` fields + `HAL_DMA_Init(hdma)` vs `HAL_DMA_Init(hdma, channel)` + `HAL_DMA_SetConfigDirectXfer()` |
| `dma_link_tx()/dma_link_rx()` | `__HAL_LINKDMA()` vs `HAL_XSPI_SetTxDMA()/SetRxDMA()` |
| weak `HAL_DMA_Abort(_IT)` stubs | legacy-only HAL compilation requirement |

Shared code (identical for both HALs): the MSPI API implementations (`dev_config`, `transceive`, `memmap_config`, `get_channel_status`, controller `config`/`init`), the transfer paths (`access`, `status_reg`, `memmap_on`, `wait_auto_polling`, indirect and memory-mapped read/write), the ISR and DMA callback, validation helpers, PM hooks and the device instantiation macros. Shared code only calls HAL functions whose names and signatures are the same in both generations (`HAL_XSPI_Receive/Transmit(_IT/_DMA)`, `HAL_XSPI_IRQHandler`, `HAL_DMA_IRQHandler`, comparisons against `HAL_OK`).

## Notes for the reviewers

The series is split so that every commit builds on its own and does one thing:

1. `use driver-local DMA priority table names` - stops redefining HAL macro names in `mspi_stm32_common.c`
2. `use one timeout define for XSPI transfers` - HAL2 has no `HAL_XSPI_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_VALUE`; same value
3. `split Zephyr-side DMA channel setup out` - the `dma_config()` part of the DMA init does not touch the HAL handle, so it can be shared later
4. `configure the XSPI handle at runtime` - moves the `Init` fields out of the device macro and carries the devicetree memory size and type through the driver config; the HAL2 handle has no `Init` member, so the macro must stay HAL-agnostic
5. `build XSPI commands from a neutral description` - the main step, introduces the command description and `send_cmd()`; the commit message lists why every sent command stays identical
6. `return errno codes from the indirect helper` - keeps HAL type names out of shared signatures
7. `gather HAL-specific code into adapter functions` - pure code movement plus small extractions; easiest to read with `git show --color-moved=dimmed-zebra`
8. `warn when the abort after autopoll timeout fails` - the only behavior change in the series, kept separate on purpose
9. `select XSPI handle types and DMA values per HAL` - `mspi_stm32.h` + `mspi_stm32_common.c`
10. `support STM32Cube2 HAL in the XSPI driver` - adds the HAL2 adapter section

## Behavior notes for the HAL2 side

- `MSPI_IO_MODE_HEX_8_8_16` falls back to 8 data lines (no 16-line support in this XSPI generation; same as the legacy `#else` branch).
- SIOO, prefetch, wrap size and delay-block bypass settings stay in the legacy branch; the HAL2 structures have no such fields, and the HAL2 reset defaults match what the legacy driver programmed for clock mode and free-running clock.
- `HAL_DMA_ConfigChannelAttributes()` has no HAL2 equivalent and is legacy-only.
- HAL2 `memmap_off()` is a no-op when memory-mapped mode is not active (the HAL2 state machine rejects a stop outside that state); the legacy branch keeps its unconditional abort.
- The mixed-line modes added in `bb3e933` are implemented in both branches.
- The delay block is enabled explicitly after configuring it: the HAL2 calibration calls restore the block to the state they found it in, which is disabled out of reset.
- The DMA transfer path compiles against HAL2 but is untested on hardware - no supported board routes DMA channels to the XSPI node yet.

## Testing 
Described in a comment, see bellow!

## Relationship to other issues/PRs

- Prerequisite for #112731 (`boards: st: nucleo_c5a3zg: add M.2 Key A serial memory support`): the twister run there fails building `sample.drivers.mspi.flash.b_m2mem_pack1_*` on `nucleo_c5a3zg` precisely because of #112732 plus the legacy-HAL-only XSPI driver.

title: modem: cellular: bound the recovery loop
body:

title: drivers: sensor: bmi270: convert RTIO path to fully async with SQE chaining
body:
## Overview

Reworks the BMI270 RTIO data path to be fully asynchronous, using SQE chaining instead of a work queue, and adds FIFO streaming support via `sensor_stream()`.

The original async RTIO rework and FIFO streaming work was authored by @sudiiyengar-en based on #105828. This PR carries it forward, rebased onto current `main`, with the review feedback from that PR addressed and two additional fixes found during hardware validation.

Since #105828 was closed as stale, this reopens the same work rebased onto current `main`, with the review feedback from that PR addressed:

- FIFO decode now converts each raw sample to Q31 with a single multiply, using a scale precomputed once per buffer instead of per frame.
- The `1000000LL` unit-conversion divisor is now a named macro (`BMI270_MICRO_UNIT_SCALE`) with a short comment explaining it.
- `bmi270_decoder_decode()` groups plain field assignments separately from ones requiring a function call.
- `write_config_file()` correctly keeps `int` (not `int8_t`), since it forwards the return of `bmi270_reg_write_with_delay()`, which is `int`.

On top of that, this adds two fixes found while validating FIFO streaming end to end on hardware:

- `bmi270_submit_stream()` was re-running its full one-time setup (FIFO config, INT map, flush, GPIO disable) on every `RTIO_SQE_MULTISHOT` cycle instead of once at stream start. It's now gated behind a `fifo_configured` flag, re-armed only after a stream abort.
- The FIFO poll fallback (`CONFIG_BMI270_FIFO_POLL_FALLBACK`) stopped rescheduling itself permanently if it ran while `streaming_sqe` was momentarily `NULL` between cycles.

## Testing

Built and run on hardware with BMI270 over SPI, using the `gesture_recognition` application from `nrfconnect/sdk-edge-ai`. FIFO streaming, IMU sampling, and the application pipeline ran continuously without stalling.

title: soc: realtek: bee: fix timing defaults
labels: area: Kernel;area: Tests;area: MAINTAINER File;area: Boards/SoCs;platform: Realtek Bee
body:
1. Remove hardcoded TIMESLICE_SIZE default (rtl87x2g, rtl8752h)

  The SoC-level default of 10 ms caused tracing samples (sample.tracing.user, sample.tracing.gpio) to stall at 115200 baud: three consecutive trace hooks after each sys-timer ISR emit ~9–12 ms of synchronous UART output, exhausting the timeslice before application threads get CPU time. Removing the override lets the kernel default (20 ms) apply, which provides sufficient headroom.

**### Delete these two related commits for root cause solve PR:** 
  2. Tune zephyr,min-timeout-cycles to 30 (rtl87x2g, rtl8752h) ->https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/113083

  With MIN_DELAY = 32 = CYC_PER_TICK, the per-ISR overhead from elapsed() and drift correction accumulates without bound until the unannounced surplus reaches 2 * CYC_PER_TICK, triggering dticks=2 and firing two k_timer callbacks back-to-back in a single ISR. This appears as a ~1-cycle (31 µs) spurious period in tests/kernel/timer/timer_behavior. Setting MIN_DELAY = 30 (drain rate = 2 cycles/tick) resolves the accumulation. The value was validated by test on both platforms.

  3. Relax IDLE_EVENT_STATS_PRECISION for 32 kHz SysTick platforms  ->  https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/113075

The default 1% precision in tests/kernel/usage/thread_runtime_stats is unachievable at 32 kHz: with peak_cycles ~ 32, a single cycle deviation already represents ~3%. Raised to 7% for SOC_SERIES_RTL87X2G and SOC_SERIES_RTL8752H, consistent with the existing relaxation for RISC-V targets.


Description Assisted By Claude

title: tests: timer: timer_behavior: disable timeslicing
body:
When TICKLESS_KERNEL is enabled on platforms using a coarse SysTick (e.g. 32 kHz on Realtek BEE SoCs), enabling timeslicing intermittently causes a ~1-cycle (~31 us) timer period to appear in the test results, far outside the expected ~1000 us period.

Root cause: the periodic timeslice yield calls sys_clock_set_timeout() from within the timer ISR path. Each call adds elapsed() plus drift compensation cycles to cycle_count (the unannounced surplus). With only 32 cycles per tick at 32 kHz, this surplus can accumulate to 2*CYC_PER_TICK=64, causing the driver to announce dticks=2 in a single ISR and fire two k_timer callbacks back-to-back with only ~1 cycle between them.

Disabling timeslicing eliminates the extra set_timeout() call and keeps the surplus below the dticks=2 threshold. This is also consistent with the intent of the test, which measures pure timer accuracy and does not require preemptive time-sliced scheduling.


Assisted By Claude

title: drivers: i2c_dw: introduce pm device runtime
body:
Add device power management and runtime PM support to the DesignWare I2C driver (i2c_dw), and enable it for the SiWG917 I2C controllers in devicetree.

Driver initialization is refactored into focused helpers so hardware bring-up can be deferred to PM_DEVICE_ACTION_TURN_ON when the parent power domain is not active at boot. pm_device_runtime_get() / put() are added around driver API paths that access controller registers (transfer, recover_bus, configure, and target register/unregister).

All snps,designware-i2c instances now use PM_DEVICE_DT_INST_DEFINE(). On platforms without a power domain or zephyr,pm-device-runtime-auto, behavior is unchanged: pm_device_driver_init() runs TURN_ON at boot and leaves the device active.

**Why ?** 

On SiWx91x, I2C controllers can be unpowered while the SoC is in a low-power state. After power is restored, the controller must be brought up again through the TURN_ON path (clock, optional reset/pinctrl, register programming, and IRQ setup). The same pattern applies to other DesignWare I2C users that adopt power-domains and zephyr,pm-device-runtime-auto in devicetree.

Tested on SiWG917 with I2C sensor transfers before and after runtime idle.

Feedback is welcome, especially around the PCIe, MMIO, and DMA init split. This series assumes that PCIe BAR mapping, MMIO mapping, and LPSS DMA setup do not require the I2C clock or pinctrl to be enabled, and therefore keeps that work in i2c_dw_initialize() while deferring clock/reset/pinctrl and controller register access to i2c_dw_turn_on().

title: net: ethernet: bridge: Resolve IPv4 dst before flooding
body:
When the bridge interface owns an IPv4 address it can originate traffic of its own (for example a TCP server bound to the bridge). Such locally originated IPv4 packets were flooded to the member ports with the family reset to AF_UNSPEC, which disables the ARP step in the Ethernet L2 send routine. The destination link address was therefore left unresolved and defaulted to broadcast, so e.g. a TCP SYN-ACK went out to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff and RFC-compliant peers dropped it.

The member ports cannot resolve on the bridge's behalf either: an ARP reply is addressed to the bridge link address, so a member port would drop it as "not for me". IPv6 is unaffected as its neighbor is resolved in net_ipv6_prepare_for_send() before the packet reaches this layer.

Resolve the destination on the bridge interface, where the ARP cache is populated, before flooding to the member ports. On a cache miss the ARP request is flooded and the packet held until the reply resolves it. Forwarded (L2 bridged) frames already carry a complete header and are left untouched.

Tested on native_sim with the tests/net/bridge regression tests.

Fixes #112408

title: boards: infineon: kit_pse84_eval: disable watchdog on m33/ns
body:
The SRSS watchdog on the PSE84 is a secure-owned platform resource. On the
`kit_pse84_eval` non-secure M33 target (`m33/ns`) the `watchdog0` node was left
enabled even though the non-secure image is not meant to drive it:

- In the TrustZone-M security model the secure image manages the system
  watchdog (it also gates the `WDT_LOCK`), and a watchdog timeout resets the
  whole SoC.
- On this SoC the SRSS block is mapped secure-only: its non-secure address
  alias does not respond on the bus, and the low-frequency clock the watchdog
  counts on is brought up by the secure world.
- The non-secure side uses the MCWDT (`mcwdt0`) for its timing needs instead.
- This board's non-secure capabilities intentionally do not advertise the
  `watchdog` feature, so the watchdog test suites are already filtered out on
  this target via the devicetree alias / `depends_on` mechanism.

Because the block is secure-only, leaving `watchdog0` enabled on `m33/ns` does
not fail cleanly. Building the watchdog sample with the node forced back on and
running it on hardware reproduces a hang: the non-secure driver's setup path
(`wdt_install_timeout()`) blocks indefinitely when it tries to configure the
timer, with the core spinning in the secure world rather than taking a fault.

Leaving `watchdog0` enabled in the non-secure devicetree is therefore
inconsistent with the board's declared capabilities and would let the driver
bind an instance the non-secure image should not manage. This change disables
the node on `m33/ns` so the devicetree matches the board's non-secure
capabilities; `mcwdt0` stays enabled. The secure M33 and the M55 targets, which
legitimately own the watchdog, are unaffected.

title: fs: FatFs CVE fixes (POSIX readdir bound + f_lseek() regression test)
labels: area: File System;area: Tests;area: Storage;area: POSIX
body:
## Summary

Fix the one Zephyr-side caller that shares the 2026 runZero FatFs disclosure
(CVE-2026-6682 … CVE-2026-6688), and add a regression test for the vendored
FatFs `f_lseek()` fix.

The five `ff.c` fixes themselves landed in the module via
zephyrproject-rtos/fatfs#23, and `main` already pins a `fatfs` revision that
carries them, so this PR no longer touches `west.yml`.

Two commits:

1. **`portability: posix: bound readdir() name copy to the dirent buffer`**:
   the POSIX `readdir()` shim copied the FatFs long file name into
   `struct dirent.d_name[NAME_MAX + 1]` clamped only to `MAX_FILE_NAME`. Those
   limits are independent: with FAT LFN, `MAX_FILE_NAME` follows
   `CONFIG_FS_FATFS_MAX_LFN` (default 255) while `NAME_MAX` is the POSIX minimum
   (14), so a long directory entry name overran the static `d_name` buffer.
   This is the caller-side FatFs long-name overflow of **CVE-2026-6688**
   (GHSA-8vm2-mjff-2gg2); the in-tree `fs_readdir()` path was already bounded by
   the CVE-2020-13598 fix. The copy is now clamped to the destination buffer.

2. **`tests: fs: fat_fs_api: cover FatFs f_lseek() past-EOF zeroing`**: a
   regression test for **CVE-2026-6686** (GHSA-h94p-vjqx-v7rr). It drives the
   FatFs API directly, because the Zephyr `fs_*` layer does not reach this path
   (`fs_seek()` clamps to the file size and `fs_truncate()` growth is
   zero-filled). It covers both the empty-file extend and the partial-cluster
   case, where a file is truncated and then re-extended within an
   already-allocated cluster.

## Testing

`filesystem.fat.ram.api` (which runs the new test, `CVE-2026-6686: PASS`) and
the four `portability.posix.fs` scenarios pass on `native_sim`.

Fixes: #121154

title: drivers: counter: infineon_tcpwm: cache input frequency for ISR safety
body:
## Summary

`counter_get_frequency()` may be called from a counter alarm or top-value
callback, which runs in the counter ISR. The Infineon TCPWM counter driver
implemented `get_freq()` by walking the peripheral clock tree on every call via
the PDL (`Cy_SysClk_PeriPclkGetFrequency` -> `Cy_SysClk_ClkHfGetFrequency`).

On non-secure builds (TrustZone-M with TF-M) that PDL clock query is serviced by
the secure world through a PSA / secure-request round-trip. Such calls are not
permitted from interrupt context, so calling `counter_ticks_to_us()` /
`counter_get_frequency()` from an alarm callback made the secure request fail and
the PDL assertion fault the core, hanging the application.

## Details

The problem is specific to the non-secure interrupt path:

- In **thread** context the same query succeeds (e.g. computing alarm ticks
  during setup works).
- On **secure** builds the PDL reads the clock registers directly with no
  secure-request round-trip, so it works there too.
- Only the **non-secure, interrupt-context** call fails.

This was observed on a non-secure Cortex-M33 TF-M target running the
`samples/drivers/counter/alarm` sample: the alarm interrupt is delivered and the
callback runs, but the core faults inside the PDL clock-frequency query, so the
sample hangs after arming the alarm and the `!!! Alarm !!!` line never prints.

## Fix

The counter input clock is fixed once the peripheral divider is assigned at
init. Cache the frequency in the driver's init routine (thread context) and
return the cached value from `get_freq()`. This makes `counter_get_frequency()`
safe to call from the counter ISR and also avoids a clock-tree walk on every
call.

With this change the sample runs to completion on the non-secure target
(`!!! Alarm !!!` fires for the 2/4/8/16 s alarms as expected), and behaviour on
secure builds is unchanged.

title: drivers: pcie: host: shell: add advanced error reporting telemetry co…
body:
Right now, our Zephyr shell subcommands don't have a way to peek into the PCIe Extended Configuration Space (offsets ≥ `0x100`) or troubleshoot low-level hardware issues while the system is running. If we hit electrical noise, receiver overflows, or protocol packet errors on critical hardware platforms, we are basically flying blind until a hard fault or data abort drops the system. This new tool helps change that!
 This patch adds a handy new runtime subcommand to our PCIe shell utility: `pcie aer status <bus:dev.func>`. 
* **Extended Capability Space Traversal:** It hops through the capability linked list to automatically find the base offset for the native PCIe Advanced Error Reporting block (Capability ID `0x0001`).
* **Friendly Register Decoding:** It unpacks the 32-bit hardware status registers and translates those scary raw bitfields into clear, human-readable terminal alerts (like Link Training failures, Poisoned TLPs, or Flow Control Protocol credit errors).
* **Fault Triage Capture:** It extracts and clean-prints the raw 16-byte Transaction Layer Packet (TLP) Header Log matrix straight to the console loop for post-fault analysis.
* **Shell Integration:** It plays nice with Zephyr's positional shell parsing conventions by keeping argument constraints neatly restricted to `2, 0` configurations.
###Terminal Output

```text
uart:~\$ pcie aer status 0:1.0 
====================================================================
   PCIe ADVANCED ERROR REPORTING (AER) STATUS MATRIX: 0:1.0
====================================================================
Uncorrectable Errors Status: 0x00002000 [Mask: 0x00000000]
   [CRITICAL] -> Flow Control Protocol Error (FCPE)
----------------------------------------------------
Correctable Errors Status:   0x00000000 [Mask: 0x00000000]
   -> No physical signal degradation faults reported.
----------------------------------------------------
Transaction Layer Packet (TLP) Header Log Matrix:
   [DW0-DW1] : 0x00000000 0x00000000
   [DW2-DW3] : 0x00000000 0x00000000
====================================================================
```

title: kernel: Add option to run the system workqueue on the main thread
body:
Add `CONFIG_SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_ON_MAIN`, which runs the system workqueue on the
main thread instead of spawning a dedicated thread, reclaiming the dedicated
thread's stack. This targets applications whose `main()` returns after boot-time
initialization and do not otherwise rely on the system workqueue from `main()`
(e.g. memory-constrained targets). On such a build, once `main()` returns the
main thread enters the system workqueue run loop and does not return.

Measured saving: ~1 KB RAM on a basic Bluetooth app.

### Contents

* **kernel: work: allow arming a work queue before its run loop** — add
  `k_work_queue_prepare()`, which marks a queue started and records the calling
  thread as its thread *without* entering the run loop. This lets work be
  submitted (and `k_work_queue_thread_get()` be used) before the same thread
  later calls `k_work_queue_run()`. Previously `k_work_queue_run()` did this
  setup itself, so work submitted beforehand was rejected (`-ENODEV`) and would
  have been discarded by its list re-initialization. `k_work_queue_run()` now
  detects an already-armed queue and skips the setup, so existing callers are
  unaffected.

* **kernel: Add option to run the system workqueue on the main thread** — the
  `CONFIG_SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_ON_MAIN` option itself. `k_sys_work_q_init()` prepares the
  queue on the main thread before `main()` runs; `k_sys_work_q_run()` enters the
  run loop after `main()` returns. The main thread is kept essential (it becomes
  the essential system workqueue thread).

* **tests: kernel: workq: cover arming a work queue before its run loop** — adds
  `test_k_work_queue_prepare` verifying that the queue thread identity is valid after
  preparing, and that work submitted before the run loop is accepted and later
  processed.

### Notes

* `k_work_queue_prepare()` is generally useful on its own for running a workqueue on
  a caller-supplied thread that must accept submissions before its run loop.

title: drivers: pcie: host: shell: add link lane margining capabilities trac…
body:
This patch implements a modular runtime subcommand utility: `pcie link margin <bus:dev.func>` within the link management utility subtree. 

### Rationale & Problem Description
When performing pre-silicon validation sweeps, early chiplet fabric bring-up, or physical multi-layer PCB layout debugging, signal integrity and hardware teams must evaluate high-speed link signaling tolerances at the physical layer (PHY). Currently, the Zephyr RTOS PCIe shell utilities lack any capability to poll or decode the standardized receiver tuning interfaces introduced in modern PCIe specifications. Hardware-firmware co-design teams require visible runtime instrumentation to audit lane tolerances directly over the serial console interface without needing invasive external oscilloscope differential probes.

### Proposed Architectural Solution
* **Extended Capability List Traversal:** Dynamically negotiates linked headers across the PCIe Extended Configuration Space (offsets ≥ `0x100`) to isolate the base register offset of the native Lane Margining at Receiver capability block (Extended Cap ID `0x001A`).
* **PHY Telemetry Profile Extraction:** Reads and parses the 16-bit Port Capabilities and Port Control registers. It decodes and exposes maximum voltage margins (up to 127 steps), maximum timing margins (up to 63 steps), exact link widths tracked, and independent per-lane software control availability.
* **Real-Time Receiver Signal Layer Auditing:** Interrogates the Lane Status registers to safely track active receiver hardware margining engine runs and flag timing/voltage step threshold limits.
* **Shell Argument Hardening:** Filters parental root tokens and strictly constrains positional shell argument requirements to a `2, 0` layout configuration.

### Output (Defensive Fallback Check)

```text
uart:~\$ pcie link margin 0:1.0 
pci_cfg_read pcie-root-port 00:01.0 @0x0 -> 0xc1b36
pci_cfg_read pcie-root-port 00:01.0 @0x100 -> 0x14820001
pci_cfg_read pcie-root-port 00:01.0 @0x148 -> 0x1000d
Target device does not implement native Lane Margining at Receiver (Cap ID 0x001A).
```

title: drivers: pcie: host: shell: add physical power gating command for pci…
body:
This patch adds a powerful, hardware-level energy-gating subcommand to our central utility tree: `pcie device state <bus:dev.func> up|down`.

While we have software-only filter mechanisms like dynamic device masking to hide malfunctioning controllers during the boot sequence, our shell utilities currently lack any mechanism to manipulate real hardware power states at the silicon level. 

This command directly targets the physical layer. By writing straight to the device's Power Management Control/Status Register (PMCSR), we can dynamically toggle transceivers between fully operational execution states and low-power hardware leakage states. This provides crucial hardware bring-up instrumentation for verifying physical energy-gating loops and power grid states on high-reliability embedded platforms.

### What This Patch Does
* **Traditional Capability Space Traversal:** Scans the base configuration capability list registers to isolate the native PCI Power Management Block (Capability ID `0x01`).
* **Silicon State Mutation:** Implements safe read-modify-write mechanics over the PMCSR, mutating bits `[1:0]` cleanly between `00b` (D0 Max Performance) and `11b` (D3hot Low Energy Suspend).
* **Deterministic Verification Readback:** Performs an immediate hardware status readback right after the bit mutation, verifying the true electrical state of the device transceiver.
* **Shell Parsing Hardening:** Enforces strict argument validation, setting positional constraint matrices tightly to `3, 0` boundaries to prevent execution errors.

### Terminal Output Trace

```text
uart:~\$ pcie device state 0:1.0 up 
====================================================================
   PCI HARDWARE TRANSCEIVER ENERGY REGISTRY STATUS: 0:1.0
====================================================================
   Current PMCSR Value Readout  : 0x00000000
   Physical Silicon Transceiver: [FULLY OPERATIONAL - D0 MAX PERFORMANCE]
====================================================================
uart:~\$ pcie device state 0:1.0 down 
====================================================================
   PCI HARDWARE TRANSCEIVER ENERGY REGISTRY STATUS: 0:1.0
====================================================================
   Current PMCSR Value Readout  : 0x00000003
   Physical Silicon Transceiver: [POWER GATED - D3hot LOW ENERGY SUSPEND]
====================================================================
```

title: soc: st: stm32: common: gpioport_mgr: don't instantiate GPIO port nodes when CONFIG_GPIO_STM32=n
body:
Since #104527, GPIO nodes are unconditionally instanced as long as the GPIOport manager module is enabled: `CONFIG_PINCTRL_STM32=y || CONFIG_GPIO_STM32=y`. The unfortunate side-effect of this approach is that it is possible to build an application that uses the GPIO API *but does not enable `CONFIG_GPIO`* without causing the usual `__device_dts_ord_N not found` linker error. #110017 introduced a hacky workaround to prevent really catastrophic consequences, but #113011 has proven that this isn't sufficient and still confuses users. Rework the GPIOport manager to instantiate the GPIO nodes as software devices when `CONFIG_GPIO_STM32=n`. This restores the old and expected behavior of "disabled driver causes `__device_dts_ord_N` **build-time** error" as the `struct device`s' names no longer match the expectations of `DEVICE_DT_GET()`, while avoiding too much external changes since *they are still instanced as proper devices*. One unfortunate side-effect of this approach is that the resulting devices don't get the fancy features from `DEVICE_DT_DEFINE()`: no initialization priority checking, no dependencies, etc. This *could* be obtained by using the raw `Z_DEVICE_DEFINE()` macro but has not been done for portability and future-proofing since that macro is internal. Given that the GPIO devices become private and are only manipulated by the STM32 Pinctrl driver when `CONFIG_GPIO_STM32=n`, I believe the currently implemented approach should be safe overall. Verified by building `samples/basic/blinky` without `CONFIG_GPIO=y` in the `prj.conf`:
Details

Before: ``` $ wb samples/hello_world/ -b nucleo_wba65ri -DCONFIG_GPIO=n -p [...] [164/164] Linking C executable zephyr/zephyr.elf Memory region Used Size Region Size %age Used FLASH: 17544 B 2 MB 0.84% RAM: 4240 B 458720 B 0.92% SRAM0: 0 B 458720 B 0.00% SRAM6: 0 B 16 KB 0.00% PM_S2RAM: 0 B 32 B 0.00% IDT_LIST: 0 B 32 KB 0.00% ``` After: ``` $ wb samples/basic/blinky/ -b nucleo_wba65ri -DCONFIG_GPIO=n -p [...] [159/164] Linking C executable zephyr/zephyr_pre0.elf FAILED: zephyr/zephyr_pre0.elf zephyr/zephyr_pre0.map ld.bfd: app/libapp.a(main.c.obj): in function `main': zephyrproject/zephyr/samples/basic/blinky/src/main.c:48:(.text.main+0x60): undefined reference to `__device_dts_ord_56' collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status ninja: build stopped: subcommand failed. ```

Tested for regression by running `samples/hello_world` (which works fine, both with and without `-DCONFIG_PM=y`) as well as `samples/basic/blinky`. --- While at it, add some cleanup, footprint optimizations and "bugfix" (in the first, third and fourth commit respectively).

title: drivers: i2c: infineon: program SCB clock divider for all CAT1 families
labels: area: I2C;area: Tests;area: Clock Control;platform: Infineon
body:
The Infineon CAT1 I2C driver only programmed the SCB oversampling-clock
divider on PSoC 4. On every other CAT1 family the runtime divider was never
set, so a `STANDARD`, `FAST` or `FAST_PLUS` configuration all ended up
producing the same SCL frequency (whatever the static devicetree divider
happened to yield) instead of the requested data rate.

## Change

- Replace the dead `USE_I2C_SET_PERI_DIVIDER` path and the PSoC 4-only
  `_i2c_set_peri_divider_psoc4()` with a single `_i2c_set_peri_divider()`
  compiled for all CAT1 families. It:
  - maps the requested data rate to the SCB oversampling-clock window,
  - reconstructs the divider source frequency as
    `source = current_output * current_ratio` (independent of the family's
    HFCLK-to-peripheral-group routing),
  - programs the integer or fractional peripheral divider, and
  - lets `Cy_SCB_I2C_SetDataRate()` derive the SCL low/high phases.
  - It now returns a negative errno on failure so
    `ifx_cat1_i2c_configure()` can propagate the error.
- Add `ifx_cat1_utils_peri_pclk_get_divider()` and
  `ifx_cat1_utils_peri_pclk_get_frac_divider()` clock-control helpers used to
  read back the current divider ratio.

## Test

Measured SCL on `kit_pse84_eval` (m33):

| Requested speed | Before | After |
| --------------- | ------ | ------ |
| STANDARD (100 kHz)   | ~100 kHz | 100 kHz |
| FAST (400 kHz)       | ~100 kHz | 362 kHz |
| FAST_PLUS (1 MHz)    | ~100 kHz | 862 kHz |

The post-fix FAST/FAST_PLUS values are the expected maxima for an integer
oversampling-clock divider on this part (the SCB never overshoots the
requested rate); before the fix every speed collapsed to the same ~100 kHz.

title: kernel: smp: ipi: do not drain self bit in signal_pending_ipi()
body:
signal_pending_ipi() used atomic_clear() on _kernel.pending_ipi, which
also drained the calling CPU's own pending bit. With directed IPIs,
arch_sched_directed_ipi() skips the calling CPU, so any IPI that had
been raised for self by another CPU was silently dropped. The lost
wakeup left the target CPU stuck until something else nudged the
scheduler.

This was latent for the existing call site in ipi_work_process(), but
became reachable on every no-swap path through do_swap() once
signal_pending_ipi() was added there, producing intermittent CPU1
starvation on SMP. tests/kernel/spinlock/spinlock_api test_trylock
(and test_spinlock_bounce on cortex_a53) reproduced it reliably on
qemu_riscv32/smp, qemu_riscv64/smp, and qemu_cortex_a53/smp: CPU0's
loop would acquire bounce_lock 10000 times in a row without CPU1
ever winning a single acquisition.

Switch to atomic_and() with the self bit as the mask, which preserves
our own pending bit (so the next interrupt entry on this CPU still
sees it and runs the scheduler) while atomically draining the bits
for the other CPUs we are about to dispatch IPIs to.

Assisted-by: Claude:claude-opus-4.7
Signed-off-by: Tom Burdick <thomas.burdick@infineon.com>

Picked out of #110717

body:
This comprehensive pull request unifies our entire low-level PCIe diagnostics and hardware instrumentation sprint into a single, cohesive subsystem release: the PCIe Runtime Telemetry & Bring-up Suite. 

By grouping these subcommands and cross-module tracking layers into a linear, single-commit architecture, we prevent tracking drift, eliminate downstream rebasing churn, and deliver a clean, modular diagnostic interface to the core shell utility tree.

### Development History & Patch Breakdown
To facilitate granular code reviews, the atomic development history can be traced through the following individual tracking branches:

When bringing up custom silicon, evaluating multi-layer high-speed PCB trace designs, or triaging fault signatures on safety-critical real-time platforms, firmware engineers cannot rely on heavy, non-deterministic high-level OS abstractions.

title: net: dns: Misc multi-server fixes
body:
* **Set dispatcher ifindex on resolver registration** — A second DNS server bound to a different interface was treated as a duplicate and never added to the socket service poll list. Late DNS replies on that socket piled up unread, each holding an RX net_pkt until the pool was exhausted.

* **Flush datagram when dispatcher buffer alloc fails** — If the DNS message pool was full, the dispatcher returned without reading the socket. The datagram stayed queued and kept its net_pkt pinned. A discard read on allocation failure releases the buffer even when the packet can't be processed.

* **Keep polling remaining servers on single close** — Removing one DNS server unregistered polling for every resolver socket and cleared dispatch entries for all of them. Servers on other interfaces could still receive traffic but nothing drained their queues, so packets accumulated and starved RX.

Fixes #112939

title: bluetooth: mesh: clamp solicitation PDU length before decryption

body:
The encrypted Solicitation PDU is defined by Mesh Protocol 1.1.1 section 6.9.1 as a fixed 17-octet Network PDU (CTL=1, TTL=0, empty TransportPDU, 8-octet NetMIC).

The mesh scan callback in adv.c restores its snapshot of the advertising buffer before dispatching, so buf->len passed into bt_mesh_sol_recv() may still cover trailing AD structures beyond the Solicitation Service Data.

Trim buf->len to the expected 17 octets after consuming the Solicitation Service Data Identification Type byte, and drop the PDU early if fewer octets remain. This aligns the input handed to sol_pdu_decrypt() with the specification.

title: drivers: wifi: nrf_wifi: Support 64-bit TWT interval range
body:
The TWT interval passed by the Wi-Fi management API is a uint64_t, but nrf_wifi_twt_us_to_float() took a uint32_t, silently truncating any interval above UINT32_MAX us (~71.6 min). On top of that, the encoder worked in milliseconds and renormalised the mantissa via frexp(), which pinned it near ~1000 and used only ~10 of the 16 mantissa bits, capping the encodable interval at ~1000 * 2^31 us (~24 days).

Take the interval as uint64_t end to end and encode it directly in micro-seconds using the full 16-bit mantissa and the 5-bit exponent (max WIFI_MAX_TWT_EXPONENT). This removes the truncation and lets the driver represent the complete range the API exposes, up to the IEEE 802.11 maximum of UINT16_MAX * 2^31 us, with exact micro-second resolution. Intervals beyond the encodable maximum are saturated.

The over-the-air value is unchanged (mantissa * 2^exponent us), so the firmware interface is untouched; only the host-side conversion changes.

This makes it impossible to release a pin with gpio_pin_configure(dev, pin, GPIO_DISCONNECTED), which applications such as debug probes and programmers need in order to tri-state shared target pins (SWD, ICSP, UPDI) when a protocol is deactivated.

title: dap: add lock API to serialize debug port access
body:
`dap_link_execute_cmd()` runs without locking. An application that also drives the same debug port from its own threads therefore cannot serialize against commands coming from the debug host, and the two interleave on the wire.

This adds a `k_mutex` to `struct dap_link_context`, statically initialized by `DAP_LINK_CONTEXT_DEFINE()` and held across command processing, and exposes `dap_link_lock()` / `dap_link_unlock()` so an application can hold the port across its own transfer sequence. +52/-1, confined to `subsys/dap/` and its header. Existing users are unaffected: the lock is uncontended unless an application takes it.

### What the application is

A USB debug probe running CMSIS-DAP for the host while its own firmware reads a log ring buffer out of the target's RAM over the same SWD interface — "watch the target's console while a debugger is attached to it". The probe's engine is driven by a poll thread; the host's commands execute on the USB device stack thread. Both reach the same DP.

### Why the lock is taken inside `dap_link_execute_cmd()`

Two reasons, and the second is the one that motivates the exported `lock()`/`unlock()` pair:

1. **Granularity.** A `DAP_TransferBlock` writes CSW/TAR once and then issues N DRW accesses. An application transfer landing mid-batch re-points TAR, and the host's remaining reads silently return the wrong data. Serializing at *transfer* granularity — in the DP driver, or in a shim below it — cannot express this; only a hold spanning the whole command can. We built the driver-level shim first and it is structurally short of what correctness needs: it sees operations, not command boundaries.

2. **It is the only interposition point that exists.** `dap_link_execute_cmd()` is declared in `subsys/dap/cmsis_dap.h`, not in a public header, and the USB backend calls it from its own completion handler. An application cannot wrap a DAP command batch through today's public API at all, short of forking `dap_backend_usb.c`. Holding the lock inside the subsystem is what gives the application a state it can make a coherent decision against — in our case, "is a host session live right now", which is armed by `DAP_Connect` from inside that very call.

### Measured

Probe FRDM-MCXA153, target Nucleo-H503RB, pyOCD 0.45.0, ten `pyocd commander` connects with the probe's own engine already polling the target:

| Probe firmware | Clean connects |
|---|---|
| no shared lock | 0 / 10 |
| this lock only | 9 / 16 |
| this lock + application-side deference | 10 / 10 |

Stated plainly: the lock alone is not sufficient — an SW-DP requires IDCODE as the next access after a line reset, which is protocol *phase*, and no lock fixes phase. Our firmware layers a deference rule on top. But the lock is what that layer stands on, and without it the setup does not work at all. Cost of the whole downstream layer on a 24 KB part: +8 bytes.

### Limits

Command execution already happens in the USB backend's transfer completion handler, so a long command stalls every USB function on the device. This patch adds a second source of that stall — an application holding the lock — hence the `@warning`. Moving command execution to a worker would remove the coupling entirely; that is a backend rework, and the lock is correct either way.

### Alternatives

- Lock in the DP driver, or in an application shim below it — wrong granularity (see above); tried, insufficient.
- Application supplies its own DAP backend — the entry point is private, and it means forking ~500 lines off upstream.
- Host-side configuration telling debuggers to drop their register caches — patches only cooperating hosts and fails corrupt rather than safe when absent.

Happy to convert this to a registered callback pair (`lock_ops` on the context, NULL by default) if you would rather no mutex existed for users that do not opt in, or to gate it behind a Kconfig. Also happy to drop the owner-recursive property — nothing in `subsys/dap` re-enters; the recursion only saves our own nesting.

Tested by building `samples/subsys/dap` for `frdm_mcxa156`.

title: Bluetooth: Mesh: delayable_msg: fix NULL deref on empty busy list (#113175)
body:
Fixes #113175.

## Problem

`delayable_msg_handler()` pops a node from `access_delayable_msg.busy_ctx` and immediately uses it via `CONTAINER_OF` without checking for NULL:

```c
sys_snode_t *node = sys_slist_get(&access_delayable_msg.busy_ctx);
struct delayable_msg_ctx *pending_msg =
        CONTAINER_OF(node, struct delayable_msg_ctx, node);

pending_msg->fired_time += 10;
```

When the busy list is empty, `sys_slist_get()` returns NULL, so `pending_msg` is also NULL (`node` is the first member of `struct delayable_msg_ctx`), and `pending_msg->fired_time += 10` performs a read-modify-write near address 0 - on Cortex-M targets this lands in the flash vector-table region and leads to a hard fault ("Bus fault on vector table read").

The issue reporter captured this deterministically on real hardware (nRF5340, BLE mesh node) during node configuration, where a data race between `bt_mesh_delayable_msg_manage()` (BT RX workqueue) and `delayable_msg_handler()` (system workqueue) - both touching the same lock-free slist with no synchronization - causes the handler to sometimes run an extra time against an already-drained busy list, hitting this exact NULL-deref path. The captured hard fault register state was byte-identical to two separate production crashes reported weeks apart.

## Fix

This applies the immediate, minimal fix the reporter proposed: add a NULL check before dereferencing. This eliminates the crash.

The underlying data race between the two execution contexts (the reporter's second, larger proposed fix - e.g. guarding the module's slists with a `k_spinlock`, or funneling both contexts through a single workqueue) is a separate, broader synchronization design question that deserves its own discussion/PR rather than being folded into this minimal crash fix.

## Verification

I don't have the nRF5340 hardware to reproduce the exact race end-to-end, so I verified the specific fix (the NULL check preventing the dereference) with a standalone C reproduction of the node-is-NULL -> `CONTAINER_OF` -> pending_msg-is-NULL -> dereference chain, confirming the pre-fix path computes a near-zero pointer that would be dereferenced, and the post-fix path returns early instead. The crash mechanism itself (NULL/near-NULL pointer dereference causing a hard fault on Cortex-M) is unambiguous from the reporter's own register dump and root-cause analysis, which I independently traced through the current upstream source to confirm still applies.

## Disclosure

Generative AI (Claude) was used to help investigate this issue, implement, and verify this fix. All changes were reviewed by me before submission.

body:
## Summary

delayable_msg.c mutates three `sys_slist_t` pools from two different threads with no synchronization. This series serializes that state, fixes a context leak on an error path, and adds a regression test that reproduces the failure deterministically.

## Problem

Two contexts mutate the module's `free_ctx` / `busy_ctx` / `free_chunks` lists:

- `bt_mesh_delayable_msg_manage()` runs in the caller of the model response send. For messages received over GATT proxy or the advertising bearer this is the BT host RX workqueue (`CONFIG_BT_RECV_WORKQ_BT=y`, `K_PRIO_COOP(CONFIG_BT_RX_PRIO)` = -8).
- `delayable_msg_handler()` runs on the system workqueue (`SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_PRIORITY` = -1).

Both are cooperative, so they cannot preempt each other arbitrarily — but the enqueuer path calls `bt_mesh_access_send()` and `bt_rand()`, which block. While the enqueuer is blocked mid-update, the sysworkq handler runs and interleaves on inconsistent list state. `push_msg_from_delayable_msgs()` compounded this by *peeking* the `busy_ctx` head rather than popping it, so both contexts could send and release the same context.

Observed symptom: `delayable_msg_handler()` used the result of `sys_slist_get()` without a NULL check. Once the other context had drained the busy list, `CONTAINER_OF()` yielded `NULL` and the following `pending_msg->fired_time += 10` read-modify-write faulted on a NULL-based address — a bus fault in the flash vector-table region on Cortex-M, ending with the CPU at `PC=0` (hard fault reported in the sysworkq context).

Separately, `release_delayable_msg_ctx()` only appended to `free_ctx` when `sys_slist_find_and_remove()` found the context on `busy_ctx`. The `-ENOMEM` path in `bt_mesh_delayable_msg_manage()` releases a context that was popped from `free_ctx` and never inserted on `busy_ctx`, so it was silently lost from both lists. This needs no race to trigger: it is reachable single-threaded whenever chunk allocation comes up short and the purge attempt hits `-EBUSY`/`-ENOBUFS` from the transport. Repeat it `CONFIG_BT_MESH_ACCESS_DELAYABLE_MSG_COUNT` times and every delayable send fails with `-ENOMEM` until reboot.

## Changes

| Commit | Description |
|---|---|
| `bluetooth: mesh: delayable_msg: fix ctx leak on manage() ENOMEM path` | Append to `free_ctx` unconditionally. `find_and_remove()` is a no-op when the context is not on `busy_ctx`, so the normal release path is unaffected. |
| `bluetooth: mesh: delayable_msg: serialize list access with a spinlock` | Add a `k_spinlock` covering every list mutation and the `fired_time` field of any context on `busy_ctx`. The lock is dropped around all blocking calls. `push_msg_from_delayable_msgs()` now atomically detaches the head, so concurrent pushers cannot send the same message. On `-EBUSY`/`-ENOBUFS` the message is reinserted with the `fired_time += 10` backoff (moved out of the handler for atomicity) and the timer re-armed. The handler no longer touches `busy_ctx` directly, eliminating the NULL dereference by construction. |
| `tests: bluetooth: mesh: delayable_msg: add concurrency regression test` | New `test_concurrent_manage` in the existing suite. |

No API, Kconfig, or devicetree changes. Critical sections contain only list manipulation; every blocking call is made with the lock released. On non-SMP builds `k_spinlock` reduces to `irq_lock()`/`irq_unlock()` with no added RAM.

## Test

`test_concurrent_manage` runs two cooperative threads — the ZTEST main thread temporarily raised to `K_PRIO_COOP(6)` and a helper at the same priority — each calling `bt_mesh_delayable_msg_manage()` 40 times, alternating via `k_yield()`. The mocked send-completion callback also yields, landing control inside `push_msg_from_delayable_msgs()` while the caller is mid-critical-section. Because the interleaving points are explicit yield sites rather than preemption timing, a regression reproduces on the first run.

Assertions track callbacks **per `cb_data` slot** rather than in aggregate. This matters: the bug delivers two callbacks to one message and zero to another, so aggregate counters coincidentally balance and hide it. The per-slot check enforces the exactly-once delivery contract.

Results on `qemu_x86`:

- Reverting the fixes and keeping the test: `test_concurrent_manage` fails with 40 of 80 slots receiving a wrong callback count.
- With the fixes: `SUITE PASS - 100.00%`, 8/8 passing.

```
west build -b qemu_x86 tests/bluetooth/mesh/delayable_msg -t run
```

Fixes #113175

title: drivers: sensor: bme280: sign-extend dig_h4/dig_h5 calibration values
body:
Fixes #112381

## Problem

`bme280_read_compensation()` (drivers/sensor/bosch/bme280/bme280.c) builds the
12-bit two's complement calibration constants `dig_h4`/`dig_h5` (BME280
datasheet Table 16, registers 0xE4-0xE6) like this:

```c
data->dig_h4 = (hbuf[3] << 4) | (hbuf[4] & 0x0F);
data->dig_h5 = ((hbuf[4] >> 4) & 0x0F) | (hbuf[5] << 4);
```

`dig_h4`/`dig_h5` are declared `int16_t` (bme280.h), but `hbuf` is
`uint8_t hbuf[7]`. Under the C integer promotion rules, `hbuf[3]`/`hbuf[5]`
promote to a *non-negative* `int` before the `<<`, so a calibration byte
such as `0xE2` (which is meant to represent a negative 12-bit value once
combined with the low nibble) is promoted to `226`, not `-30` — the shift
never sign-extends it.

Any sensor whose calibration byte has its top bit set (a negative
correction value, which is a normal and frequently-occurring case for
these constants) gets silently reinterpreted as a large positive number.
Both fields feed directly into `bme280_compensate_humidity()`, producing a
wrong `%RH` reading with no indication anything is wrong.

Reported in #112381, where the maintainer (@teburd) confirmed the fix
approach:

> Please propose a PR, you have proposed fix in the issue already. There's
> also a sign extension API in Zephyr, see sign_extend()

## Fix

Use the project's existing `sign_extend()` helper
(`include/zephyr/sys/util.h`) with index `11` (0-based sign-bit position
for a 12-bit value) — the same idiom already used for other 12-bit two's
complement fields elsewhere in the tree, e.g.
`drivers/sensor/als31300/als31300.c`
(`sign_extend(value, ALS31300_12BIT_SIGN_BIT_INDEX)`, where the constant
is `11`) and `drivers/sensor/bosch/bmm350/bmm350.c`.

```c
data->dig_h4 = sign_extend((hbuf[3] << 4) | (hbuf[4] & 0x0F), 11);
data->dig_h5 = sign_extend(((hbuf[4] >> 4) & 0x0F) | (hbuf[5] << 4), 11);
```

`#include <zephyr/sys/util.h>` is added for `sign_extend()`. The change is
scoped to these two lines plus the include and an explanatory comment; no
other file defines or re-implements this parsing (checked
`bme280_async.c`, `bme280_decoder.c`, `bme280_i2c.c`, `bme280_spi.c`).

## Verification

I wrote and ran a standalone C harness that copies the exact parsing
statements and the exact `bme280_compensate_humidity()` formula verbatim
from `bme280.c` (the only stub is the register read itself, replaced with
a fixed test buffer). `sign_extend()` is copied verbatim from
`include/zephyr/sys/util.h`. A third, independent implementation
(`ground_truth_12bit()`, a subtraction-based 12-bit two's-complement
decode that shares no code path with either the buggy or fixed parsing)
is used as the cross-check oracle.

Compiled with `gcc -std=c11 -O0 -Wall -Wextra`, run result: `PASS: 0
mismatch(es)`, exit code 0.

- **Boundary vectors** (`0`, `+2047`, `-2048`, `-1`, `-30`, and the
  issue's own example `0xE2 0x03`): the fixed parsing matches the
  independent ground truth on every vector. The current (buggy) parsing
  *diverges* from ground truth on every vector whose sign bit is set, and
  matches it on every vector whose sign bit is clear — i.e. the bug
  reproduces exactly where expected and nowhere else.
- **Realistic scenario** (`dig_h2=100, dig_h6=0, dig_h3=0, dig_h1=75,
  t_fine=100000, adc_humidity=8000`, chosen to avoid the 0%/100%
  saturation clamps):
  - `dig_h4`: buggy = `3619`, fixed = `-477` (ground truth `-477`)
  - `dig_h5`: buggy = `3616`, fixed = `-480` (ground truth `-480`)
  - Reported humidity: buggy = `50.60%RH`, fixed = `59.31%RH`,
    delta = `-8.71%RH`
- **Regression check**: for a buffer whose sign bits are all clear
  (`hbuf[3..5] = 12 03 34`), buggy and fixed parsing produce identical
  results — the fix does not change behavior for positive calibration
  values.

## Disclosure

Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to investigate this issue,
implement the fix, and write/run the standalone verification harness
described above. All changes were reviewed by me before submission.

title: net: ptp: fix 32-bit overflow in foreign clock record time window
labels: area: Networking;area: Tests;backport v3.7-branch;area: PTP;backport v4.3-branch;backport v4.4-branch
body:
`foreign_clock_cleanup()` computes the announce record aging timeout in
32-bit arithmetic before storing it into an `int64_t`. For positive
`log_msg_interval` values the product `4 * 2^log * NSEC_PER_SEC` wraps
around: with `log_msg_interval = 1` the 8 s window becomes ~3.7 s, so
announce messages still inside the window are aged out prematurely and
the port can wrongly lose its foreign time transmitter records
(Coverity CID 487738, OVERFLOW_BEFORE_WIDEN / CWE-190).

- The first commit casts the first factor to `int64_t` in both branches
  so the expression is evaluated in 64-bit arithmetic.
- The second commit adds a `foreign_master` regression test pinning the
  scaled window behavior: it fails without the fix (records dropped,
  `ptp_port_best_foreign()` returns `NULL`) and passes with it.

**Testing:** `west twister -T tests/net/ptp -p native_sim/native/64` —
all suites pass; the new test was verified to fail with the fix
reverted. `./scripts/ci/check_compliance.py` clean locally.

Fixes #84696

title: irq: multilevel: avoid bit-field layout dependency
labels: area: Kernel;area: Tests;area: Architectures;area: Interrupt Controller
body:
## Summary

Multilevel IRQ values use a numeric encoding with each interrupt level placed at configuration-defined bit offsets.

The inline helpers in `irq_multilevel.h` currently access those fields through a C bit-field overlay. Since bit-field allocation order is implementation-defined, the helpers can interpret the numeric IRQ value differently from `IRQ_TO_L2()` and `IRQ_TO_L3()`.

This change:

* replaces the bit-field overlay with named masks and the existing `FIELD_GET()` / `FIELD_PREP()` helpers;
* preserves the existing multilevel IRQ encoding and public API;
* adds coverage for encoding, decoding, level detection, parent lookup, interrupt-controller lookup, and increment operations.

Before the fix, the new tests pass on little-endian Malta but fail on big-endian Malta and LEON3.

## Testing

```text
west twister -G -T tests/arch/common/irq_multilevel --inline-logs
```

Results: 12/12 test configurations and 102/102 test cases passed, with no warnings.

Tested on:

```text
qemu_malta/qemu_malta
qemu_malta/qemu_malta/be
qemu_leon3/leon3
```

title: drivers: sensor: bmi270: fix ANY_MOTION_2 threshold field width
body:
## Problem

`BMI270_ANYMO_2_THRESHOLD_MASK` is defined as `BIT_MASK(10)` (10 bits, 0..1023), but the
ANY_MOTION_2 feature-config word's threshold field is actually 11 bits wide (bits `[10:0]`):
`BMI270_ANYMO_2_OUT_CONF_POS` is 11 and `OUT_CONF` occupies bits `[14:11]`, so bit 10
legitimately belongs to the threshold field and is currently left unused, wasting one bit
of resolution.

`bmi270_write_anymo_threshold()` (drivers/sensor/bosch/bmi270/bmi270.c:554-578) uses the
mask constant directly as the scaling denominator when converting a requested g threshold
into the register's raw LSB count:

```c
uint16_t lsbs = (val.val2 * BMI270_ANYMO_2_THRESHOLD_MASK) / 1e6;
```

Per Bosch's official BMI270 Sensor API (any_motion threshold documented as "5.11g
format... Range is 0 to 1g"), the field is a Q5.11 fixed-point fraction of g (LSB =
1/2048 g) — i.e. genuinely 11 bits. With the current 10-bit mask, every requested
threshold is scaled using half the intended denominator, so the raw LSB count programmed
into the sensor represents roughly half of the value the caller asked for: e.g. requesting
the datasheet's own default of 83 mg produces a raw count that the sensor's fixed Q5.11
decode interprets as ~41 mg, and requesting the documented max of 1 g (the `val1 > 0`
"set to max" path) can only reach a raw count representing ~0.5 g. The any-motion
interrupt therefore fires at roughly twice the sensitivity the caller configured, for
every value in range.

The same field-width mistake exists in the neighboring `BMI270_ANYMO_1_DURATION_MASK`,
defined as `BIT_MASK(12)` although `ANY_MOTION_1.duration` is 13 bits (`SELECT_X/Y/Z`
occupy bits `15:13`, so duration legitimately owns bits `12:0`). This constant is not
currently used as a scaling factor anywhere (`bmi270_write_anymo_duration()` just shifts
the LSB count into position without consulting the mask), so it has no observed runtime
effect yet, but it documents the wrong field width and would corrupt any future code that
relies on it (e.g. for range clamping). Fixed for consistency with the same datasheet
section, which documents the duration range as 0..163 s at 20 ms/LSB
(163000 / 20 = 8150, which needs 13 bits; 12 bits only reaches 81.9 s).

Fixes #111249

## Fix

- `drivers/sensor/bosch/bmi270/bmi270.h`: `BMI270_ANYMO_2_THRESHOLD_MASK` `BIT_MASK(10)` →
  `BIT_MASK(11)`; `BMI270_ANYMO_1_DURATION_MASK` `BIT_MASK(12)` → `BIT_MASK(13)`.
- `drivers/sensor/bosch/bmi270/bmi270.c`: updated the accompanying comment
  (`/* max = BIT_MASK(10) ... */` → `/* max = BIT_MASK(11) ... */`) to match.

Minimal, 2-file, +3/-3 diff. Confirmed by `grep` that both constants are only referenced
within this driver, so no other code depends on the old (wrong) values.

## Verification

Built and ran a standalone C harness that verbatim-copies the `ANYMO_1`/`ANYMO_2`
`#define`s from `bmi270.h` and the full body of `bmi270_write_anymo_threshold()` from
`bmi270.c` (only Zephyr-specific types/log macros are stubbed — no arithmetic/logic was
rewritten), compiled once against the unpatched 10-bit mask and once against the fixed
11-bit mask. An independent reference model — hardcoding Bosch's documented Q5.11 decode
directly (LSB = 1/2048 g), not sharing any code with the driver — computes what the sensor
would actually trigger at for each raw register value the driver produces.

```
requested   unpatched (buggy)      patched (fixed)
 83 mg  ->  triggers at  41.02 mg   triggers at  82.52 mg
250 mg  ->  triggers at 124.51 mg   triggers at 249.51 mg
500 mg  ->  triggers at 249.51 mg   triggers at 499.51 mg
900 mg  ->  triggers at 449.22 mg   triggers at 899.41 mg
max(1g) ->  triggers at 499.51 mg   triggers at 999.51 mg

duration field:
  unpatched BIT_MASK(12) = 4095 -> max representable 81.9 s  (datasheet: 0..163 s)
  patched   BIT_MASK(13) = 8191 -> max representable 163.8 s (matches datasheet)
```

This confirms the unpatched driver silently programs roughly half of the
requested/documented threshold for every value in range, and the patched driver matches
the requested value (within the normal Q5.11 quantization already inherent to this
field). Duration max representable value now matches the datasheet's documented 163 s
range.

`checkpatch.pl --no-tree` on the code diff: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

Cross-checked against the currently open issue #111249 ("BMI270 driver ANYMO threshold
conversion is incorrect"), filed independently by another user against the Bosch
datasheet, which reports the identical root cause and the identical corrected mask
values (`BIT_MASK(11)` / `BIT_MASK(13)`).

## Disclosure

Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to investigate this issue, implement the fix,
and write/run the standalone verification harness described above. All changes were
reviewed by me before submission, and I take full responsibility for the contribution.

title: fs: ext2: reject sub-1024 block_size in ext2_format() before it underflows
body:
## Description

`ext2_format()` computes the superblock's `s_log_block_size` field as:

```c
uint8_t block_log_size = find_msb_set(cfg->block_size) - 11;
```

`find_msb_set()` returns `unsigned int` (`include/zephyr/arch/common/ffs.h`), so this
subtraction is unsigned arithmetic. `validate_config()` only substitutes the default
block size when `cfg->block_size == 0` — it never enforces a minimum — so any caller
that passes a `block_size` smaller than 1024 (the sector size 512 is an easy, plausible
mistake to make here) causes `find_msb_set(cfg->block_size) - 11` to underflow, and the
truncated garbage is written straight into the on-disk superblock:

| `block_size` | `find_msb_set()` | `block_log_size` written to disk |
|---|---|---|
| 512 | 10 | 255 |
| 256 | 9 | 254 |
| 100 | 7 | 252 |
| 1 | 1 | 246 |

`ext2_format()` returns success while silently writing a corrupt, unmountable file
system, instead of failing cleanly at format time with a clear error.

This is the root cause flagged by Coverity CID 487768 / issue #84678, and independently
confirmed there by @de-nordic: *"it is possible to set block_size to 512 bytes, even
though it seems that other code expects block_size to be multiply of 1024."*

Note: PR #111241 already added a mount-time bound check (`s_log_block_size > 11U` is
rejected in `ext2_verify_disk_superblock()`), so a superblock corrupted by this bug can
no longer cause Zephyr's own mount path to compute an out-of-bounds shift. That is a
separate, already-fixed concern; it does not address the format-time bug itself, which
still lets `fs_mkfs(FS_EXT2, ...)` silently produce a corrupt, unmountable file system
for any `block_size < 1024`.

## Fix

Extend `validate_config()` to reject any nonzero `block_size` that is not a power of two
`>= 1024`, and propagate that error from `ext2_format()` before the shift-count
calculation is reached. `block_size == 0` still resolves to the documented default, and
every currently-legal value (1024/2048/4096/...) is unaffected — verified with a
standalone reproduction of the exact arithmetic (see Testing).

## Testing

- Reproduced the underflow and validated the fix with a standalone host program that
  copies `find_msb_set()` and the exact expressions verbatim (gcc, `-Wall -Wextra
  -std=c11`): all four bad inputs (512/256/100/1) are rejected with the new check before
  the shift-count is ever computed, and all legal inputs (0/1024/2048/4096) resolve to a
  `block_log_size` byte-identical to what the current code already produces for them.
- Ran `scripts/checkpatch.pl` against the diff: 0 errors, 0 warnings.
- I do not have a Zephyr SDK / `west` toolchain available in this environment, so I was
  not able to run an in-tree `west build` / twister test for `tests/subsys/fs/ext2`
  (that suite currently only exercises `block_size` 2048/4096, never a value below
  1024, so it would not have caught this regardless). Flagging this limitation
  explicitly rather than claiming in-tree verification I didn't do.

Fixes #84678

## Disclosure

Generative AI (Claude) was used to help investigate this issue and implement this fix.
All changes were reviewed by me before submission.

title: Samples lvgl benchmark native sim fixes
body:
Summary
     
  Fixes a segfault in the LVGL benchmark demo sample on native_sim, and makes the on-screen performance
  monitor report real CPU usage.
     
  Running the benchmark demo on native_sim crashes with a segmentation fault roughly two minutes in,
  during the widgets scene:

  west build -b native_sim/native/64 samples/modules/lvgl/demos -p \
      -- -DCONFIG_LV_Z_DEMO_BENCHMARK=y

  Root cause
     
  The benchmark demo selects the widgets demo, which rotates/transforms images. The layer and
  image-transform scratch buffers allocated for that rendering (lv_draw_sw_img.c) exhaust the LVGL memory
  pool part-way through the run. The allocation failure is not caught: LVGL's LV_ASSERT_MALLOC maps to
  Zephyr's __ASSERT, which is a no-op unless CONFIG_ASSERT is set (it is not, in the default sample
  config). The resulting NULL buffer is then dereferenced by the SW renderer, producing the segfault.
     
  Confirmed under gdb (crash in transform_argb8888, writing to a NULL transformed_buf) and reproduced
  cleanly as an out-of-memory assert in a debug build with CONFIG_ASSERT=y + LVGL logging enabled:

  <err> lvgl: transform_and_recolor: Asserted at expression:
        transformed_buf != NULL (Out of memory) lv_draw_sw_img.c:519
     
  The memory pressure is specific to native_sim, which runs at 32-bit color depth
  (CONFIG_LV_COLOR_DEPTH_32). The dynamically allocated layer and transform buffers are sized by
  bytes-per-pixel, so at 32bpp they are twice the size of a 16-bit target's, and that is what overflows
  the pool. This was verified with a controlled build: native_sim/native/64 at 16-bit color runs the same
  benchmark to completion with the old pool size, and the same demo runs fine on real 16bpp hardware
  (mimxrt700_evk + rk055hdmipi4ma0) with its existing 81920-byte pool. Lower-color-depth targets are
  therefore unaffected.

Changes
                                       
  - Enlarge the pool for native_sim. Set CONFIG_LV_Z_MEM_POOL_SIZE to 128 KiB in both
  native_sim.conf and native_sim_native_64.conf so the benchmark runs to completion. The shared prj.conf
  default (58368) and all other boards' overrides are left unchanged, since the overflow is a
  32bpp-native_sim condition.
  - Report real CPU load. The performance monitor shows 0% CPU usage unless CONFIG_CPU_LOAD is enabled.
  Enable it in prj.conf so the monitor reports real usage on targets that support it (Cortex-M/A, RISC-V,
  Xtensa). Because CPU_LOAD depends on the CPU architecture and is unavailable on native_sim, it is
  overridden to n in both native_sim board configs to avoid an unmet-dependency Kconfig warning; the idle
  percentage simply stays 0 on the simulator.

  Testing

  - native_sim and native_sim/native/64: benchmark runs through all scenes and reaches the summary
  without crashing; pool resolves to 131072 and no Kconfig warnings are emitted.
  - mimxrt700_evk/mimxrt798s/cm33_cpu0 + SHIELD=rk055hdmipi4ma0: flashed and run on hardware; benchmark
