title: scripts: ci: request reviewers in batches of 15
body:
A single GitHub review request accepts at most 15 users, but _request_reviews() sent the whole candidate list in one call and, when GitHub rejected it, retried with only the first 15 and gave up on the rest. Those left over were merely mentioned in a comment, and only a later run of the script - where the first 15 are filtered out as existing reviewers - added them. That is why a PR received a subset of its reviewers on the first run and more on the second.

Split the candidates into batches of REVIEWER_REQUEST_BATCH (15) and issue one request per batch, so every eligible reviewer is added on the first run. A rejected batch is now retried one user at a time, so a single bad candidate (deleted account, lost collaborator status) no longer costs the rest of its batch their review request; only the users that still fail are mentioned instead.

Also delete the reviewer-mention comment once a run has nobody left to mention, so the PR stops claiming that people could not be requested after they have been.

Verified with scripts/tests/ci/test_set_assignees.py, extended with tests for the batching, the per-user fallback and the comment cleanup.

title: net_buf: buf: avoid rewalking the chain in net_buf_append_bytes
body:
## Problem

`net_buf_append_bytes()` links each newly allocated fragment with `net_buf_frag_add()`, which calls `net_buf_frag_last()` and walks the whole chain from the head to find the tail. That tail is already known (it is the fragment the loop has just filled), so appending a payload that spans multiple fragments can incur O(n^2) fragment traversals.

The redundant search occurs each time a new fragment is linked. When a single call links many fragments, repeatedly searching the growing chain produces quadratic traversal work. A call linking only one fragment still repeats the search for the existing chain’s tail. The in-tree callers are the hl7800 and wncm14a2a modem receive paths, which append UART reads into a growing chain.

## Change

Keep the chain tail in a local variable and link the new fragment behind it with `net_buf_frag_insert()`. For a non-NULL head that is exactly what `net_buf_frag_add()` does, and the function already requires a non-NULL buffer, so the fragment reference is still consumed and the resulting chain order is unchanged. The tail is re-derived from the returned fragment, so an allocator callback that hands back a chain keeps its previous behaviour.

Allocation-failure behaviour is unchanged: the function returns the number of bytes appended so far, retaining any data and fragments already added during the call.

## Evidence

Deterministic count of ->frags traversal steps, taken with a temporary counter in net_buf_frag_last() on native_sim/native/64, with an identical build and configuration on both sides:

| Case | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4096 bytes appended in one call over 32 x 128-byte fragments | 465 | 0 |
| The same chain built with 32 single-fragment appends | 930 | 465 |

The first row is the case the O(n^2) bound describes. The second is the shape of the in-tree hl7800 and wncm14a2a modem receive paths, which read at most one fragment's worth per call: for them the chain is walked once per call instead of twice. The remaining 465 steps are from the net_buf_frag_last() calls at function entry, which the head-pointer argument requires and which this change does not address. (The claim is a reduction in executed pointer traversals, not a measured wall-clock figure.)

## Testing

Executed with Twister, host/gnu toolchain:

- `libraries.net_buf.buf` on `native_sim/native` and `native_sim/native/64`
- `libraries.net_buf.buf_simple` and `libraries.net_buf.buf_simple.hardening`
  on `unit_testing/unit_testing`
- `net.packet`, `net.packet.preempt`, `net.packet.large_buffer` and
  `net.packet.allocation_stats` on `native_sim/native` and
  `native_sim/native/64`

12 of 12 configurations passed, 329 of 329 executed test cases passed. I've added `net_buf_append_long_chain`, which builds a ten-fragment chain over two appends and checks the fragment count, that every fragment is filled, the payload order across the join between the two appends, and that an additional append to an already-full chain leaves it unchanged when the pool is exhausted.. The change is semantics-preserving so this test passes before and after, i.e. it guards the chain ordering that the tail tracking must maintain. 

`checkpatch.pl` reports no issues; ClangFormat, Identity, YAMLLint, TextEncoding and BinaryFiles compliance checks pass.

## Limitations

For callers that append a single fragment's worth per call, the chain is still walked once per call from the head, so this change removes the second walk, not the first. The two in-tree callers are vendor modem drivers that were not built locally because their target toolchains were unavailable. No physical-target timing or cross-compiled code-size measurements were taken.

title: drivers: sensor: adxl372: support op mode/WUR via sensor API
body:
The ADXL372 driver had no way to change its operating mode or wake-up rate (WUR) from application code:

- adxl372_set_op_mode() was declared only under CONFIG_ADXL372_STREAM, so it could not be called unless RTIO streaming was enabled.
- Even with that Kconfig on, nothing routed SENSOR_ATTR_CONFIGURATION (or any other sensor attribute) to adxl372_set_op_mode(), so the operating mode set at init from the config struct's hardcoded op-mode field could never be changed afterwards.
- adxl372_set_wakeup_rate() had the same problem: it was only ever called once at init with cfg->wur, with no attribute wired up to call it again at runtime.

In practice this made the chip's own low-power Wake-Up mode unreachable from application code - only ADXL372_FULL_BW_MEASUREMENT (continuous conversion, the highest-current mode the chip has) could ever be selected, since that is the config struct's default and nothing could change it later.

Fix this by:

- Moving enum adxl372_op_mode into a new public header, include/zephyr/drivers/sensor/adxl372.h, so application code has something to include for the mode values without pulling in the private driver header.
- Un-gating the adxl372_set_op_mode() declaration from CONFIG_ADXL372_STREAM in the private header - the function definition itself was never actually gated, only its declaration.
- Wiring SENSOR_ATTR_CONFIGURATION to adxl372_set_op_mode(), and SENSOR_ATTR_SAMPLING_FREQUENCY - while the device is in ADXL372_WAKE_UP mode - to adxl372_set_wakeup_rate(), converting the requested frequency to the nearest supported wake-up period. Both the current op mode and WUR are now tracked in struct adxl372_data so attr_set() knows which of ODR or WUR "sampling frequency" currently refers to.
- Adding an op-mode devicetree property so the mode selected at init is configurable too, not just at runtime. Defaults to ADXL372_OP_MODE_FULL_BW_MEASUREMENT, so existing users see no behavior change unless they opt in.

Tested on real ADXL372 hardware (Thingy:91, nRF9160): switched between ADXL372_FULL_BW_MEASUREMENT and ADXL372_WAKE_UP at runtime via sensor_attr_set(), and set several wake-up rates via SENSOR_ATTR_SAMPLING_FREQUENCY, confirming each is applied.

Fixes: #118373

title: drivers: watchdog: sam0: add Always-On (ALWAYSON) support
labels: area: Watchdog;platform: Microchip SAM;area: Devicetree Binding
body:
The SAMC21/SAMD21/SAME51 WDT has an Always-On bit (CTRLA.ALWAYSON, bit 7) that, when set, makes the watchdog run continuously and prevents disabling it. CONFIG and EWCTRL registers become read-only, so timeout and window configuration cannot be changed.

The driver previously ignored this bit entirely, causing:
- wdt_disable() to silently fail (returned 0 but WDT kept running when ALWAYSON was set by the NVM User Row fuse)
- wdt_is_enabled() to return false when only ALWAYSON was set, misleading callers about the WDT state
- CONFIG_WDT_DISABLE_AT_BOOT to silently fail when ALWAYSON was programmed in the NVM User Row

Fix this by:
- Reading CTRLA.ALWAYSON at init and storing the state
- Making wdt_is_enabled() check both ENABLE and ALWAYSON bits
- Returning -ENOTSUP from wdt_disable() when ALWAYSON is set
- Handling disable-at-boot with a warning when ALWAYSON is active
- Letting install_timeout() and setup() skip CONFIG/EWCTRL writes when ALWAYSON is set (those registers are read-only), but still allowing callback and interrupt configuration

When ALWAYSON is set by software on a previous boot, it persists across warm resets. The driver now handles this by accepting the current configuration and continuing operation. The NVM User Row fuse always takes priority over devicetree.

Add an 'always-on' boolean devicetree property so applications can request Always-On mode from the devicetree without programming fuses.

Also remove a redundant declaration of wdt_sam0_data.

Tested on SAMC21N Xplained Pro (samc21n_xpro):
- With always-on property: wdt_disable() returned -ENOTSUP, the watchdog kept running and was correctly fed every 3 seconds
- Without always-on (and after POR): wdt_disable() worked, re-enable succeeded
- Warm resets with always-on active: install_timeout() and setup() detected the persisted ALWAYSON state and continued operation

title: drivers: watchdog: sam0: protect against feed during closed window
body:
In window mode, writing 0xA5 to the WDT CLEAR register during the closed window period causes an immediate hardware reset. The driver previously made no attempt to detect the current window phase and fed blindly, exposing callers to a hard reset if wdt_feed() was called before the Early Warning interrupt fired.

The SAMC21/SAMD21 WDT has no hardware status register for the current window phase, so the only signal is the Early Warning interrupt, which fires at the start of the open window in window mode.

Fix by tracking the window phase in the ISR:
- Add window_mode and window_open flags to dev_data
- The ISR sets window_open = true when the EW fires (window opens)
- wdt_feed() returns -EAGAIN if the window is closed, allowing the caller to retry without crashing the system
- wdt_feed() clears window_open after a successful feed
- Always enable the EW interrupt in window mode even when the user does not provide a callback, since the driver needs it to track the window state

Also update the wdt_feed() documentation in watchdog.h to clarify that -EAGAIN may also indicate a closed window in window mode.

Tested on SAMC21N Xplained Pro (samc21n_xpro):
- Feed at 5s with 4s-8s window: EW fires at ~4s, feed succeeds at 5s
- Feed at 2s with 4s-8s window: feed rejected with -EAGAIN, no reset
- Feed stopped: early warning fires, then system resets at 8s (normal)

title: bluetooth: classic: l2cap: Fix data drop waiting for config rsp sent
body:
In commit 15bb270 (bluetooth: classic: l2cap: Fix race condition in config rsp handling), the channel transitions from the `CONFIG` state to the `CONNECTED` state of L2CAP channel will be set after the configuration response frame has been sent via the sent callback `l2cap_br_config_rsp_sent_cb()`. The sent callback will be called by `hci_num_completed_packets()` when the HCI event `NUM_COMPLETED_PACKETS` is notified. However, the time duration between the completion of the configuration response transmission and the arrival of the `NUM_COMPLETED_PACKETS` HCI event is indeterminate; it depends entirely on the controller.

From the peer's perspective, the L2CAP channel is successfully established once the configuration response is received, whereas the local side remains in the `CONFIG` state until the `NUM_COMPLETED_PACKETS` event arrives. Consequently, it is possible for the peer to transmit data over the established channel before the `NUM_COMPLETED_PACKETS` event arrives. Since the local side is still in the `CONFIG` state, this data will be discarded.

Add `L2CAP_FLAG_CONF_RSP_SENDING` flag, set before queuing the configuration response and cleared in the sent callback. In the receive path, attempt to complete the configuration state when this flag is set, so that data arriving before the HCI `NUM_COMPLETED_PACKETS` event does not get silently discarded.

The change aims to prevent the dropping of received data while waiting for the HCI event `NUM_COMPLETED_PACKETS`.

body:
Add a native SRTP (RFC 3711) implementation to the RTP stack, built on the PSA Crypto API: platforms with hardware crypto drivers benefit automatically and no second crypto stack is pulled in. Sessions opt in with `rtp_session_set_srtp()` on both the socket and net_pkt transports; the core `srtp_protect()`/`srtp_unprotect()` also work standalone on serialized RTP packets. All state is caller-allocated.

**Supported transforms**

- AES-128-CM with HMAC-SHA1-80/32, the RFC 3711 mandatory-to-implement suites
- AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM (RFC 7714), with AES_256_CM_PRF key derivation (RFC 6188)
- NULL cipher, and NULL authentication behind an explicit opt-in

**Implementation**

- Key derivation with a configurable rate, rollover counter tracking with packet index estimation
- Sliding-window replay protection and the 2^48 packets-per-master-key limit
- Master key identifiers: appended and matched per stream (one master key; rekeying via MKI is out of scope)
- Transmit stream keyed by the session SSRC; receive streams late-bound per source SSRC

**Out of scope**

- Key exchange (DTLS-SRTP, SDES, MIKEY): master keys are provisioned by the application
- SRTCP, as RTCP is not implemented

This is a native alternative to #118267.

title: Bluetooth: Add HCI lockstep command helper and use it in hci_silabs_siwx91x
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Tests;platform: Silabs;area: Bluetooth Controller;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth HCI;area: Bluetooth Classic;Release
body:
Adds `hci_lockstep.h`, a helper on top of the HCI packet helpers of #117228 for HCI drivers that exchange commands with the controller over their own transport, one command at a time, without the Host's command machinery and in any build type. The header lives with the HCI driver API under `include/zephyr/drivers/bluetooth/`, and the implementation is part of every `CONFIG_BT` build, like the packet helpers. Its shape follows what drivers have: the send callback receives the HCI device so a driver's raw send function serves as-is, received packets are fed as bytes, a NULL command buffer means no parameters, the command timeout (one deadline covering the wait for the controller to allow the command and the wait for its response) defaults to the Host's 10 s, and failures are logged by the helper. Command flow control still applies: the helper sends only once the controller allows a command, which every response fed to it announces through Num_HCI_Command_Packets, the NOP Command Complete included. The siwx91x driver is the first user: it sends its RF power vendor command from `open()` through the helper and drops its `setup()` implementation, so the configuration also runs in controller-only builds. Why this matters is in #117228.

title: soc: nordic: nrf71: extract early init into nordicsemi_nrf71_init
body:
soc_early_init_hook() is a generic Zephyr SoC API, called automatically by the kernel during a normal Zephyr boot. TF-M's
platform/ext/target/nordic_nrf/common/core/target_cfg_71.c also needs this same hardware bring-up to run during the Secure boot, which never goes through Zephyr's kernel init and so never calls the hook automatically and has to call the function by name instead.

Because target_cfg_71.c declared its own prototype for soc_early_init_hook() rather than sharing a header with this file, and TF-M's standalone fallback in nrf71_init.c happened to reuse the same name with a different (int) signature, the two independent declarations of the same symbol silently disagreed. The compiler cannot catch this across translation units, so it went undetected until it caused TF-M to read an uninitialized register as a bogus error code and panic on every boot, before any log output was even possible.

Extract the actual init logic into a new, TF-M-specific function nordicsemi_nrf71_init(), matching the pattern already used by nRF54L (nordicsemi_nrf54l_init()). soc_early_init_hook() becomes a thin wrapper that just calls it, so Zephyr's normal boot is unaffected, while TF-M can now call nordicsemi_nrf71_init() by a name that isn't also a generic Zephyr API with its own, unrelated contract.

title: bluetooth: mesh: fix dfu applying step
body:
Commit 1de08e0b6e08 ("bluetooth: mesh: dfu_cli, dfu_srv: accept SUCCESS
and APPLYING as terminal") made the Firmware Update Client acknowledge any
target that answers a Firmware Update Apply message with status Success
and phase Applying Update, ending the Apply step on the first response.

MshDFUv1.0 Section 6.2.2.4 requires the Confirm step of the Distribute
Firmware procedure to wait until the Target nodes have applied the new
firmware update before starting the Retrieve Firmware Information
procedure. The Apply step retry loop was the only thing implementing
that wait. Without it the client reads the Current Firmware ID while the
target is still installing, the Table 7.3 comparison in Section 7.1.2.9
fails, and the target is marked Apply Failed. A PTS test caught this.

Keep repeating Firmware Update Apply to a target reporting Applying
Update, as Section 7.1.2.6 permits, until it reports Idle. Once the
install completes the target answers Wrong Phase with phase Idle, which
the branch above already accepts as the end of the Apply step.

Keep acknowledging the self-target, which is why 1de08e0b6e08 touched
this branch in the first place: a Distributor that is also a Target
defers its own apply until the Confirm step completes, so it never
leaves Applying Update on its own and would otherwise stall the Apply
step until the retry budget is exhausted.

Revert the accompanying dfu_srv change as well. Its -ETIMEDOUT branch
applied the firmware although the Firmware Update Status response was
never acknowledged, assuming a client treats Success + Applying Update
as terminal and does not retry. That assumption no longer holds.
Reverting the phase to Verification Succeeded on any send error is
correct for a retrying client: the retry is accepted as a fresh apply
per Section 6.1.3.6.

title: secure_storage: allow custom AEAD en/decrypt function

When this option is enabled, the key provider is disabled as the crypt function is assumed to take care of the key itself, and the AEAD scheme as well as the key size are not configurable by default to avoid leaking Kconfig options in case the custom implementation would not be using them.

title: net: route: fix IPv6 ping from AIL host to Thread device
body:
Without this fix, a simple IPv6 ping from a host on an adjacent link
    (e.g. the AIL) to a device reachable via a different egress interface
    fails: when the next hop is not yet in the neighbor cache,
    net_route_ipv6_packet() returned -ENOENT and the packet (for a ping,
    the ICMPv6 Echo Reply) was dropped by the router.
    
    Instead of dropping it, clear the link-layer destination the packet was
    received with. net_send_data() then re-enters net_ipv6_prepare_for_send(),
    which already solicits the next hop and queues the packet until the
    Neighbor Advertisement arrives, reusing the existing forwarding path
    (hop-limit decrement, egress interface selection, NULL NS source address
    when forwarding). This mirrors the unknown-neighbor handling already used
    for locally-originated packets. When CONFIG_NET_IPV6_ND is disabled the
    previous -ENOENT behavior is kept.
    
    Add a regression test (net.route.ipv6.forward_nd): forward a packet to an
    unresolved next hop on an Ethernet interface, verify one NS is sent and
    the packet is queued, then resolve the neighbor and verify the queued
    packet is transmitted on the outbound interface.

title: Bluetooth: Host: Extended scanner filter policy and directed advertising reports
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Tests;area: Bluetooth Controller;area: Bluetooth Host;platform: nRF BSIM;Release
body:
Adds host support for the extended scanner filter policies and for the LE Directed Advertising Report event, so that an application can be told about a directed advertisement whose target address is a resolvable private address the Controller was unable to resolve.

Fixes #114103
Fixes #114236

## Background

`subsys/bluetooth/host/scan.c` has always requested one of the basic scanning filter policies. `BT_HCI_LE_SCAN_FP_EXT_NO_FILTER` (0x02) and `BT_HCI_LE_SCAN_FP_EXT_FILTER` (0x03) are defined in `hci_types.h` but had no users anywhere in the tree, and `BT_HCI_EVT_LE_DIRECT_ADV_REPORT` had neither an event mask bit nor a handler. The Controller side already implements the feature end to end under `CONFIG_BT_CTLR_EXT_SCAN_FP`, which is `default y` on nRF, so the gap was entirely on the host.

The practical effect is that a peripheral directing advertisements at an identity the local Controller cannot resolve is invisible to a Zephyr observer or central, even though the specification provides this mechanism precisely to surface that case. A typical use is a central that has lost its bonding information noticing that a peer is still trying to reconnect to it, and offering to pair again.

## What this adds

`BT_LE_SCAN_OPT_EXT_FILTER_POLICY` selects the extended variant of whichever filter policy would otherwise be requested, so all four policies are now reachable. It is gated by the new `CONFIG_BT_SCAN_EXT_FILTER_POLICY`, which depends on `BT_CTLR_EXT_SCAN_FP` when the Controller is built in tree.

Not every Link Layer supports the extended scanner filter policies, and one that does not shall reject the scan parameters with Invalid HCI Command Parameters. `bt_le_scan_start()` therefore checks LE feature bit 7 and returns `-ENOTSUP` before any HCI command is sent. That bit had no accessor, so `BT_FEAT_LE_EXT_SCAN()` is added alongside the other feature test macros.

The report itself is delivered through the existing scan callback, with the target address in the new `bt_le_scan_recv_info.direct_addr` member and the address type set to `BT_ADDR_LE_UNRESOLVED` when the Controller could not resolve it. The same on-air advertisement arrives as an LE Directed Advertising Report with the legacy scanning commands and as an LE Extended Advertising Report with the extended ones, so both paths populate the same member and applications need only one code path. The extended report already carried this address and the host was discarding it.

## Backwards compatibility

The change is additive. `valid_le_scan_param()` rejects the new option bit unless the Kconfig symbol is enabled, `bt_le_scan_param.options` is unchanged in width, and the filter policy sent to the Controller is unchanged for anyone not setting the option. No migration guide entry is needed.

Two behaviour changes are worth calling out explicitly:

- `le_adv_recv()` drops directed reports when scanning explicitly without privacy and without `CONFIG_BT_SCAN_WITH_IDENTITY`, to avoid reporting advertisements for the local identity while scanning with a non-resolvable private address. An unresolved target address is by construction not the local identity, so it is excluded from that rule; without this the feature would be a no-op in the default configuration. Per specification a Controller only reports an unresolved target address while using a filter policy the host requests exclusively for this option, so existing users cannot be affected.
- Both scan start paths now select the filter policy through one helper that gates the filter accept list on `BT_FILTER_ACCEPT_LIST`. The legacy path already did this, the extended one did not. This only changes the extended path when `BT_FILTER_ACCEPT_LIST` is disabled and the application sets `BT_LE_SCAN_OPT_FILTER_ACCEPT_LIST` anyway, in which case it now asks for no filtering rather than filtering against an accept list that `bt_le_filter_accept_list_add()` is compiled out to populate, so the scanner previously reported nothing at all.

## Controller

`le_ext_adv_legacy_report()` reported the target address verbatim without consulting `node_rx->rx_ftr.direct`, so an advertisement accepted only because of an extended filter policy was indistinguishable from one addressed to the local identity. It now reports `BT_ADDR_LE_UNRESOLVED` for that case through a `legacy_adv_direct_addr_type()` helper, mirroring what `le_ext_adv_report()` already does through `ext_adv_direct_addr_type()`. This is the path taken for legacy advertising PDUs received while scanning with the extended scanning commands, so without it the feature is only usable with `CONFIG_BT_EXT_ADV=n`.

## Testing

- `tests/bluetooth/host_direct_adv_recv` — native_sim with a fake HCI driver, driving the host through `bt_enable()` and the public scan API. The fake Controller records what the host asks for, so the suite asserts the scanning filter policy requested for each combination of `BT_LE_SCAN_OPT_EXT_FILTER_POLICY` and `BT_LE_SCAN_OPT_FILTER_ACCEPT_LIST`, and the LE event mask. It also covers the reported type, properties and target address for an unresolved target, multi-report, truncated and empty events, discarding while no scanner runs, the legacy report carrying no target address for both `ADV_IND` and `ADV_DIRECT_IND`, the unsupported case where the event stays masked off and `bt_le_scan_start()` returns `-ENOTSUP`, and the filter accept list compiled out, where the accept-list option is accepted and then ignored. Four configurations, 45 cases; the legacy and the extended scan parameter commands are covered between them.
- `tests/bsim/bluetooth/host/scan/ext_filter_policy` — end to end on `nrf52_bsim/native`, a peer directing at an RPA the scanner cannot resolve, run with both the legacy and the extended scanning commands. Reverting the Controller commit fails the `CONFIG_BT_EXT_ADV=y` run.
- Build coverage through `tests/bluetooth/init` with a new `prj_scan_ext_fp.conf`, and for the shell option through a new `tests/bluetooth/shell` entry.
- Every commit builds and passes its tests on its own.

Nothing was run on hardware.

title: modem: cellular: silence the implicit switch fallthroughs
body:
A `CONFIG_CODING_GUIDELINE_CHECK` build compiles this driver with `-Wimplicit-fallthrough=2`, which flags two case reaches.

The await power on handler means its one, as the comment there already says, so it just wants the marker. The RING case in the await ppp dead handler does not: it is the only RING case in the driver that does not end, and nothing marks the reach as deliberate.
Ending it is a deliberate behaviour change on one path. Three of the four entries into that state arm the timeout at the call site, so the `start_timer` the fallthrough reached was a no-op there. The fourth, the deregistered case, arms none, and leaving the registered state cancels any pending one, so a RING arriving there used to arm the settling timeout and now does not. 

In practice the state's own `net_if_dormant_on` provokes the PPP_DEAD that arms it in the same millisecond, so the window is sub-millisecond and recovery is unaffected either way.

title: modem: cellular: handle a PPP drop while awaiting registration
body:
`MODEM_CELLULAR_EVENT_PPP_DEAD` had no case in the await registered state, so it was discarded. A vendor with no network script enters that state after a successful dial, with PPP attached and the carrier on, so a data call dropping there goes unnoticed. The registration event that follows routes to the registered state, which clears the dormant flag and announces a bearer that is already gone, and the driver then stays there indefinitely because the periodic script keeps passing on a module that is itself healthy.

Handle the event as the registered state already does, entering await ppp dead so its existing timeout re-dials.

title: AGENTS.md: clarify the Signed-off-by rule
body:
The first bullet of "Rules for agents" reads "Never add a `Signed-off-by:`
line", which states the opposite of the DCO requirement: every Zephyr commit
must carry one, and it must come from the human responsible for the work. As
written it also contradicts the "Commits" section further down, which requires
exactly one sign-off matching the commit author and forbids removing an
existing one.

The intent was that an agent must not manufacture a sign-off on someone's
behalf. Reword the bullet to require the trailer, say whose identity it
carries, and narrow the prohibition to inventing or copying one.

title: drivers: i2c: it51xxx: Fix read OOB in target FIFO ISR
body:
The write direction of the it51xxx target FIFO ISR pre-checks `w_index`
before every copy, but the read direction has no equivalent bound. Two
commits, each an independent defect.

### `drivers: i2c: it51xxx: bound the target FIFO read index`

In target buffer mode the `SMB_RCS` branch of `target_i2c_isr_fifo()`
pushes a fixed 16 bytes out of `target_out_buffer` on every data
interrupt and then advances `r_index` by 16, without ever checking it
against the size of the buffer. `r_index` is cleared only on the timeout
path and on the STOP path, so within one transaction it just grows: a
controller that keeps clocking read bytes without issuing a STOP walks
`r_index` past the end of the buffer after sixteen interrupts, and each
interrupt after that transmits 16 bytes read from beyond
`target_out_buffer`.

This adds `target_i2c_fifo_write_from_buf()`, which pre-checks `r_index`
against `sizeof(target_out_buffer)` the way the existing
`target_i2c_fifo_read_to_buf()` checks `w_index`, with the 16-byte
transmit loop and the `r_index` advance moved inside it. Once the buffer
is exhausted the guard logs and fills the FIFO with a chunk of `0xff`
rather than transmitting past the end, leaving `r_index` parked so that
every later interrupt refills the same way until the STOP or timeout
path resets the transfer state.

Filling rather than emptying is deliberate, per review: an emptied
transmit FIFO raises a data interrupt for every further byte the
controller clocks, so resetting it would trade the overread for an
interrupt storm. The `#ifdef CONFIG_SOC_IT51526AW` register selection
used by the fill and by the transmit loop is shared in a
`target_i2c_fifo_put()` helper.

### `drivers: i2c: it51xxx: handle a missing target read callback`

Both target read paths declare the transfer length uninitialised and
call the optional `buf_read_requested()` callback without checking that
it is registered. A target that provides no read callback therefore
leaves `rdata` NULL and `len` indeterminate, and the code then compares
that indeterminate length against the destination size; whenever the
comparison happens to pass, `memcpy()` runs with a NULL source.

`len` is now initialised at its declaration, and the length check and
the copy are skipped when the callback leaves no buffer behind. The same
shape appears twice, in `target_i2c_isr_fifo()` and in the shared-FIFO
arm of `target_i2c_isr_pio()`, and both get the same treatment.

### Build coverage

Built for `it51xxx_evb/it51526aw` against `tests/drivers/i2c/i2c_target_api`,
whose board overlay already enables target mode, with
`CONFIG_I2C_TARGET_BUFFER_MODE=y` confirmed in the generated
`autoconf.h`. Without that the edited region is preprocessed away and a
green build proves nothing. checkpatch is clean on the series.

Two things I could not cover, for reviewers who know the part:

- There is no runtime or hardware test path for this driver, so this is
  build coverage only.
- `it51526aw` is the only in-tree board variant, so the `#else`
  (non-`CONFIG_SOC_IT51526AW`) arm of `target_i2c_fifo_put()` gets no
  compile coverage. Its body is moved byte-for-byte with no edits.


Fixes: #118633

title: bluetooth: mesh: skip the self-target during the DFU apply step
body:
Commit 5bdbd5015736 ("bluetooth: mesh: defer self-target apply until
distribution completes") special-cased the self-target in three Firmware
Update Client message paths: send_info_get(), confirmed() and
handle_status().
    
Use the blob broadcast skip mechanism instead, as the Transfer step
already does. The self-target takes no part in the Apply and Confirm
broadcasts, so all three special cases go away and handle_status()
returns to plain Section 7.1.2.6 behaviour. The Distribution Server
drives the deferred apply from dfu_confirmed() as before.
    
The local server no longer receives Firmware Update Apply, so
bt_mesh_dfu_srv_apply_deferred() now makes the Section 6.1.2.3
transition to Applying Update and persists it before the apply callback,
which may reboot the node. bt_mesh_dfu_srv_apply_cancel() accepts the
same phases.
    
Split the phase bookkeeping out as bt_mesh_dfu_srv_apply_settle(). The
resume path must move the local server to Idle so it reports the new
Firmware ID, but must not report the apply as complete, which would end
the distribution before the Confirm step re-runs and turn a failed apply
into a successful one. The self_update flag suppressed that notification
and is dropped; bt_mesh_dfd_srv_self_applied() now takes the applying
server and verifies it is the Distributor's own target.

title: tests: arch: derive Nordic VPR test IRQ lines from devicetree
body:
The gen_isr_table and interrupt tests both select their test IRQ lines on Nordic VPR cores from a hardcoded ladder of SOC_SERIES conditionals. The values in that ladder are VEVIF task lines, which devicetree already describes: every VPR core has a nordic,nrf-vevif-task-rx mailbox node whose interrupts property enumerates the CLIC lines that are not wired to a peripheral and can therefore be triggered from software. The node is disabled in both tests, so the VEVIF mailbox driver does not claim those lines.

Read the lines from that node instead, taking the highest ones: the two highest for the nested interrupt test and the three highest for gen_isr_table. Selecting from the top rather than the bottom keeps the choice inside nordic,tasks-mask on every target, as the nRF54H20 reserves the low tasks for other domains (0-3 on the PPR, 0-15 on the FLPR).

The lines picked on the already-listed targets change, and all remain within the VEVIF range and the task mask. The nested interrupt test moves from 16/17 to 21/22 on the nRF54L and nRF71 FLPR, from 19/20 to 21/22 on the nRF71 FLPR, from 16/17 to 30/31 on the nRF54H20 FLPR, and is unchanged at 14/15 on the nRF54H20 and nRF92 PPR. gen_isr_table moves to 20/21/22 on the nRF54L and nRF71 FLPR, 29/30/31 on the nRF54H20 FLPR, and 13/14/15 on the nRF54H20 and nRF92 PPR.

title: Bluetooth: Classic: Support SCO voice over HCI feature

title: Modem cellular: get active cellular registration status
body:
This PR is a proposal to discuss and if makes sense to others, to change cellular modem registration status getter. Current modem API, required the caller to pass in a specific access technology to get the registration status for.  The caller had to already know which one to ask about. This is awkward in practice, since a modem device has a primary/serving access technology which is active at a time.

For applications quering the registration status, is more useful to ask “Am I currently connected, and over what technology?” rather than "Am I currently connected with NB-IoT?".

This PR reworks the API so cellular_get_registration_status() reports the currently active access technology together with its registration status, instead of requiring the technology as an input. The tech parameter becomes an output.

title: modem: ppp: report a link death on an in-band NO CARRIER
body: An in-band NO CARRIER drops the carrier, and on an interface that is not up that tells nobody: net_if notifies only on a transition into or out of `NET_IF_OPER_UP`, so while a PPP interface is still dormant the carrier drop is silent, the PPP L2 never changes phase, and no `NET_EVENT_PPP_PHASE_DEAD` reaches a driver waiting on one. The L2 cannot cover that window itself, since its phase is already `PPP_DEAD` and `ppp_change_phase` returns early on an unchanged phase; notifying on dormant-to-down in net_if and clearing dormant at dial success both leave the failure unchanged for the same reason. So the event is raised where the death is detected

title: modem: cellular: dial only once registered
body:
The EG2x dial script raises the radio and dials tens of milliseconds later, so a module that has to search answers CONNECT with no PDN behind it and PPP runs over nothing. Vendors with a network script already wait for registration. The EG2x has none, and `modem_cellular_init` rejects one alongside on-demand connect. Give the EG2x a network script holding its radio raise, run the network script on a dial request instead of in place of it, and drop that rejection: the admin state gates whether to dial, the script gates when.

Also, a hang-up during the network script parks the modem, and a dial or network script that finds the chat busy retries on the timer. Script results carry the script that produced them, so a state only acts on a result it started, which covers the non-periodic results #116989 filters per state and replaces those checks. The event queue is sized in events through `MODEM_CELLULAR_EVENT_QUEUE_DEPTH` since some odd configurations can get more than 8

title: kernel: skip redundant runtime usage stop locking
body:
Return before taking usage_lock when the current CPU's accounting window is already stopped. This avoids a redundant global-lock acquisition when architecture IRQ-entry accounting precedes scheduler IRQ-exit accounting.

The hook already requires local interrupts to be masked, and only the local CPU writes usage0. Keep the existing lock for every shared-counter update and preserve runtime-statistics behavior.

Microbenchmarks on a quad-core ARMv8 SMP platform with runtime statistics enabled showed 2.5-4.4% lower latency and up to 12.8% higher throughput.

title: drivers: bluetooth: userchan: size RX frame buffer from BT_BUF_RX_SIZE
body:
## Problem

The `userchan` HCI driver's `rx_thread` assembles a whole HCI packet in a single static `frame` buffer before handing it to the host. That buffer was hardcoded to **512 bytes**.

A full ACL data packet can exceed this. The host's receive buffer is `CONFIG_BT_BUF_ACL_RX_SIZE` bytes (defaults up to 1300 for Classic), and an A2DP media packet fills it. When such a packet arrives:

```
<err> bt_driver: HCI Packet is too big for frame (512 bytes). Dropping data
<err> bt_conn: Unexpected L2CAP continuation
```

The driver drops the packet, the host sees a truncated stream and rejects it, and **no A2DP media is ever received**.

## Fix

Size the frame buffer from `BT_BUF_RX_SIZE` instead of a fixed 512:

```c
#define RX_FRAME_SIZE BT_BUF_RX_SIZE
```

`BT_BUF_RX_SIZE` is what the host already uses for its RX buffers. It includes the H4 transport octet and the maximum of the ACL, event and ISO receive-buffer sizes, so the frame buffer holds every packet type `get_rx()` accepts. This also covers H4 ISO packets, whose `CONFIG_BT_ISO_RX_MTU` can exceed both 512 and the ACL RX size; the ISO term is zero when `CONFIG_BT_ISO` is disabled, so no memory is added for configurations that do not use ISO.

## Testing

Verified on `native_sim` with a real Bluetooth dongle (HCI User Channel):

- **Before:** A2DP media reception failed with the errors above; zero SBC media packets received.
- **After:** an A2DP SBC stream from a phone is received continuously — packets both below (498 B) and above (581 B) the old 512-byte limit — with no dropped-frame or L2CAP continuation errors. HFP hands-free call setup/teardown during playback also works.
- Compile-tested: `samples/bluetooth/classic/a2dp_sink` builds clean for `native_sim` on current `main`.

title: subsys: shell: count messages dropped while log backend disabled
body:
## Summary

The shell's log backend (`shell_log_backend.c`) starts in `SHELL_LOG_BACKEND_DISABLED`
and is only enabled once `shell_start()` runs — normally whenever the shell thread
first gets scheduled, via `CONFIG_SHELL_AUTOSTART`. Any `printk()`/`LOG_*` message
that reaches `process()` before that happens currently falls into the
`SHELL_LOG_BACKEND_DISABLED` case and is silently discarded, with **no counter
incremented and no way for the user to ever know something was lost**.

This is asymmetric with the existing deferred-mode buffer-full path, which already
calls `dropped()` and gets reported via `log_output_dropped_process()` once the
backend is enabled ("N messages dropped"). This PR extends the same accounting to
the disabled case.

We hit this concretely: an app-level `SYS_INIT(..., APPLICATION, 0)` boot banner was
reliably lost on one sample's thin boot and reliably preserved on a heavier one,
purely depending on whether anything in `POST_KERNEL` init happened to block long
enough for the (lowest-priority) shell thread to get scheduled before `APPLICATION`
level ran. Total silence made this very slow to diagnose - this PR doesn't remove
the race (see the linked discussion issue for that), but makes it observable.

## Change

- `process()`: the `SHELL_LOG_BACKEND_DISABLED` case now calls `dropped(backend, 1)`,
  same as the existing buffer-full path.
- `z_shell_log_backend_enable()`: no longer resets `dropped_cnt` to 0.
  `z_shell_log_backend_process()` already atomically reads-and-clears it the next
  time it runs (right after enable, from the shell thread's own loop), so the count
  is reported instead of clobbered before it can be. This also means log output
  manually toggled off/on via the shell's log-toggle command now reports what was
  missed while off, consistent with the buffer-full case.

## Test plan

- [x] `samples/subsys/shell/shell_module` builds cleanly for `native_sim` with this
      change (145/145 objects, including `shell_log_backend.c.obj`).

title: shell: CONFIG_SHELL_AUTOSTART timing races with early printk()/LOG_* via CONFIG_LOG_PRINTK
body:
## Describe the bug / question

With `CONFIG_SHELL` enabled and the default `CONFIG_LOG_PRINTK=y`, `printk()` is
routed through the logging core, which dispatches to the active log backend - the
shell's own `shell_log_backend` when `CONFIG_SHELL_LOG_BACKEND` is set (default).
That backend starts in `SHELL_LOG_BACKEND_DISABLED` and is only enabled by
`shell_start()` (`shell.c`), which is only called from `shell_thread()`, gated by
`CONFIG_SHELL_AUTOSTART` (default y) - i.e. whenever the shell thread first happens
to get scheduled.

Any `printk()`/`LOG_*` call before that point is silently dropped (see #118690 for
a small PR that at least makes this observable via the existing dropped-message
counter - this issue is about the underlying timing itself).

### Concrete case that surfaced this

An application-level boot banner (`printk()` from a `SYS_INIT(..., APPLICATION, 0)`
hook, so it runs at the very end of kernel init, before `main()`) was **reliably
lost** on one sample and **reliably preserved** on another, on the same SoC family.
Tracing it down: the shell thread runs at `K_LOWEST_APPLICATION_THREAD_PRIO`,
strictly below a typical main/init thread's priority - so per Zephyr's scheduler,
it can only get the CPU if the main/init thread genuinely blocks (sleep/semaphore/
mutex wait) somewhere in `POST_KERNEL` init, never via preemption or time-slicing
between different priorities. The sample with a thin `POST_KERNEL` sequence (no
blocking calls between the shell UART backend's own init and `APPLICATION` level)
lost the banner every single time. The sample with heavier `POST_KERNEL` init
(networking stack, filesystem/settings, etc., several of which block) won the race
every time and kept it.

So this isn't really platform-specific or non-deterministic in a probabilistic
sense - it's fully determined by how much blocking work an app's `POST_KERNEL`
init happens to do, which is an accident of app composition, not something an app
author would think to check.

### Question for maintainers

Would it make sense for shell backends (at least the synchronous ones, e.g. UART)
to call `shell_start()` directly from their own `SYS_INIT`, instead of deferring to
whenever `CONFIG_SHELL_AUTOSTART` causes the shell thread to call it? That would
make "shell is started" (and thus its log backend enabled) deterministic relative
to kernel init levels rather than scheduler-dependent.

I'm aware this could be wrong for backends where "device ready" doesn't imply
"transport actually usable yet" (e.g. USB CDC ACM before host enumeration) - so
this might need to be opt-in per-backend rather than a blanket change, or there
may be a reason `shell_start()` is currently expected to run from the shell
thread's own context that I'm not seeing. Filing this as a question/RFC rather
than a PR, since it's a behavior change affecting every shell backend
(UART/RTT/USB CDC/BT NUS/telnet/MQTT/...) and needs subsystem maintainer input
before anyone should attempt it.

### Environment

- Zephyr main (traced against a downstream fork tracking a recent main)
- Affects: `subsys/shell/shell.c`, `subsys/shell/backends/shell_uart.c`,
  `subsys/shell/shell_log_backend.c`

title: net: ipv6: handle reflected DAD NS self-probes (MAC + RFC7527 nonce)
body:
In an IPv6-only Wi-Fi setup (SLAAC, no DHCPv6), the device sends DAD NS multicast after Router Advertisement (RA). Since this DAD NS is a multicast frame, it is reflected by AP. When was testing on `nRF7002` and on `nRF7120`, I saw the following difference:
- On `nRF7002` the reflected (by AP) DAD NS does not reach host RX path (and thus doesn't show up in IP stack).
- On `nRF7120` the reflected DAD NS reaches host RX path

When the reflected DAD NS reaches host side, it is passed to the IP stack and causes false DAD failure: IP stack treats it as someone using the address already.

What specs say about this:
- RFC 4862 Appendix A states loopback detection is implementation-dependent and warns that MAC-only self-source filtering can break DAD correctness in some cases.
- RFC 7527 defines Enhanced DAD nonce processing to safely detect and drop looped-back self-probes.

This pull request fixes this false IPv6 Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) failures when a device receives its own DAD Neighbor Solicitation (NS) back on RX by implementing RFC 7527 nonce support:
- add and validate DAD nonce
- ignore reflected self-probes with matching nonce.

It also adds regression tests for the implemented behaviors.

title: dap: bound and yield in the DAP_SWJ_Pins wait
body:
### Why

`DAP_SWJ_Pins` lets the host say "set these pins, then wait until they read back". That wait is a 32-bit microsecond field, so a perfectly conformant host is allowed to ask the probe to wait **up to 71 minutes**.

Two things go wrong while it runs:

1. **The whole USB device stops responding.** `dap_link_execute_cmd()` is called directly from the USB class request handler in `subsys/dap/dap_backend_usb.c`, so this loop runs on the `usbd` thread — the thread that dispatches endpoint completions for *every* function on the device. On a probe that is only CMSIS-DAP nobody notices. On a composite device that also exposes, say, a CDC-ACM port, that port is dead for the whole wait.
2. **It spins at 100% CPU.** The loop polls without ever sleeping, and `usbd` is a cooperative thread, so a loop that never sleeps also never yields. Nothing else on the system runs at all.

This is not a corner case. Any time a host waits on a pin that does not reach the expected level — a target that does not release nRESET, for instance — the loop runs the host's full timeout.

We found it on our own composite probe firmware (CMSIS-DAP + a CDC-ACM UART bridge on one USB device, FRDM-MCXA156 / FRDM-MCXA153) built on this driver and `subsys/dap`.

### What this changes

- **Clamp** the wait to a new `CONFIG_CMSIS_DAP_SWJ_PINS_MAX_WAIT_MS`. The default is **3000**, which is the same cap ARM's reference implementation applies in [`DAP.c`](https://github.com/ARM-software/CMSIS-DAP/blob/main/Firmware/Source/DAP.c) (`if (wait > 3000000U) { wait = 3000000U; }`, in the timestamp-clock path). So out of the box nothing changes for any wait a reference probe would have honoured. Composite devices that share the transport can set it far lower.
- **Yield** — `k_usleep(100)` between polls. The pins are read over a bit-banged transport and cannot change faster than that, so the sleep costs no responsiveness.
- Expiry is checked **before** the sleep, so the common `wait == 0` request — what every stock host issues simply to set and read pins — stays a single read with no sleep, exactly as in the reference implementation.
- The per-iteration `LOG_INF` becomes `LOG_DBG`. At one line per poll it is itself a source of stall, and it is a debug aid rather than an info-level event.

### Supporting data

Measured on the probe firmware described above, with a CDC-ACM bridge carrying a 115200-baud stream on the same USB device. "Bytes lost" is data dropped from that stream while a single `DAP_SWJ_Pins` request is in flight.

| stall | bytes lost |
| --- | --- |
| 40 ms | **0** |
| 50 ms | 64 ← knee |
| 200 ms | 1 760 |
| 1000 ms | 10 752 |

The knee lands where the arithmetic puts it: a 512-byte ring at 11 520 B/s holds 44.4 ms.

**CPU cost of not yielding**, from idle-thread cycle counts read over SWD on two images differing only in the `k_usleep()`:

| | idle |
| --- | --- |
| spinning (before) | 2.7% |
| sleeping (after) | 88.1% |

**With the clamp applied**, a request asking for the 32-bit maximum returns in **40.5 ms** with pin state intact, and costs **0 bytes** on the concurrent bridge stream (worst observed HID latency 30.9 ms, against 1994 ms before).

Worth noting that the two halves do different work: yielding alone recovers about 58% of the loss at a 200 ms stall, because `sysworkq` drains the ring while the thread sleeps. So **yielding reduces loss, bounding removes it** — which is why this patch does both.

### A note on the response

The clamp is deliberately not visible to the host. The `DAP_SWJ_Pins` response carries pin state and has no field for "I stopped waiting early", so the device stays truthful about what it actually observed and is silently non-literal about duration. Inventing a wire signal for it would be a larger conformance departure than the clamp itself.

### Relationship to #117238 / #114549

Independent, and the files do not overlap — those change `sw_set_pins()`/`sw_get_pins()` in `drivers/dp/swdp_bitbang.c`; this changes the loop in `subsys/dap/cmsis_dap.c` that calls them.

They do interact in one direction worth mentioning: this loop's exit condition is `(value & select) == (state & select)`, so it depends on set and get agreeing about level convention. While they disagree — the bug #117238 reports — the compare can never match for the affected bit, and every such request runs the host's full timeout instead of returning early. That makes the unbounded wait easier to hit today, and it is a reason to bound it regardless of which convention #117238 settles on.

### Testing

- `samples/subsys/dap` builds and links for `nrf52840dk/nrf52840`.
- `scripts/checkpatch.pl` clean.
- Bench: FRDM-MCXA156 and FRDM-MCXA153 probes against FRDM-MCXN947 and STM32H503 targets — pyOCD connect / halt / memory read / flash / resume unaffected; our full firmware test suite shows no regression against a control image without the change.

title: dap: DAP_Delay's parameter is microseconds, not milliseconds
body:
### Why

The CMSIS-DAP `DAP_Delay` command carries a 16-bit delay **in microseconds**. `dap_delay()` multiplies it by `USEC_PER_MSEC` before busy-waiting, so every delay is **1000× longer than the host asked for**.

A host requesting 10 ms — i.e. sending 10000 — is held for **9.93 s**. Measured, not inferred.

And, as with `DAP_SWJ_Pins`, `dap_link_execute_cmd()` is called straight from the USB class request handler in `subsys/dap/dap_backend_usb.c`, so that wait runs on the `usbd` thread, which dispatches endpoint completions for every function on the device. For those 9.93 s the device services nothing at all — not just DAP.

### The unit is microseconds

- ARM's CMSIS-DAP specification, [DAP_Delay](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS-DAP/latest/group__DAP__Delay.html): *"Delay: wait time in µs."*
- ARM's reference [`DAP.c`](https://github.com/ARM-software/CMSIS-DAP/blob/main/Firmware/Source/DAP.c) scales the parameter by `CPU_CLOCK/1000000U` — i.e. treats one unit as one microsecond — before calling `PIN_DELAY_SLOW()`.
- CMSIS-Pack debug sequences pass `10000` where they mean 10 ms.

The existing `LOG_DBG` string says `"dap delay %u ms"`, which is consistent with the same misreading; it is corrected here too.

### What this changes

- Treat the parameter as microseconds — drop the `USEC_PER_MSEC` scaling.
- **Sleep rather than busy-wait** once the delay is long enough for sleeping to be accurate. Below a millisecond, busy-waiting is the only way to be accurate, so that path is kept.
- **No clamp is added**, deliberately. The field is 16-bit, so the worst legal delay is 65535 µs and no host can make it longer; and a delay is a deliberate request that the reference implementation honours exactly. Clamping it would refuse legal, intended delays for no gain in bound.

### Supporting data

| | requested | delivered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | 10 ms (10000 µs) | 9.93 s (×993) |
| after | 65535 µs — the worst legal case | 65.65 ms |

After the fix, the worst legal `DAP_Delay` costs **0 bytes** on a concurrent 115200-baud CDC-ACM stream sharing the same USB device, measured on our composite probe firmware (CMSIS-DAP + UART bridge, FRDM-MCXA156 / FRDM-MCXA153) built on `subsys/dap`.

### Compatibility — please read

This is a behaviour change, not only a bug fix: every existing host's delays become 1000× shorter. That is what the host asked for, but it is worth stating plainly.

The reason we think it is safe is asymmetry. The current bug makes delays *longer* than requested, and a delay that is too long is functionally invisible — it shows up as slowness, never as a protocol failure. So no existing user can have come to depend on the overshoot for correctness; they can only have been paying for it. Anything that was working keeps working, faster.

We have kept this separate from #118729 (the `DAP_SWJ_Pins` bound) on purpose, precisely because this one has an argument attached and that one should not be held hostage to it.

### Testing

- `samples/subsys/dap` builds and links for `nrf52840dk/nrf52840`.
- `scripts/checkpatch.pl` clean.
- Bench: FRDM-MCXA156 and FRDM-MCXA153 probes against FRDM-MCXN947 and STM32H503 targets — pyOCD connect / halt / memory read / flash / resume unaffected; our full firmware test suite shows no regression against a control image without the change.

title: Bluetooth: host: GATT: silently cancel CCC write on unsubscribe
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Tests;area: Bluetooth Host;platform: nRF BSIM
body:
## Commits 1. **att: fix NULL channel request dereference** -- a pre-existing NULL-deref guard in `bt_att_find_req_by_user_data()`, no behaviour change, so it can be applied on its own. 2. **gatt: silently cancel CCC write on unsubscribe** -- the fix proper. 3. **tests: bsim: ... stress subscribe/unsubscribe reuse** -- three bsim scenarios covering the reuse. checkpatch reports 0 errors / 0 warnings on all three commits. ## Problem Subscribing and unsubscribing to a notification are asynchronous, callback-driven procedures. Each is a CCC write, i.e. one ATT request, and a single `bt_gatt_subscribe_params` backs one such write at a time (it owns one `value`, one list node, one flags word). `bt_gatt_subscribe()` sends the enable CCC write to the peer as an ATT transaction with the 30-second ATT timeout running (Bluetooth Core Specification v6.3, Vol 3, Part F, Section 3.3.3: a transaction not completed within 30 seconds shall time out). An unsubscribe reuses the same params for the disable CCC write. With the subscribe CCC write still in flight (`WRITE_PENDING` set), `bt_gatt_unsubscribe()` called `bt_gatt_cancel()` to abort it. `bt_gatt_cancel()` runs the aborted request's completion synchronously, so `gatt_write_ccc_rsp()` ran with `BT_ATT_ERR_UNLIKELY`: the subscribe callback saw a spurious failure and the subscription was torn down (NULL notification, node removed). `bt_gatt_unsubscribe()` then queued the disable write on the same params, whose completion delivered the subscribe and NULL callbacks a second time. One unsubscribe thus produced a spurious subscribe failure and duplicate completions, with the params and its list node reused while the first completion was still unwinding. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant App as Application participant Host as GATT/ATT host participant Peer App->>Host: bt_gatt_subscribe(params) Host->>Peer: enable CCC write (ATT request) Note over Host,Peer: in flight, WRITE_PENDING set,
30 s ATT timeout running App->>Host: bt_gatt_unsubscribe(params) Note over Host: WRITE_PENDING set →
bt_gatt_cancel() runs the completion synchronously Host-->>App: subscribe cb (BT_ATT_ERR_UNLIKELY) — spurious failure Host-->>App: NULL notification, subscription torn down Host->>Peer: disable CCC write (same params reused) Peer-->>Host: Write Response Host-->>App: subscribe cb (SUCCESS) — second time Host-->>App: NULL notification — second time Note over App,Host: duplicate completions, params and its node
reused while the first completion is still unwinding ``` ## Fix Cancel the in-flight write silently instead. Factor the body of `bt_gatt_cancel()` into a helper taking whether to run the completion, and call it from `bt_gatt_unsubscribe()` without the completion, clearing `WRITE_PENDING` in its place. The superseded write's response is then ignored, the disable write is queued behind it exactly as before, and the application sees one NULL notification, as for any other unsubscribe. No new flag (`gatt.h` is unchanged), and no locking beyond what `bt_gatt_cancel()` already takes -- the same two round trips on the air as a sequential subscribe followed by unsubscribe. `bt_att_find_req_by_user_data()` now runs while a channel may hold no active request, so guard its `chan->req` dereference with a NULL check; the request lookup the silent cancel relies on would otherwise fault (e.g. under EATT, with the request queued or on another channel). ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant App as Application participant Host as GATT/ATT host participant Peer App->>Host: bt_gatt_subscribe(params) Host->>Peer: enable CCC write (ATT request) Note over Host,Peer: in flight, WRITE_PENDING set,
30 s ATT timeout running App->>Host: bt_gatt_unsubscribe(params) Note over Host: WRITE_PENDING set → gatt_cancel() drops the
request without running its completion
clear WRITE_PENDING, queue the disable write Peer-->>Host: enable Write Response Note over Host: response absorbed silently
(completion already dropped) Host->>Peer: disable CCC write (now on air) Peer-->>Host: disable Write Response Host-->>App: NULL notification (unsubscribe complete) Note over App,Host: one NULL notification, as for any other unsubscribe
no spurious failure, no duplicate completions ``` If the peer never answers the superseded enable write, the 30-second ATT timeout that was armed when it went on the air still fires and tears the bearer down, exactly as without this change; the silent cancel touches neither the timeout nor the bearer's busy state, so ATT's one-transaction-at-a-time rule is preserved and the disable write stays queued until the enable write resolves. ## Tests Adds three bsim scenarios under `tests/bsim/bluetooth/host/gatt/notify` that reuse a single `bt_gatt_subscribe_params` across subscribe/unsubscribe cycles: - **racy** subscribes and then immediately unsubscribes the same params with no scheduling point in between, so the subscribe CCC write is still in flight when the unsubscribe is issued (in bsim no simulated time passes between the two calls, so this is deterministic). It asserts the application sees a single NULL notification and no spurious subscribe failure for the superseded write. - **reentrant** repeats settled and racy enable/disable cycles and checks the unsubscribe return codes: an unsubscribe with no active subscription returns `-EINVAL`; one issued while the enable write is still in flight returns 0 and drops the subscription, so an immediately repeated unsubscribe returns `-EINVAL`; and after a settled unsubscribe a repeated unsubscribe returns `-EINVAL` too. - **cross-traffic** interleaves the CCC writes with ordinary read requests, write requests and write commands on the same bearer, both when the (un)subscribe settles cleanly and when it races an in-flight enable write. A writable characteristic on the server and a matching UUID in `common.h` support the new traffic. All three fail on the old cancel-and-reuse path and pass with the silent cancel. Fixes: #120008

title: scripts: checkpatch: Recognize C++ template angle brackets

`checkpatch.pl` treated C++ template angle brackets in `.h` files as comparison operators (false `SPACING` and `CONSTANT_COMPARISON`). This marks high-confidence template lists (`template <...>`, named casts, qualified names such as `std::vector<T>`, `typename`) and ignores only those offsets. Regression tests live in `scripts/checkpatch/test_checkpatch.py` and run in the scripts-tests workflow.

- Unqualified `Foo<T>` (ambiguous with C `MAX<value`)
- Space before a qualified list: `std::vector <int>`
- Unparenthesized non-type template parameters: `N > 0`, `a<b`, `<<`, `>=` (parenthesized forms are fine)

title: boards: renesas: ek_ra8p1: hook up the DA7212 audio CODEC
body:
Enables the DA7212 audio CODEC fitted on the EK-RA8P1: the control interface on `iic1` at 0x1a, the DAI on SSIE0, and the master clock on GPT2.

Independent of #118803 (PDM microphones), but note both branches allocate board interrupt slots starting at 32 — whichever lands second needs renumbering, since git will not conflict on it.

### Wiring

| Signal | Pin | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SDA / SCL | P511 / P512 | IIC1 |
| BCLK | P403 | SSIE0 SSIBCK0 |
| WCLK | P404 | SSIE0 SSILRCK0 |
| DATIN | P405 | SSIE0 SSITXD0 |
| DATOUT | P406 | SSIE0 SSIRXD0 |
| MCLK | PD06 | GPT2 GTIOC2A |

P405 and P406 are shared with the parallel camera behind the J41 links, so the CODEC and the camera are mutually exclusive. Speaker output is on J33; the headphone/line header J38 is not populated.

This makes EK-RA8P1 the first board in tree to enable `renesas,ra-i2s-ssie`.

### The clocking is not exact, and that is the interesting part

PD06's only output function is GTIOC2A, so the CODEC master clock has to come from GPT2 — and the same GPT2 output feeds the SSIE audio clock over the internal route, which is what the pin choice is clearly designed around: at 12.288 MHz, a bit-clock divider of 8 gives 1.536 MHz, exactly 48 kHz for 16-bit stereo.

The problem is that 12.288 MHz is not reachable. GPTCLK on this board is PLL2P/2 = 300 MHz and the GPT period is an integer count, so the neighbours are 300/24 = 12.5 MHz and 300/25 = 12 MHz. The 24 MHz crystal cannot produce the 24.576 MHz audio family by integer division at all, and re-sourcing GPTCLK to reach it would break the 12 MHz camera clock on `pwm12`.

Zephyr's `da7212` driver runs the CODEC with its PLL bypassed, so SYSCLK is simply MCLK. This branch therefore sets `audio_clock` to 12.5 MHz, the closest reachable rate, which puts every sample rate 1.7% high (~29 cents). Fine for voice, wrong for music. The proper fix is DA7212 PLL support in the driver, which would accept 12 MHz and synthesize a correct SYSCLK — worth doing as a follow-up, but it needs the datasheet's feedback-divider formula, which I did not want to guess at.

### Two other things reviewers should weigh

- **`RA_PSEL_GPT1` for PD06.** Every RA board in tree uses `RA_PSEL_GPT1` (0x3) for GTIOCnA/B pins and none uses `RA_PSEL_GPT0` (0x2), so that is what this uses. Not confirmed against the RA8P1 PFS table for this specific pin.
- **Footprint.** `CONFIG_CLOCK_CONTROL_PWM` is `default y` when a `pwm-clock` node is enabled and it `select`s `PWM`, so enabling the CODEC's clock pulls both into every build of this board. Gating the audio chain behind an overlay instead would avoid that, at the cost of the CODEC not being usable out of the box.

### Driver change

`da7212` read the MCLK specifier with a hardcoded `name` cell, which only exists on controllers modelled like the NXP syscon; a `pwm-clock` names its cell `id` and failed to build. It now falls back to subsystem 0 when there is no `name` cell. No change for the two existing NXP users.

### Testing

Not built and not run on hardware. `check_compliance.py` passes, and the devicetree was parsed with `edtlib` to confirm the nodes, clocks, pinctrl and interrupts all resolve. Nothing here has been verified against real audio.

body:
Add two opt-in Kconfig options that remove the per-frame memcpy in the NXP ENET data path.

ETH_NXP_ENET_TX_ZERO_COPY builds an enet_buffer_struct_t scatter list directly from the outgoing net_buf fragments and hands it to ENET_StartTxFrame, instead of copying each frame into a driver TX buffer. The net_pkt is referenced until the transmit DMA completes and released from the Tx-done reclaim callback, so the HAL txDirtyRing (frame-info array) and ENET_SetTxReclaim are enabled for this config. Zero-copy TX submits into the ready ring and reclaims through the dirty ring, so ETH_NXP_ENET_TX_BUFFERS defaults to 4 when it is enabled; a single-descriptor ring stalls every transmit with
kStatus_ENET_TxFrameBusy.

ETH_NXP_ENET_RX_ZERO_COPY hands the Rx DMA cache-line aligned full-frame buffers from a k_mem_slab via the HAL rxBuffAlloc/rxBuffFree callbacks, then wraps each received buffer into a net_pkt fragment with net_buf_alloc_with_data (no copy). A net_buf pool destroy handler returns the external buffer to the slab once the stack unreferences the packet.

Both options depend on !ETH_NXP_ENET_USE_DTCM_FOR_DMA_BUFFER and !PTP_CLOCK_NXP_ENET, and default off so existing behavior is unchanged.

Built for mimxrt1170_evk/mimxrt1176/cm7 with both options enabled. Not run on hardware as part of this commit.

title: Bluetooth: BAP: BSNK: Re-request broadcast code after bad code
body:
When a broadcast sink fails to decrypt a BIG due to a bad broadcast code, the BASS receive state is left at Bad_Code. If the broadcast assistant subsequently requests BIS sync again before providing a new broadcast code, the sink did not notify Broadcast_Code_Required again, leaving the assistant with no indication that a new code is expected.

Reset the receive state back to Broadcast_Code_Required whenever a new sync attempt is requested on a BIG known to be encrypted, matching the BASS requirement to request a Broadcast_Code whenever the server does not have a key to decrypt a BIS it is trying to sync to.

Extend the bsim BAP broadcast sink/assistant tests to cover the retry-after-bad-code scenario: the assistant requests BIS sync again before sending the correct code, and the test verifies the receive state changes back to Broadcast_Code_Required instead of staying at Bad_Code.

Tested by running the extended
bap_broadcast_audio_assistant_incorrect_code bsim test, which fails without the fix (times out waiting for the repeated Broadcast_Code notification) and passes with it. Not built or tested on hardware.

Fixes #111790

title: soc: st: stm32u5: wait for the regulator switch before using the new supply
body:
RM0456 requires PWR_SVMSR.REGS to be polled after writing PWR_CR3.REGSEL. The switch is not instantaneous, and until REGS agrees with REGSEL the supply actually feeding VCORE is the previous one. ST's own HAL does this: HAL_PWREx_ConfigSupply() sets REGSEL, spins on REGS with a timeout, and returns HAL_TIMEOUT if it never settles.

soc_early_init_hook() set REGSEL and moved straight on. It runs before PRE_KERNEL_1, so the very next code to touch the supply is the RCC driver, which raises the voltage scaling range, enables the EPOD booster and locks PLL1 - all against a regulator that may still be in transition.

On an STM32U575VIT6Q board selecting SMPS, this draws 280 mA with a hot MCU instead of the expected 15 mA. The A/B is a single image pair from the same tree, same devicetree, same configuration, differing only by this poll loop, 24 bytes of binary: without it the board overheats within seconds of boot, with it the board runs at 15.4 mA awake and 1.95-2.3 mA asleep. The supply network was verified against AN5373 first, and reading REGS from a shell seconds after boot reports SMPS either way - the failure is confined to the microseconds during which the clock driver acts.

Poll REGS with a bounded budget, expressed the way the HAL expresses it, since this runs before the kernel and no timer API is available yet. On timeout fall back to the LDO: a board wired for the LDO, or one whose SMPS network is not fitted, can never make SMPS ready, and the reset default is always available. Proceeding against an unknown supply state is worse, and a pre-kernel hook has no way to report the failure.

Fixes #118845

labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Samples;area: Tests;area: Bluetooth Controller;area: Bluetooth Host;platform: nRF BSIM
body:
The central_gatt_write and peripheral_gatt_write samples only exercise
the GATT Write Without Response path, which is a full-duplex flow driven
from both peers. This does not cover the GATT server to client
notification path, which has a different code path and is a common
real-world throughput scenario.

Add two Kconfig options that extend both samples:

- USE_NOTIFY switches the workload from GATT Write Without Response to
  GATT Notifications. The shared gatt_write_common.c gains a vendor
  specific throughput service with a single notify characteristic and
  CCC. The former write_cmd_cb() metrics body is factored into
  record_and_step() so the same rate accounting is reused by the notify
  send and receive callbacks.
- USE_FULL_DUPLEX (default y) selects bidirectional transfers to load
  both link directions and uncover stack regressions such as
  deadlocks/livelocks (for example on supervision timeout). GATT Write is
  inherently full-duplex; for Notifications both peers subscribe to and
  notify each other. When disabled, Notifications run one-directional
  (peripheral notifier, central subscriber).

For BSIM CI
- overlay-notify.conf enables CONFIG_USE_NOTIFY (full-duplex by default).
- overlay-notify_simplex.conf additionally sets CONFIG_USE_FULL_DUPLEX=n for the one-directional path.


closes #118638

title: drivers: gpio: mcp23xxx: use the chip's interrupt features
labels: area: GPIO;area: Tests;area: Devicetree Binding;platform: Microchip
body:
The MCP23xxx driver only ever wrote one IOCON bit (MIRROR) and otherwise treated the chip as a generic expander with a single active-low interrupt line. Reading the MCP23017 and MCP23018 datasheets against the driver turned up several gaps and two real bugs. This series closes them, one per commit:

- **Byte-oriented bus accessors** (refactor, no functional change) so the core can burst over consecutive registers.
- **Port reads no longer lose interrupts.** Reading GPIO clears the pending interrupt and discards INTCAP (datasheet 3.6.4). If an application read the port before the work handler ran, the event was gone and an error was logged. Port reads now burst INTF+INTCAP+GPIO in one transaction and stash the interrupt for the handler. The handler also reads INTF+INTCAP in one burst instead of two.
- **INT line re-checked after servicing.** DEFVAL-compare (level) interrupts keep INT asserted as long as the mismatch exists (datasheet 3.6.5), so an edge-triggered host never sees another edge. The old code relied on a ~2 ns pulse the chip emits when INTCAP is read, as its own comment admitted.
- **MCP23x09/x18 interrupts now clear.** Those parts have an INTCC bit that defaults to "clear on GPIO read", but the driver acknowledges by reading INTCAP, so INT never deasserted after the first event.
- **INT polarity and drive are configurable.** IOCON.INTPOL follows the `GPIO_ACTIVE_*` flag on `int-gpios`; a new `int-open-drain` boolean sets IOCON.ODR for boards sharing one interrupt line between expanders.
- **Separate INTA and INTB.** `int-gpios` accepts a second entry; with two entries MIRROR is left clear and each port's line gets its own host callback. A single entry keeps the mirrored behaviour, so existing device trees are unaffected.
- **No spurious callback on enable.** Found on hardware: interrupt-on-change compares against the pin value at the last GPIO/INTCAP read, so enabling a pin that changed since then fired immediately. The reference is now refreshed right before GPINTEN is set.

The build_all GPIO overlay gains both binding forms so the new paths are compiled. Each commit builds on its own on `native_sim/native/64` and `qemu_cortex_m3`.

**Hardware testing** (MCP23017 breakouts on an ESP32, I2C at 400 kHz, GPA0 jumpered to GPB0 so the output drives the input on the other port):

| Case | Mirrored, one INT line | Two lines (INTA, INTB) |
|---|---|---|
| Edge both / rising / falling, 200 toggles | 200 / 100 / 100 exact | 200 / 100 / 100 exact, both directions |
| Edge both while another thread hammers `gpio_port_get_raw` | 200 exact | 200 exact |
| Level low held | re-fires continuously (~480 per 100 ms), once when disabled from the callback | same |
| Level low armed while high, then driven low | 0 before, fires after | same |
| Level high, disabled from callback | exactly 1 | exactly 1 |
| Host-side edge counters on INTA/INTB | n/a | port B input: 0 on INTA, 200 on INTB; port A input: 200 on INTA, 0 on INTB |

Tested on two separate MCP23017 boards in mirrored mode and one in two-line mode. Not yet tested: `int-open-drain`, and the INTCC change on an MCP23x09/x18, so review from anyone with one of those on hand would be welcome.

title: logging: fix lost wakeup when attaching the first backend
body:
The log processing thread does not poll periodically: when no autostart backend is pending activation it parks on log_process_thread_sem with K_FOREVER, and the first flush of the boot messages depends on the single wake token given by z_log_notify_backend_enabled().

The token is given before backend_attached is set, and that flag is a plain bool the woken thread reads without synchronization. On SMP the log thread runs on another core and can observe a stale backend_attached == false, return from log_process() without claiming any message, and park again. The semaphore limit is 1, so the token is gone. Messages buffered before the log thread first ran never armed the one-shot trigger timer, and as long as their count stays below CONFIG_LOG_PROCESS_TRIGGER_THRESHOLD nothing wakes the thread again.

The shell log backend opens a second window: it sets its state to SHELL_LOG_BACKEND_ENABLED only after log_backend_enable() returns, so a log thread dispatched in between finds the backend active but still in the SHELL_LOG_BACKEND_UNINIT state and process() silently discards the claimed messages.

Fix both windows:

- make backend_attached an atomic_t and set it before giving the semaphore, so the woken thread always observes the backend as attached;

- set the shell backend state, output context and dropped count before activating the backend, so messages dispatched right after activation are processed instead of dropped.

The two changes are interdependent: closing only the first window makes the woken thread hit the second.

Verified on a quad-core rk3588 board, where the race is reachable at every boot with the shell as the only non-autostart log backend: without the fix, boot logs appeared late or not at all; with it, 100 consecutive boots flushed all boot logs before the first prompt. The logging test suite passes on native_sim; builds were verified in deferred and immediate modes.

Fixes #118927

title: drivers: ethernet: nxp_imx_netc & dsa: gptp deadlock fix
body:
Using gPTP with the NXP iMX NETC driver together with DSA caused two
separate TX-path deadlocks, both rooted in mismatched criteria for
"does this frame need to wait for a TX timestamp":

1. netc_eth_tx() gated its TX-timestamp reclaim/wait loop on
   opt.flags (kEP_TX_OPT_REQ_TS), which is only set for endpoint
   timestamp requests. DSA conduit-port frames signal their
   timestamp request through a separate txDesc TSR_MASK flag that
   never touches opt.flags. When a frame's only timestamp request
   came from the DSA path, the wait loop was skipped, so its TX
   descriptor was never reclaimed, the TX ring filled up, and the
   thread blocked forever on tx_sem.

2. dsa_xmit() decided whether to wait for a TX timestamp callback
   based on the raw Ethernet type (NET_ETH_PTYPE_PTP) rather than
   the packet's actual timestamp-request flag
   (net_pkt_is_tx_timestamping(pkt)). This let DSA wait for a
   timestamp on PTP-typed frames (e.g. a gPTP announce) that the
   NETC driver never generates, hanging the TX path.

Both fixes align the timestamp-wait condition with the actual
timestamp-request signal instead of an incidental/legacy proxy for
it, eliminating the deadlocks.
