title: modem: cellular: on-demand GNSS power control
body:
This PR adds on-demand control of the GNSS receiver integrated in a cellular modem API

Integrated GNSS receivers are common in asset trackers, where power consumption is critical: the receiver should only run while the application needs a fix, and switching it on or off should not disturb the cellular link. The driver of the GNSS receiver is the owner of that decision, so this PR gives it an API to switch the receiver through the modem driver, at any point in the modem's lifecycle. First user of this is U-blox SARA-R4. Some fixes landed additionaly in `modem_cellular` as they were found while testing it on hardware.

## On-demand GNSS power control
  - Two new optional chat scripts in struct modem_cellular_config_scripts: 
    - `gnss_power_on` GNSS power on AT commands
    - `gnss_shutdown` GNSS shutdown AT commands
  - Two new functions added, `modem_cellular_gnss_power_on` and `modem_cellular_gnss_shutdown`. The caller blocks until the above mentionedscripts has run, at most `CONFIG_MODEM_CELLULAR_GNSS_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S` (default 60 s).
  - A request runs from a new `RUN_GNSS_REQUEST_SCRIPT` state, entered from `WAIT_FOR_APN`, `AWAIT_DIAL`, `AWAIT_REGISTERED` or `REGISTERED` when no other script is running on the AT channel. The modem returns to the same state afterwards, so the cellular link, including a running PPP session, is not affected.
  - Events that arrive while the GNSS script runs, such as registration changes or the interface going up or down, are queued and handled once it completes.
  - A request made while the modem is suspended or still starting up waits until the modem reaches one of these states. 
  - Before the modem powers off, `gnss_shutdown` runs over the AT channel. The last known receiver state is tracked, so a script for the state the receiver is already in is not sent again.

For the SARA-R4, `CONFIG_MODEM_CELLULAR_U_BLOX_SARA_R4_GNSS` provides the scripts (`AT+UGPS=1,0,15` and `AT+UGPS=0`) and adds `AT+UGPRF=2` to the init script. It routes the GNSS data to a muxed virtual port and must be sent before CMUX is started.

Modems without these scripts are not affected: the API returns `-ENOTSUP` and the new state is never entered, however slight code and RAM memory increase is noticiable. Will take care of it after review. 

## Power management

  - **Child devices:** with `CONFIG_DEVICE_DEPS`, the modem refuses to suspend (`-EBUSY`) while one of its devicetree children is in use: a child under runtime PM that holds a usage reference, or any other child in
  `PM_DEVICE_STATE_ACTIVE`. Previously the modem powered off underneath it. The application now suspends the children, such as the GNSS receiver, before releasing the last modem reference. An asynchronous runtime suspend cannot  report the refusal, so this order matters.
  - **Suspend during PPP teardown:** a suspend arriving in `AWAIT_PPP_DEAD`, typically right after the interface is brought down, was dropped, so `pm_action()` waited for its 30 s timeout and the modem stayed powered. It is now
  handled once the PPP teardown has settled.

## Fixes

  - `cmd_pipe` was left pointing at DLCI2 after dialing, so power-off scripts ran on the PPP data channel instead of the AT channel.
  - The `+CME ERROR` abort match is extended to `"+CME ERROR: "`, so `argv[1]` holds only the error code.
  - `modem_chat_release()` now also cancels the script timeouts, so a script started right after releasing a running one no longer inherits its deadlines.

  ## Testing

**Setup:** custom board with an nRF5340 and a u-blox SARA-R422M10S. An out-of-tree u-blox GNSS driver on CMUX DLCI3 calls the new API from its own PM handling. This out-of-tree driver, I plan to share next month together with extra related functionality.

  | Scenario | Result |
  |---|---|
  | Start-up with the GNSS option | `AT+UGPRF=2` accepted before `AT+CMUX`. A power-on request made during the power pulse waits and runs from `AWAIT_DIAL`, `AT+UGPS=1,0,15` answers `OK` in about 1.2 s, the receiver initialises on DLCI3 and GNSS driver initializes and gets fixes. |
  | Receiver off/on while idle and connected | 5 cycles in `AWAIT_DIAL` and 6 in `REGISTERED` with PPP up: all `OK`, the link and the periodic script unaffected. |
  | Request while a periodic script runs | 18 requests at a 300 ms poll interval of which 4 that arrived during a poll started only after it completed. All completed. |
  | Request for the state the receiver is already in | Completes with no additional AT command sent. |
  | Interface brought up during a GNSS script | The dial waits for the script, then runs once. Link comes up. |
  | Suspend while a request waits or runs | From `REGISTERED` state, 50, 300 and 800 ms after the request: `-ECANCELED`. The running `AT+UGPS=1` completes before `AT+UGPS=0` and the power-off, and the next dial connects. During modem  start-up (3.5 and 4.4 s after resume): `-ECANCELED`, normal power-off. |
  | Request while the modem stays suspended | Waits, then `-ETIMEDOUT` after the configured timeout. No state change. |
  | Suspend while the GNSS receiver is in use | Refused with `-EBUSY` (`Refusing to suspend: child device ... is still in use`). The modem stays up. |
  | Interface down from a connected state, then suspend | The suspend arrives in `AWAIT_PPP_DEAD`, is handled when that state is left, and the modem reaches `IDLE` about 1.1 s later with a 10 s periodic interval. Before this change, `pm_action()` timed out after 30 s with the modem still on. |
  | Power-off with the receiver state known off | `gnss_shutdown` is skipped. |
  | Power-off with the receiver state unknown | `AT+UGPS=0` is sent, the module is either responding with OK or refuse with`+CME ERROR: 1799` aborting the script at once, and the power-off continues normally. |
  | Cycle tests | 50 cycles of receiver off, interface down, suspend, resume, interface up, receiver on: 50/50, no script failures, no dropped events. |

Built with `tests/drivers/build_all/modem` on native_sim, also with `CONFIG_GNSS=y` and `CONFIG_MODEM_CELLULAR_U_BLOX_SARA_R4_GNSS=y`.

Only the SARA-R4 has been tested. The mechanism is generic and could be applied to other cellular modems that attach the GNSS receiver on MUX, regardless if they have user pipe available or not. All it needs is its own `gnss_power_on` and `gnss_shutdown` scripts. Feedback from anyone with such hardware is welcome.

components that submit work to the system workqueue, not from Bluetooth being
enabled. This adds a hidden `BT_SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_COOP` symbol and applies the
range only when one of those components is enabled. See the commit message for
the reasoning.

Motivated by an out-of-tree application that drives an external controller and
deliberately runs the system workqueue as its lowest-priority thread, so that
the watchdog it services is only fed while the whole system is still making
progress. Today that application cannot enable `CONFIG_BT` at all.

### Testing

Built against `main` with Zephyr SDK 1.0.1.

| Configuration | Board | `BT_HCI_RAW` | `BT_CTLR_PRIVACY` | `BT_SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_COOP` | `SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_PRIORITY` |
| :--- | :--- | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| `samples/bluetooth/hci_uart_3wire` | nrf52840dk/nrf52840 | y | y | y | -1 |
| `samples/bluetooth/hci_uart` | nrf52840dk/nrf52840 | y | y | y | -1 |
| `samples/bluetooth/peripheral` | nrf52840dk/nrf52840 | n | y | y | -1 |
| minimal app, `BT_HCI_RAW=y` + userchan, asking for `SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_PRIORITY=10` | native_sim | y | n | **n** | **10** |

The first three are unaffected by this patch; note that two of them are
`BT_HCI_RAW` builds that still require the cooperative range, which they get
through `BT_CTLR_PRIVACY`. The fourth is the case being addressed.

Reverting only `subsys/bluetooth/Kconfig` to `main` and rebuilding that fourth
configuration fails, as expected:

```
warning: user value 10 on the int symbol SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_PRIORITY (defined at
kernel/Kconfig:536, subsys/bluetooth/Kconfig:40,
subsys/ipc/ipc_service/lib/Kconfig.icmsg:92) ignored due to being outside the
active range ([-256, -1]) -- falling back on defaults
error: Aborting due to Kconfig warnings
```

title: Bluetooth: Classic: GOEP RX buffer allocation and SDU reassembly bounds
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Bluetooth Classic;backport v4.3-branch;backport v4.4-branch
body:
Two related correctness fixes in the BR/EDR receive path.

### `Bluetooth: Classic: GOEP: Do not wait for L2CAP RX buffers`

The `alloc_buf` callback of a GOEP v2 L2CAP channel allocates from `goep_rx_pool`
with `K_FOREVER`. L2CAP calls that callback from the Bluetooth RX workqueue, both
to start a new SDU and for every further fragment appended to it, and it is that
same workqueue that releases the buffers once the SDU has been handed to OBEX.
The pool is shared by all GOEP v2 channels and a single SDU can take several
buffers, so once it runs dry the wait can never be satisfied and HCI receive
processing stops.

The callback also has no timeout parameter, so a caller that asks for a
non-blocking append (`net_buf_append_bytes()` with `K_NO_WAIT`, reaching the
callback via `l2cap_br_alloc_frag()`) has no way to say so. The callback has to
decide, and here the only workable answer is not to wait.

This is the same change made for the sibling AVCTP and AVRCP browsing channels in
8529242080de and c8c2438f0516; GOEP is the remaining one. L2CAP already turns a
failed allocation on a retransmission-mode channel into `-ENOBUFS` and reports
the channel as locally busy to the peer, so the graceful path already exists.

### `Bluetooth: Classic: L2CAP: Bound BR/EDR SDU reassembly`

`bt_l2cap_br_recv_seg()` takes the declared SDU length from a `SAR_START` segment
and never compares it against the channel's negotiated receive MTU, so a peer can
announce an SDU of up to 65535 bytes on a channel configured for far less. The
`seg_recv` twin `bt_l2cap_br_recv_seg_direct()` already rejects such an SDU, and
so does the LE path; this applies the same check with the same log wording.

The running total the function compares against that declared length is also
wrong. Segments are appended with `net_buf_append_bytes()`, which chains a new
fragment when the current buffer fills up, so once reassembly spills past the
head buffer `_sdu->len` stops growing while data keeps arriving in the chain. All
three reads of the accumulated length now use `net_buf_frags_len()`. That matters
in both directions: the overflow guard stops under-counting, and the `SAR_END`
completeness check stops rejecting a correctly received fragmented SDU as short.

I checked every in-tree profile that registers an `alloc_buf` callback (a2dp via
avdtp, avctp, avrcp browsing, goep, and the bredr shell): all set `rx.mtu` at or
above the size of the buffers their callback hands out, so none of them needs to
receive an SDU larger than the MTU it advertised.

### Build coverage

Compile-tested only; there is no GOEP test coverage in the tree.

- `qemu_x86`, `tests/bluetooth/shell` with `CONF_FILE="prj_br.conf"`
  (`CONFIG_BT_GOEP=y`): builds clean, compiles both `goep.c` and `l2cap_br.c`.
- `qemu_x86`, `tests/bluetooth/classic/l2cap_s` plus `CONFIG_BT_L2CAP_ENH_RET=y`
  and without `CONFIG_BT_GOEP`: builds clean, compiles `l2cap_br.c`. Note that
  `bt_l2cap_br_recv_seg()` sits inside `#if defined(CONFIG_BT_L2CAP_RET_FC)`,
  which plain `l2cap_s` does not set, so that overlay is needed for the changed
  lines to compile at all.

Neither build exercises the changed code at runtime. `CONFIG_BT_L2CAP_SEG_RECV`
was not set in either, so `bt_l2cap_br_recv_seg_direct()` did not compile; this
series does not change that function.

Fixes: #121162

title: gitlint: ignore the whole trailer block in commit messages
body:
The commit message rule filtered out only lines starting with "signed-off-by" before counting body lines when determining whether the body-min-line-count was sufficient.  Every other trailer, such as "Co-authored-by" or "Assisted-by" would be counted as body lines in the commit message.  This allowed commit messages with an empty body to pass the CI.  Example:

```
tests: drivers: fixing stuff in tests

Assisted-by: Claude:my-ai-best-friend
Signed-off-by: My Name <my.name@somedomain.com>
```

Strip the trailer blocks from the end of the message instead.  The final paragraph is dropped only when it opens with a trailer and holds nothing but trailers and their continuation lines.  This allows trailer-shaped comments earlier in the message to still count as a body.

title: bluetooth: mesh: fix rpl storage timeout
body:
The replay protection list and the solicitation replay list shared the
pending-store work item with every other settings flag. Scheduling any
other flag, such as model data, rescheduled that work item to
CONFIG_BT_MESH_STORE_TIMEOUT, and the handler then stored every flag
that was set, the replay lists included. CONFIG_BT_MESH_RPL_STORE_TIMEOUT
was therefore only honored while nothing else was pending, and the
replay lists were written to flash far more often than configured.

Give the replay lists a work item of their own, armed with
CONFIG_BT_MESH_RPL_STORE_TIMEOUT. store_pending_flags() now takes a mask
so that each work item stores only the flags it owns, and the generic
item masks the replay list flags out. bt_mesh_settings_store_pending()
cancels both items and flushes everything, leaving the synchronous path
unchanged. Both replay lists keep sharing one deadline, and each is
still stored only when its own flag is set.

plus unit tests to check that there is no interference among stored groups and
all groups behave as designed.

title: kernel: pipe: notify pollers only when data is stored
body:
k_pipe_write() reported K_POLL_STATE_PIPE_DATA_AVAILABLE before it put anything into the ring buffer, and did so whether or not the write stored any data. A thread blocked in k_poll() on
K_POLL_TYPE_PIPE_DATA_AVAILABLE was therefore woken by writes that left the pipe with nothing to read.

The case that always misreports is an unbuffered pipe, which k_pipe_init() accepts with a NULL buffer and a size of zero. Such a pipe has no storage, so data only moves by direct copy to a pending reader. A write that finds no reader transfers nothing and returns -EAGAIN, yet it still told pollers that data was available. A write consumed entirely by pending readers, and a write that stores nothing because the pipe is full, misreport the same way.

Store the data first and report availability only when ring_buf_put() accepted at least one byte. Data handed straight to a pending reader never reaches the pipe, so it is not reported.

The pipe test suite never built the CONFIG_POLL paths of the implementation, which is why this went unnoticed. Add a scenario that enables CONFIG_POLL and a test for the unbuffered case.

Ran tests/kernel/pipe and tests/kernel/poll on native_sim, native_sim/native/64, qemu_x86 and qemu_cortex_m3: the new test fails without this change and 292 of 292 test cases pass with it. Ran tests/kernel on native_sim and qemu_x86 with no failures. Not run on hardware.

Fixes: a9ab8cb7797d ("feat: enable polling support for k_pipe interface")

title: drivers: mfd: ad559x: wait for reset recovery after hardware reset
body:
The AD559x needs up to 250 us to recover after a reset, per the datasheet, before it will accept new data on the bus. The driver previously issued the software reset immediately after de-asserting `reset-gpios`, without waiting for this recovery time.

Add a `reset-recovery-time-us` devicetree property (default 250 us) and busy-wait for it in `mfd_ad559x_init()`, after de-asserting `reset-gpios` and before the software reset. The delay is only applied when `reset-gpios` is present. Boards whose reset line needs extra settling time can increase the property to match their hardware.

This delay only applies at driver init (`mfd_ad559x_init()`), which runs on every boot regardless of reset cause. It doesn't cover a RESET-pin toggle triggered outside the driver at runtime, since no such API exists in this driver.

Tested on an STM32 Nucleo-H563ZI paired with a MikroElektronika ADAC Click board (AD5593R). The click board's RESET pull-up was replaced with a pull-down so RESET is guaranteed low until the MCU drives it high, matching what the driver assumes.

A Saleae logic analyzer captured RESET and I2C activity at startup to measure the delay between RESET going high and the first I2C transaction. A test application swept reset-recovery-time-us across several values: with the delay set to 0, the software reset write in `mfd_ad559x_init()` failed and `device_is_ready()` returned false, logging "AD559x device is not ready". With the datasheet's 250 us default restored, init and the following I2C traffic succeeded reliably. The reset-recovery delay is applied in `mfd_ad559x_init()` before the bus-specific init, so this exercises the same code path used by the SPI variant.

title: net: ipv6: nbr: Pending packets leaks fixes
body:
Packets queued on a neighbor while waiting for an NA hold two references, one handed over by the sender and one taken when queued. Several drain paths released only one of them, and the NS reply timeout re-ran queued packets through the send path, which re-queued them with a third reference and, with more than two packets queued, stopped soliciting altogether. Sustained traffic to an unresolved neighbor exhausted the TX packet pool.

Fixes:
- `nbr_clear_ns_pending()` releases both references.
- The NA and RA handlers drain the queue through a shared `nbr_send_pending()` helper, which releases the queue reference of every packet it sends. The RA handler skips the drain when the RA carried no SLLAO, as sending to a still unresolved neighbor looped forever.
- The NS reply timeout no longer re-runs queued packets. It drops the oldest, sends a fresh NS for the rest so they keep their order and references, sends everything if the neighbor resolved meanwhile, and releases the neighbor when it ends unresolved with nothing queued.

Tests:
- New `tests/net/ipv6` cases queue packets toward an unresolved neighbor and check the TX pools are back to their initial state after NS timeouts, after an RA with and without SLLAO, after resolution through `net_ipv6_nbr_add()`, and after neighbor removal.
- Test packet allocations are bounded so a leak turns into a reported failure instead of a twister timeout, and the NS reply timeout is shortened to 300 ms to keep the suite fast.

Fixes #119443

The address stayed `PREFERRED`, so new connections kept picking it as source and could postpone the removal indefinitely. A repeat removal also dropped a reference that belonged to a connection, so the address could be freed while still in use.

A removed address is now demoted to `DEPRECATED` until it is added again, a repeat removal leaves the remaining references alone, and the IP config release no longer depends on the removal consuming references. Tests cover both IPv4 and IPv6.

title: drivers: timer: arm_arch: start the counter before seeding the core
body:
sys_clock_driver_init() seeded the timer core's announce baseline from the counter and only then enabled the timer. QEMU's Cortex-A9 global timer model reports the time since machine start while the timer is disabled and restarts the count from zero once it is enabled, so the baseline ended up ahead of the counter for the first few milliseconds of the run. Every sys_clock_elapsed() in that window computed a wrapped delta that clamps to UINT32_MAX ticks, so a timeout queued then was placed about 2^32 ticks out and never expired. Which timeouts land in the window depends on the boot timing, so an unrelated change in code layout made tests/net/lib/mqtt_sn_client hang in its first test case on qemu_cortex_a9.

Enable the timer before timer_core_init() so the baseline is taken from the running counter, and keep the compare interrupt masked until the core has armed the first deadline.

title: net: dhcpv4: Give the whole lease up on every path that abandons one
body:
The client removed the bound address on some paths that give a lease up and not
on others. Stopping it while rebinding, or an interface going down while renewing
or rebinding, left the address on the interface with nothing referring to it: it
stayed preferred with no lifetime, was picked as the source for new connections
after a subnet change, and with a single IPv4 address slot blocked every later
lease. The lease's DNS servers and the gateway from the router option were left
behind on more paths still.

The series gives the whole lease up in one place wherever a lease is abandoned,
in a fixed order: gateway, then DNS servers, then the address last. The gateway
is put back to whatever the interface carried before the lease installed its own
rather than cleared, because the interface records no source for it, so a gateway
set by hand survives. A refusal of the request that follows an offer, and a
decline, now wait the ten seconds of RFC 2131 3.1 plus jitter before restarting,
while a refused renewal restarts at once instead of waiting out the retransmit
the renewal had armed.

Giving a lease up now removes things, so it raises events: the lease's DNS
servers going away, then the leased address, which is deliberately last. An
application may call back into the client from those handlers, and with
synchronous event delivery that re-enters the client mid-teardown; the series
makes that work and tests it. The stop event therefore has to come first,
otherwise a handler that restarts the client would announce the start before the
stop. The order seen on a stop is thus reversed, from address, DNS servers, stop
to stop, DNS servers, address, which the migration guide covers.

The rework is quite substantial but I hope the heavily extended test suite covers for it. 
It was also tested against a real DHCP server (dnsmasq) on host.

Fixes #119441

title: Bluetooth: HCI: ipm_stm32wb: Configure the controller from open()
body:
The STM32WB IPM driver sends its two vendor-specific initialization commands, the public address derived from the device UID and the transmit power level, from `open()`, through the HCI lockstep helper added in #118479 and the driver's own send path, instead of implementing the `setup()` driver API op on top of the Host's `bt_hci_cmd_send_sync()`. The responses are consumed in the driver's receive thread by feeding received packets to the helper before delivering them to the host.

The commands no longer depend on the Host, so they now also run in controller-only builds. There they were both compiled out and never reached, since `bt_enable_raw()` opens the driver without calling `setup()`, which left the controller with its default address and transmit power. The driver no longer selects `CONFIG_BT_HCI_SETUP`.

An unanswered address command now fails `open()` instead of being logged and followed by a second command that waits out the same timeout; a controller that answers with an error status is still only logged, as before. `open()` aborts the receive thread it started when the vendor initialization fails, so that a second `bt_enable()` does not create a thread that is still running.

A second commit does the same for `close()`, which sent its vendor-specific reset command through `bt_hci_cmd_send_sync()` and was therefore compiled only into builds with a Host. It did not work with the Host either: `bt_disable()` marks the transport closed before it calls `close()`, after which the Host refuses the command with `-EHOSTDOWN`, so `bt_disable()` failed. The command now goes through the lockstep helper over the driver's own transport, while the receive thread is still running to feed the response, and with that the driver calls no Host API any more.

Build-tested on nucleo_wb55rg with `samples/bluetooth/peripheral_hr` and `samples/bluetooth/hci_uart`. Not run on hardware: I have no STM32WB board here, so a check by someone who has one is welcome.

Part of #116316, W5(c).

title: Bluetooth: HCI: ambiq: Configure the controller from open()
body:
The Ambiq driver sends its vendor-specific NVDS configuration command from `open()`, through the HCI lockstep helper added in #118479 and the driver's own SPI send path, instead of implementing the `setup()` driver API op on top of the Host's `bt_hci_cmd_send_sync()`. The responses are consumed in the driver's receive thread by feeding received packets to the helper before they reach the host.

The command no longer depends on the Host, so the two code paths that existed for it, one building the packet by hand for controller-only builds and one going through the Host, collapse into one, and the driver no longer selects `CONFIG_BT_HCI_SETUP`. The hand-built path was in fact unreachable: `bt_enable_raw()` opens the driver without calling `setup()`, so a controller-only build sent neither the NVDS command nor the reset that follows it. Both now run there, which also means the reset that makes the NVDS parameters take effect is sent in every build rather than only where the Host would send its own a few transactions later. That is the one behavioural change I would like Ambiq to confirm.

`open()` aborts the receive thread it started when the controller initialization or the vendor command fails, so that a second `bt_enable()` does not create a thread that is still running. That path could already fail before this change.

Build-tested on apollo4p_blue_kxr_evb and apollo3_evb with `samples/bluetooth/peripheral_hr`. Not run on hardware: I have no Apollo board here, so a check by someone who has one is welcome.

Part of #116316, W5(c).

title: Bluetooth: Add a reset entry point to the HCI lockstep helper
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Tests;area: Bluetooth Controller;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth HCI;area: Bluetooth Classic;Release
body:
The HCI lockstep helper documented that initializing it again restores the initial command allowance, for a controller that has been reset by other means than an HCI command. That is not safe. `bt_hci_lockstep_init()` calls `k_sem_init()`, which with `CONFIG_OBJ_CORE_SEM` calls `k_obj_core_init_and_link()`, so initializing the same helper twice links the same object core twice and corrupts the tracking list. No in-tree driver does it today, since the one user initializes the helper from its device initialization function, so this is a contract that invites the defect rather than an active one.

`bt_hci_lockstep_reset()` restores the allowance and forgets the outstanding command without re-initializing the semaphore, and initialization is now documented as the once-only call it has to be. The transport send function and the caller's timeout survive the reset, so a driver that resets its controller while opening it does not have to repeat what it set up at device initialization.

The reset may be called from any context and takes the helper's lock, so it may run while packets are being fed, which a driver that is fed from a callback it cannot stop needs. It signals the change of state by giving the helper's semaphore, as feeding does, so a sender that is waiting for the controller to allow its command goes ahead, as when a recovery path resets a controller that has stopped responding.

A driver is expected not to reset its controller while a command is outstanding, since it cannot be known which side of the reset the command ended up on. If it does, the command is abandoned: its response is no longer consumed and its sender fails at its deadline, deliberately not earlier, so that a response which still arrives cannot be taken for that of a later command with the same opcode. What the reset cannot do either is tell packets the controller sent before it from the responses to what follows, so those must not be fed afterwards: a stale response to the same opcode would pass for the new one and a stale response allowing no command would revoke the restored allowance.

The helper keeps its view of the command allowance from one opening of the transport to the next, and the group documentation now says so. #119576 and #119577 need this call once it lands: both reset their controller across a close/open cycle, and with their vendor initialization no longer going through the Host, which starts every enable with a fresh allowance, nothing else restores it. #119575 does not reset its controller and needs nothing.

Unit test on native_sim, native_sim/native/64 and qemu_cortex_m3: 156 cases pass, five of them new, one of which resets the helper from an ISR. Also built for siwx917_rb4338a, the only in-tree user of the helper. Not run on hardware.

Part of #116316, W5(c).

title: Bluetooth: HCI: ambiq: Do not close the transport mid-transfer
body:
`close()` takes the controller down and aborts the receive thread with no regard for an SPI transfer in progress. The receive thread holds `sem_spi_available` while it talks to the controller, and `k_thread_abort()` does not give a semaphore back for the thread it stops, so a `close()` that lands in the middle of a transfer leaves the semaphore taken and the next send blocks forever. Before that, the controller is put in reset and its clocks are turned off with the transfer still in flight.

The semaphore is now held across both, so `close()` waits for the transfer in progress to finish before it touches the controller or the thread. `bt_apollo_controller_deinit()` does no SPI transfer of its own, so it cannot end up waiting for the semaphore `close()` holds. Holding the semaphore does not stop a send that is already under way, though: the send path gives it back between its attempts, which it repeats for up to five seconds, so that the receive path can drain the controller in the meantime. The driver therefore keeps track of whether the transport is open and of how often that has changed. `open()` and `close()` update both while holding the semaphore, and the send path gives up with `-ENETDOWN` if on getting the semaphore the transport is closed or the count has moved on since the send began. The count is what stops a send that slept through a `close()` and the `open()` after it from delivering the old session's packet to the new one; the flag is what stops a send that starts while `close()` is finishing. The count is atomic because a send notes it before it has the semaphore: what counts is the session the call began in, not the one in which it first gets the semaphore. `open()` makes its update before the controller initialization, which already sends through the same path.

A `close()` called from the receive callback aborts the calling thread, which never returns to give the semaphore back, so that case gives it back before the abort.

Found while reviewing #119577, which uses the same order on its failed-open path. The two are independent; this one is a bug that predates it.

Build-tested on apollo4p_blue_kxr_evb and apollo3_evb with `samples/bluetooth/peripheral_hr`. Not run on hardware: I have no Apollo board here, so a check by someone who has one is welcome.

title: drivers: gpio: sam0: add drive strength flag
labels: area: GPIO;platform: Microchip SAM;area: Devicetree Binding
body:
Add SAM0_GPIO_DRIVE_STRONG, a SAM0 specific GPIO devicetree flag that sets PORT PINCFG.DRVSTR on pins configured as outputs.

gpio_sam0_config() rebuilds PINCFG from zero on every call, so a drive strength selected through pinctrl is cleared as soon as the pin is configured through the GPIO API. Carrying it on the gpios specifier selects the stronger driver where the pin is declared, alongside the existing SAM0_GPIO_DEBOUNCE.

On SAM D5x/E5x this raises the rated output current from 2 mA to 8 mA at VDD >= 3.0 V (DS60001507, Table 54-13).

title: Bluetooth: HCI: Provide the public address to drivers before open()
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Tests;area: Bluetooth Controller;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth HCI;area: Bluetooth Classic;Release
body:
The public identity address that the Host hands to a driver's `setup()` op is also stored in the common HCI driver data, through `bt_hci_set_public_addr()`, before the HCI transport is opened. A driver reads it with `bt_hci_get_public_addr()` and can apply it during `open()`, from vendor-specific initialization that does not depend on the Host's command APIs being available. `bt_hci_get_public_addr()` returns `BT_ADDR_ANY` while no public address has been set, which is what `setup()` receives in that case, so a driver moving from one to the other keeps the check it has.

The `setup()` path keeps receiving the address exactly as before, so both channels coexist until the drivers implementing `setup()` have migrated. So that enabling the new channel does not pull in the mechanism it replaces, `CONFIG_BT_HCI_SET_PUBLIC_ADDR` stops selecting `CONFIG_BT_HCI_SETUP`, and the three drivers that apply the address in `setup()` now select that option themselves, matching the conditions their `setup()` implementations are compiled under.

One in-tree configuration changes as a result: a BlueNRG build with `CONFIG_BT_HCI_RAW` no longer has `CONFIG_BT_HCI_SETUP` enabled. That is harmless, since the driver's `setup()` callback is already excluded from such a build, and it removes a case where the option was enabled for a driver that could not use it.

This is the prerequisite for the five remaining `setup()` conversions: BlueNRG over SPI, STM32WBA, NXP, CYW208xx and the h4 vendor backends all program the controller's public address today and cannot move their vendor initialization into `open()` without it.

Build-tested on nrf52dk/nrf52832, nucleo_wb55rg and nrf52840dk/nrf52840 with `samples/bluetooth/peripheral_hr`. Not run on hardware.

Part of #116316, W5(c).

title: Bluetooth: HCI: Deprecate the setup() driver API op
body:
`setup()` is Host code living in the HCI driver vtable: most implementations call `bt_hci_cmd_send_sync()`, which is why the op exists at all, and why a driver's vendor-specific initialization has nowhere to run in a build without a Host. A driver does that work inside `open()` instead, over its own transport, with the helpers of `hci_pkt.h` and `hci_lockstep.h`, and takes the public address from `bt_hci_get_public_addr()`.

This deprecates the op, `bt_hci_setup()`, `struct bt_hci_setup_params` and `CONFIG_BT_HCI_SETUP`, so that an out-of-tree driver still implementing `setup()` is pointed at the replacement. The Host keeps calling the op through the deprecation window; the op, its Kconfig and the h4 vendor hook go two releases from now.

No attribute is put on the op or the function, deliberately: the Host reads the member in order to call it, so an attribute would warn on the Host rather than on the drivers the deprecation is aimed at. Selecting the deprecated Kconfig symbol is what makes a build say so, and that fires for exactly the drivers that have not moved. Verified: a build for `nrf52dk/nrf52832` is clean, a build for `nucleo_wb55rg` prints `warning: Deprecated symbol BT_HCI_SETUP is enabled.`

It builds on the public-address channel (#119615), which besides being the prerequisite for five of the conversions also removes a false positive here: without it, a BlueNRG build with `CONFIG_BT_HCI_RAW` would warn although that build has no `setup()` callback at all. The warning is suppressible with `CONFIG_WARN_DEPRECATED=n`, and it reports an enabled Kconfig selector rather than an implementation, so it reaches an out-of-tree driver that selects the option and stays silent for one that implements the op without selecting it.

All in-tree drivers are converted, so nothing in the tree selects `CONFIG_BT_HCI_SETUP` any more and no in-tree build warns.

### Conversion status

| Driver | Vendor | State |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hci_silabs_siwx91x` | Silicon Labs | done, #118479 |
| `hci_infineon_psoc6_bless` | Infineon | merged, #119575 |
| `ipm_stm32wb` | ST | merged, #119576 |
| `hci_ambiq` + `apollox_blue` | Ambiq | merged, #119577 |
| `hci_spi_st` (BlueNRG) | ST | merged, #119734 |
| `hci_stm32wba` | ST | merged, #119733 |
| `hci_nxp` | NXP | merged, #119735 |
| `hci_infineon_cyw208xx` | Infineon | merged, #119736 |
| `h4.c` vendor backends: `hci_nxp_setup.c`, `hci_uart_infineon.c` | NXP, Infineon | merged, #120078 |

Five of those needed the public-address channel, `bt_hci_set_public_addr()` and `bt_hci_get_public_addr()` (#119615, merged), because they program the controller's public address from the value the Host passes to `setup()` today.

Part of #116316, W5(c).

title: drivers: video: native_sim host FIFO video source
labels: area: Build System;area: Samples;area: Devicetree;area: Tests;area: native port;area: Video;area: Devicetree Binding;area: Boards/SoCs;Release
body:
Add a video capture driver for `native_sim` that reads fixed-size raw frames from a named pipe on the host and exposes them through the video API as an ordinary `zephyr,camera` device.

A host process such as ffmpeg feeds the pipe. Create the FIFO and start the application on it:

    mkfifo /tmp/zephyr-cam.fifo
    zephyr.exe --video-fifo=/tmp/zephyr-cam.fifo

then feed it a test pattern from another terminal:

    ffmpeg -re -f lavfi -i testsrc2=size=320x240:rate=10 \
      -pix_fmt rgb565le -f rawvideo -y /tmp/zephyr-cam.fifo

The source can equally be a real V4L2 webcam:

    ffmpeg -f v4l2 -i /dev/video0 \
      -vf "scale=320:240:force_original_aspect_ratio=increase,crop=320:240,fps=10" \
      -pix_fmt rgb565le -f rawvideo -y /tmp/zephyr-cam.fifo

This lets video applications and the video subsystem be exercised on `native_sim` with real, moving image content, rather than only the static `video-sw-generator` pattern. It is meant to complement that driver rather than replace it: `video-sw-generator` stays the right choice for deterministic, assertable tests that also run on real hardware, while this one is aimed at developing and demonstrating code that interprets pixels.

Paired with the stock `native_sim` SDL display, whose default geometry is also 320x240 and which accepts RGB565, the capture sample renders the stream in a window on the host with no hardware involved at all.

### Design

The driver uses the usual native_sim split. `video_native_sim_fifo_bottom.c` is built in the native simulator runner context and is the only part that touches the host C library; `video_native_sim_fifo.c` contains the Zephyr video driver and never sees a host header. Errors cross the boundary through `nsi_errno`.

The pipe is opened `O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK` and polled from a dedicated thread, so the simulation is never blocked, whether or not a writer is attached. The thread reads straight into the buffer at the head of the input queue and only takes it off the queue once exactly `width * height * bpp` bytes have been read, so stop and flush never lose it. Frames are delivered as soon as they arrive: while the host has data pending and a buffer is free, the driver keeps reading without waiting, so the frame rate is entirely the one the host writer produces. `poll-interval-ms` (default 10) only applies once the host has nothing more to offer.

While the application holds every buffer, the driver stops reading and the host writer blocks once the pipe is full, so no frame is dropped. A rate-limited writer such as `ffmpeg -re` is recommended: an unpaced one is read as fast as the application returns buffers.

A writer disconnecting mid-frame makes `read()` return 0; the partial frame is then discarded while the descriptor stays open, so the next writer to attach is guaranteed to be frame aligned. Likewise, a flush that cancels a frame half way skips the rest of it, so later frames stay aligned.

The application selects the format with `set_format()`, as with the other video drivers. `get_caps()` lists the formats of `video-sw-generator` that ffmpeg can write (RGB565, RGB24, BGR24, XRGB32, BGRX32, YUYV and GREY), any size up to 1920x1080 with an even width for YUYV, and the default is 320x240 RGB565. The host writer does any scaling and pixel format conversion, so it must produce frames of the selected format. A buffer queued before a larger format was selected is returned unfilled rather than overrun. The FIFO path comes from the optional `fifo-path` property, or defaults to `/tmp/zephyr-<device>-<pid>.fifo` so that several simulator instances do not collide, and can be overridden at runtime with `--<device>=<path>`. The driver creates the FIFO when streaming starts, unless it already exists, and logs its path. A FIFO created by the driver is removed when the simulator exits.

### Contents

- `drivers: video:` the driver, bottom half, binding, Kconfig and CMake glue
- `snippets:` a `video-native-fifo` snippet, mirroring `video-sw-generator`
- `boards: native_sim:` a peripheral entry and a 4.5 release note
- `tests: video:` build_all coverage plus a ztest suite
- `samples: video: capture:` how to run the capture sample against it

### Testing

Run on Linux with ffmpeg 8.1.2.

- **Twister.** `tests/subsys/video/native_sim_fifo` passes 28/28 test cases on `native_sim` and `native_sim/native/64`, and 14/14 on `native_sim/native/64` with ASan, UBSan and asserts enabled. The build_all video suite passes on `host/gcc`. The suite brings its own host writer, in the runner context, so it needs no ffmpeg and stays deterministic. It covers the default format, `get_caps()`, every advertised format at its minimum and maximum size, the rejection of other formats (compressed, planar, too large, zero, odd YUYV width), undersized buffers, the no-writer case, a whole frame arriving byte for byte, a frame in another format (RGB24), a non-cancelling flush, a mid-frame disconnect, the host waiting while every buffer is held, a flush cancelling a frame half way, and a larger format selected half way through a frame.
- **Mutation checks.** Each of these makes exactly one test fail, and all pass again once restored: keeping the partial frame when the writer disconnects (mid-frame disconnect test), not skipping the rest of a frame cancelled by a flush (cancel test), dropping the width step check (odd YUYV width accepted), and dropping the size check of the reading thread or its skipping of the interrupted frame (larger format selected half way through a frame).
- **End to end.** `samples/subsys/video/capture` built with `-S video-native-fifo` for `native_sim/native/64` and run as above for 20 s, with the writer `kill -9`'d mid-stream and restarted 2 s later. Over four runs: 172 to 173 frames, every frame exactly 153600 bytes, and capture resumes with the new writer with no error. Deltas are exactly 100 ms (the requested 10 fps), apart from the restart gap, the first few frames of each writer, which ffmpeg writes back to back when it starts, and a single frame that came 40 ms early in one run.
- **Runtime format.** The same sample built with `CONFIG_VIDEO_FRAME_WIDTH=640`, `CONFIG_VIDEO_FRAME_HEIGHT=480` and `CONFIG_VIDEO_PIXEL_FORMAT="YUYV"` lists the 7 formats, selects 640x480 YUYV and gets it from `ffmpeg -pix_fmt yuyv422`, every frame exactly 614400 bytes. 64x32 YUYV and GREY frames written by ffmpeg as `yuyv422` and `gray` come back byte for byte.
- **Pixel format and mid-frame disconnect.** A writer sent half a frame and closed the pipe, then a single still was looped in and two captured frames were dumped back out: the incomplete frame warning was logged once, and both frames are byte-identical to `ffmpeg -pix_fmt rgb565le` output for the same image.
- **Path override.** `--video-fifo=<path>` uses the given path, and the default FIFO is not created.
- **Cleanup.** A FIFO created by the driver is removed on exit, including on Ctrl+C; one created by the user is left in place.
- **Bad path.** A path that exists but is not a FIFO is rejected with a clear error, `video_stream_start()` fails, and the file is left untouched.
- **Compliance.** `check_compliance.py -c main..HEAD` is clean, and all the C files in the series are clang-format clean.
- **Documentation references.** The docs cannot be built locally here, so every `:ref:` in the changed files is checked offline against every label in the tree, including whether a bare reference is allowed to target it.

Not covered: I do not have a webcam on the machine I developed this on, so the `-f v4l2 -i /dev/video0` input is documented but untested; its filter chain was exercised on a 640x480 `lavfi` source instead. `host/llvm` configurations were not run (no clang locally). BGR24, XRGB32 and BGRX32 are only covered by the format tests, not end to end. Frame rate control and video controls are not implemented yet; `set/get/enum_frmival` parity with `video-sw-generator` would come next, followed by controls and error injection, which is where a simulated source can offer things real hardware cannot.

Known limitation: a frame larger than the host pipe capacity, 64 KiB by default on Linux, arrives over several polls, which caps the frame rate of large formats. With the default 100 Hz tick of native_sim, 640x480 YUYV runs at about 5.5 fps. I will address this in a follow-up, for instance by growing the pipe with `F_SETPIPE_SZ`.

The driver still selects `EXPERIMENTAL`. I am happy to drop it here or later, as you prefer.

### Note on AI assistance

This series was written with AI assistance (Antigravity / Gemini). Every commit carries an `Assisted-by:` trailer. I have reviewed the code, run the verification above myself, and I take responsibility for it; the `Signed-off-by` is mine.

title: Bluetooth: Classic: L2CAP: Remove `K_FOREVER` from sig chan buf alloc
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth Classic;Release
body:
Add a retry mechanism to handle buffer allocation failures in L2CAP BR/EDR signaling channel. When buffer allocation fails, the operation is deferred and retried after a random interval to prevent deadlocks and improve reliability.

Add `retry_work` delayed work to handle deferred operations. Implement `l2cap_br_retry_handler()` to process pending operations.

Introduce `allocated_buf` to pre-allocate buffer for the response or request.

Add flags to track pending retry operations, including `CONN_RSP`, `CONFIG_REQ`, `DISCONNECT_REQ`, `INFO_REQ`. Add `BUILD_ASSERT` to verify L2CAP flags fit within available bitmap.

Modify signaling functions calling by the function `l2cap_br_sig_handle()` to use pre-allocated buffer. Add `recv_pending` buffer to handle incomplete L2CAP packets and schedule retries on allocation failure in function `l2cap_br_recv()`.

Modify `l2cap_br_recv()` to queue incoming packets when a previous packet is still being processed. Allocate from the memory slabs `br_recv_pending_pool` and append to the pending queue.

Update `l2cap_br_retry_signaling_handler()` to process the current pending buffer and automatically load the next queued buffer when processing completes via `l2cap_br_recv_pending_done()`.

Add `l2cap_br_drop_recv_pending_bufs()` to properly clean up all queued pending buffers. Ensure proper cleanup of allocated buffer, free allocated memory slabs, and retry work on channel disconnect.

Also update the doxygen comments of the functions `bt_l2cap_br_chan_connect()` and `bt_l2cap_br_chan_disconnect()`.

The changes prevent the `bt_workq` from blocking when the signaling buffer pool is exhausted and ensures L2CAP operations can complete successfully under memory pressure.

Tested by https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/112391
